title: Autonomy software selected for Proteus uncrewed rotorcraft development
body:
LONDON, United Kingdom. Leonardo will use Shield’s Hivemind software to further develop mission-autonomy capabilities for its Proteus autonomous uncrewed rotorcraft under a new agreement between the companies, Shield announced in a statement
Using the Hivemind Software Development Kit, Leonardo engineers will work to integrate and develop autonomy functions for rotary-wing missions including anti-submarine warfare, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, and contested logistics. Shield says the software environment is intended to allow Leonardo to build, test, update, and sustain its own mission-autonomy capabilities as platform, sensor, and mission requirements change.
Proteus is an uncrewed vertical takeoff and landing technology demonstrator developed by Leonardo with the Royal Navy and UK Defence Innovation under the Rotary Wing Uncrewed Air System program. The aircraft completed its maiden flight earlier in 2026 with Leonardo-developed autonomy software already onboard; Hivemind is intended to support further development of those capabilities.

title: Gulf War Air Campaign Map Featured in New Smithsonian Exhibit
body: A map pinned to the wall in a basement 36 years ago will go on display in November at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum. The map, used to identify strategic targets across Iraq in the fall of 1990, was used in the planning of Operation Desert Storm, and will be included in the museum’s new “Modern Military Aviation” gallery in Washington D.C., tracing advances in airpower from the Korean War to the present. The exhibit seeks to expose visitors to the advances that changed the nature of warfare. The map is one of two created at the time by now-retired Lt. Gen. David Deptula, Dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. Deptula was the principal air attack planner for Operation Desert Storm—identifying strategic targets across Iraq and developing the blueprint for the coalition air campaign. Two Gulf War maps remain in Deptula’s possession, and both are on display at AFA’s headquarters in Arlington: one depicting Baghdad hangs in AFA’s Heritage Hall, while a larger map of Iraq hangs in Deptula’s office, surrounded by other mementos and artifacts from throughout his career. A reproduction of the map will be displayed as a large-format graphic panel at the Smithsonian. Dr. Michael Hankins, the Smithsonian’s Curator of U.S. Air Force, Navy, and Marine Corps post-World War II Aviation, learned about the maps during a chance conversation with the Mitchell Institute’s Executive Director Doug Birkey. Hankins was aware the maps had existed, but did not know they had been carried back from Saudi Arabia after the war. Hankins immediately recognized the narrative the maps could tell and saw them as a perfect bridge for the exhibit he was creating, one that could help tell the story of the evolution from conventional airpower to the age of stealth and precision bombing that has defined military strike operations ever since. Given the map’s fragility and size, Hankins decided a reproduction would be more accessible to visitors at the Smithsonian. “As we were planning the layouts for some of these different labels, we had an opportunity, particularly in that section, to have a large-scale photo as an introduction to the Desert Storm section of the gallery,” Hankins said. “What better visual image to use than this to speak to that? … [It shows] how the thought process of using military aviation was different in 1991 than it might have been in previous conflicts.” A rendering of the Modern Military Aviation gallery at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C. The gallery is scheduled to open on Veterans Day, Nov. 11, 2026. Smithsonian Institution The Map, Deptula, and the Black Hole While the map tells the story of Operation Desert Storm, it is also a pivotal artifact in the career of the officer who led the planning of that operation over countless 20-hour days in a basement room in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, that came to be known as “the Black Hole.” On Aug. 2, 1990, Iraqi forces under dictator Saddam Hussein invaded neighboring Kuwait and conquered the country within days. In response, a coalition led by the United States was formed to eject Saddam’s forces from Kuwait. Deptula, then a lieutenant colonel working in the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force, was pulled into a Pentagon strategic planning cell known as “Checkmate,” led by Col. John Warden III. The Checkmate team had been developing a new strategic air doctrine for the post-Cold War era when it was tasked to create an operational concept for countering Iraq’s invasion with airpower. They dubbed their plan “ Instant Thunder .” After briefing Army Gen. Norman Schwarzkopf, who as commander of U.S. Central Command would oversee the operation, as well as Gen. Colin Powell, then the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, Warden, Deptula and a couple of others flew to Saudi Arabia to brief Gen. Chuck Horner, the top air commander for the theater, on the plan. Horner, unconvinced of Warden’s ability to lead the actual planning, accepted Warden’s concept, but sent Warden back to Washington, while retaining the others. Among them, only Deptula stayed long term, becoming the principal target planner for the entire campaign. Based in the Royal Saudi Air Force headquarters basement, their “Black Hole” office was defined by secrecy, the sensitive political nature of American forces planning offensive operations on Saudi soil, and the punishing hours demanded of its occupants—and, Deptula recalled, once “someone was allowed to come into it, they were never allowed to go out.” Here Deptula created his map and the Master Air Attack Plan that would ultimately orchestrate every strike of the campaign. On the map, Deptula and his team pinpointed strategic targets, coded by category: air defense, leadership, military bases, Scud ballistic missile launchers, command and control systems, and electricity and telecommunications networks. The map helped planners to identify relationships between targets, coordinate force packages across multiple objectives simultaneously, and find gaps in Iraqi defenses that a list of coordinates alone could not reveal. For example, the map revealed a gap in Iraqi border monitoring stations that allowed Deptula to safely route F-15E attack aircraft to strike Scud launchers in western Iraq before they could fire on Israel. “It wasn’t just a pretty map that hung on the wall in our planning cell,” Deptula said. “That’s what the visualization of a map does that a bunch of target coordinates and names doesn’t.” Then-Lt. Col. David Deptula, right, briefs (from left) then-Lt. Gen. Chuck Horner, then-Brig. Gen. Buster Glosson, and Gen. Norman Schwarzkopf in the “Black Hole” in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, 15 hours before the first bombs fell on Iraq. David Deptula Underlying the Instant Thunder concept was the conviction that airpower could systematically dismantle Iraq’s war-making ability. Each mark aimed to take a specific capability off the table. It was a deliberate break from what Deptula called “an attritional, intelligence-based philosophy” that had defined air campaigns in Vietnam, where success was measured by the percentage of damage inflicted rather than by what capability had actually been removed. Using the F-117 Nighthawk’s stealth capability to lead the attack, and precision munitions to ensure rapid success, coalition air forces disabled Iraq’s command and control almost instantly, and took away other war-making capabilities within weeks—all while greatly minimizing overall infrastructure damage across the country. By targeting electrical transformer yards, rather than power plants, planners saw they could shut down the electrical grid while keeping reconstruction manageable. In some cases, Deptula recalled, Iraqi power plant managers switched off their facilities, and the coalition chose not to strike them. “By the third night of the war, there hadn’t been an electron flowing in the Iraqi power grid,” said Deptula. “So that’s the objective.” For Hankins, the map illustrated the evolution of airpower in a way no other artifact could. He said, “I think the map shows that in an interesting way, because you can see who’s targeting what, what kinds of things they are able to target, what kinds of things they were successful at. It’s different than something you would see in the sections on the Korean War or the Vietnam War.” Serving as the visual introduction, the map opens the gallery’s Desert Storm section, which focuses on the new technologies that defined the conflict: a scale model of an F-117 stealth fighter and an interactive display explaining how stealth technology works and why it proved so decisive. Separately, the museum’s Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center near Dulles Airport received an original F-117 in October, so Washington visitors can see the real thing up close. The Desert Storm section will also serve as a bridge to the conflicts of the Global War on Terror that the United States has fought over the past three decades, including the Predator drone Deptula would later help pioneer as an armed platform. After the September 11 attacks, Deptula was directing the Combined Air Operations Center for the opening of the Afghanistan campaign when the United States fired a Hellfire missile from an RQ-1 Predator at al-Qaeda targets, the first combat use of an armed remotely piloted aircraft. For Deptula, the map’s display at the Smithsonian represents an acknowledgment of a turning point in how America wages war and as validation of the campaign itself. “I think it’s recognition of the significance of the operation,” Deptula said. “It was the birth of how we conceive air operations.” For Hankins, the map’s greatest value may be what it teaches visitors who know nothing about the Gulf War. “It’s not just let’s launch a bunch of airplanes and go drop a bunch of weapons,” he said. “It’s much more careful than that. It takes a lot of people a lot of time.” The Modern Military Aviation gallery, the final chapter of the Smithsonian’s eight-year renovation, is scheduled to open to the public on Veterans Day, Nov. 11, 2026. The post Gulf War Air Campaign Map Featured in New Smithsonian Exhibit appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Patrick Stewart of Star Trek and X-Men dies, aged 86
body: Patrick Stewart, of Star Trek and X-Men fame, has died at age 86. Stewart rose from poverty in the UK to become an accomplished Shakespearean stage actor and then achieved global stardom as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in TV's Star Trek: The Next Generation and ​the telepathic ​Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films. A post on his X account said that he had died after a "brief and poignant battle" with Alzheimer's and Lewy Body Dementia. "He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayers, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," his family said in the post. Stewart, knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth II for his contributions ⁠to drama, died at his home in Los Angeles. He became an actor at age 18 and gained acclaim ⁠on the stage as a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company beginning in the 1960s. But it was not until after he was hired at age 47 for Star Trek: The Next Generation - a TV series that ran from 1987 to 1994 as a sequel to the original 1960s Star Trek - that he gained mainstream fame, acting into his 80s. "His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre," the social media post read. He became a critical part of another big-money franchise starting with the first entry X-Men in 2000 and followed by several more. Stewart was married three times and had two children. His third marriage, in 2013, was to American musician Sunny Ozell.

title: Netanyahu’s Likud leads with all votes counted — election committee
body:
TEL AVIV, October 29. /TASS/. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has won the majority of votes in the October 27 parliamentary election, with all ballots counted, according to preliminary figures released by the Central Elections Committee (CEC).
Likud is projected to win 27 seats in the 120-member Knesset, Israel’s parliament, followed by Yashar, led by Netanyahu’s main opposition rival Gadi Eisenkot, with 21.
The bloc comprising Likud and the far-right and Orthodox parties that support Netanyahu and make up the current governing coalition also retains its lead. It is set to secure 53 seats, compared with 48 for the opposition. Arab parties are projected to win 19 seats, although neither Likud nor the opposition is expected to be willing to form a coalition with them.
The official final results are expected no later than November 4, once appeals are reviewed. President Isaac Herzog will then consult representatives of the parties elected to the Knesset before tasking one of its members with forming a new governing coalition.
A coalition needs at least 61 Knesset seats to form a government, a threshold no political bloc has reached. The leader of the party with the most seats usually becomes the candidate for prime minister. However, the president may also task a politician whose party did not win the majority of votes with forming a government if that politician can assemble a coalition.
The first candidate will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible two-week extension. If that attempt fails, the president will give another lawmaker two weeks to form a coalition, without the possibility of an extension.
If no lawmaker succeeds in forming a stable coalition, new elections will be called after 90 days. Netanyahu will continue to lead Israel’s government until a new cabinet is sworn in.

title: African CEOs remain confident in growth, but economic uncertainty, AI readiness will shape next phase of investment – KPMG
body: African business leaders remain confident about growth, but converting that confidence into sustained performance will depend on how effectively organisations navigate economic uncertainty, geopolitical disruption, technological change and structural constraints, according to the 2026 KPMG Africa CEO Outlook. The third edition of the KPMG Africa CEO Outlook examines the priorities shaping business leadership across the continent, from investment and growth expectations to emerging risks, artificial intelligence (AI), talent and sustainability. The findings point to a business environment in which ambition remains strong, but execution is becoming increasingly important. While 66% of African CEOs are confident in the global economy, broadly in line with the global benchmark of 65%, confidence in their domestic economies stands at 72%. A further 79% are confident in the growth prospects of their own organisations. This confidence is supported by recent performance, with 86% of African CEOs reporting revenue growth in their latest financial year. However, only 58% expect annual earnings growth of at least 2.5% over the next three years, compared with 68% globally, suggesting that translating revenue gains into sustained profitability remains a priority. Economic uncertainty reinforces the need for resilience African businesses operate in an increasingly interconnected global environment, where geopolitical tensions, energy-market volatility, supply-chain disruptions, and shifting trade relationships can influence investment decisions and operating costs. For African economies, these pressures coexist with significant opportunities. The continent’s energy resources, critical minerals, expanding consumer markets and potential to develop local manufacturing and value chains position it to benefit from changes in global investment and supply-chain strategies. Realising this potential, however, will depend on infrastructure, reliable energy, skills, connectivity and predictable regulatory environments. Resilience moves to the centre of the growth agenda Cybersecurity and data security, alongside supply-chain resilience, are the leading threats to growth among African CEOs, each cited by 31% of respondents. The integration of AI into operating models and workflows follows at 27%. Investment priorities reflect the need to strengthen operational resilience. Some 45% of African CEOs are increasing investment in cybersecurity and digital-risk resilience, 36% in regulatory compliance and reporting, and 31% in AI integration. The findings suggest that resilience is no longer simply about protecting organisations against disruption. It is increasingly a condition for growth, enabling businesses to adapt to changing market conditions, protect critical operations and make investment decisions with greater confidence. For businesses operating across diverse African markets, this requires balancing immediate operational pressures with longer-term investment in infrastructure, technology, governance and capabilities. Tola Adeyemi, Senior Partner & CEO – KPMG One Africa, said: “African businesses are demonstrating confidence in their ability to grow, but the next phase of growth will require more than ambition. Leaders must make deliberate choices about where to invest, how to strengthen resilience and how to build organisations that can adapt to disruption. The opportunity is to translate the continent’s resources, markets and entrepreneurial capacity into more productive, competitive and sustainable businesses.” AI ambition is outpacing organisational readiness AI remains a strategic investment priority for African business leaders, with 72% of CEOs identifying it as a top investment priority, compared with 79% globally. Yet only 14% believe their organisations are moving at the right pace or ahead of AI developments, against 66% of global CEOs. This 52-percentage-point gap highlights a central challenge: African businesses recognise AI’s potential, but many are still working to develop the capabilities required to deploy it effectively and at scale. Expectations around returns also differ. While 48% of African CEOs expect AI investments to deliver returns within one to three years, compared with 71% globally, 42% expect returns after three years, against 12% globally. The longer investment horizon may reflect the work required to strengthen underlying data capabilities, integrate AI into existing systems, establish appropriate governance and develop the skills needed to realise value. It also reinforces the importance of evaluating AI against tangible business outcomes rather than adoption alone. The opportunity for African businesses is not simply to adopt new technology, but to use it to improve productivity, strengthen competitiveness and develop new products and services suited to local and regional markets. Workforce transformation becomes a growth imperative Technology investment is also reshaping workforce strategies. Despite the growing role of AI in business operations, 84% of African CEOs expect headcount to increase over the next three years, compared with 89% globally. At the same time, 86% intend to retain and retrain high-potential employees, 82% are redesigning roles, career paths and team structures for human-AI collaboration, and 74% are hiring AI and technology talent. Skills remain a significant constraint, with 59% identifying workforce skills gaps, 58% citing AI upskilling and training, and 52% pointing to challenges in attracting and retaining talent. These findings underline the relationship between technology adoption and workforce development. Businesses will need to invest in both if they are to translate digital ambition into productivity gains. For African economies, developing relevant skills and expanding access to technology capabilities will also be important to ensuring that digital transformation supports broader economic participation. Sustainability shifts towards measurable business value African CEOs are increasingly approaching sustainability through the lens of commercial performance, operational resilience and reporting readiness. Almost half, or 48%, report embedding sustainability more deeply into core business strategy, compared with 63% globally. Meanwhile, 40% are narrowing their focus to sustainability issues most critical to business performance, against 21% globally. Energy choices reflect the practical realities of operating across African markets. Some 41% of African CEOs prioritise energy demand optimisation, compared with 37% globally; 40% plan to diversify towards renewable or lower-carbon external energy supply, compared with 49% globally; and 15% plan to add dedicated generation or storage capacity, against 13% globally. Reporting readiness provides one of the clearest year-on-year indicators in the findings. The proportion of African CEOs who say their organisations have the capability to meet new sustainability reporting requirements has risen from 55% in the previous year to 65% in 2026. The improvement points to progress in organisational preparedness, although the broader challenge remains embedding sustainability into business decisions in ways that support resilience, efficiency and long-term value creation.

title: When Will US Transfer Operational Control to South Korea? Debate Rages
body: For years, U.S. and South Korean officials have said they want to reach an arrangement where, should war break out on the peninsula, Seoul’s military commanders would have operational control of American forces there. Such a setup would be unprecedented in modern times, and what it would mean for U.S. Airmen, Guardians, and other troops remains to be seen. But recent comments from U.S. and Korean leaders underscore just how complex and even controversial the idea remains. Since World War II, the U.S. has been the ultimate authority for all its combined forces’ wartime operations. But South Korea—officially called the Republic of Korea—has been pressing to finalize the transfer of wartime operational control, or OPCON. Since taking office last year, President Lee Jae Myung has publicly stated his goal is to reach OPCON before his term ends in 2030, and likely earlier. But the commander of U.S. Forces Korea, Army Gen. Xavier T. Brunson, sounded far more cautious at a Center for Strategic and International Studies summit on Oct. 14. Evolving security concerns, such as recent ballistic missile launches, have created “new standards” that must be met before OPCON can be transferred, Brunson said. Brunson said the transfer must be “conditions-based” and not follow a political timeline. Air Force Maj. Mathew Dickson, an F-35A Lightning II pilot, climbs aboard an F-35 at Cheongju Air Base, Republic of Korea. (Air Force photo by Tech. Sgt. Noah J. Tancer) His comments spurred immediate backlash from Korean officials, including Defense Minister Kan Shin-chul and National Security Advisor Wi Sung-lac, who claim that Brunson’s remarks about new conditions amount to shifting the goalposts and will make the planned transfer impossible. On Oct. 29, Sung-lac said during a parliamentary audit that the government had been consulting with Washington to complete the transfer by or before 2030. But a planned Security Consultative Meeting scheduled for December in Washington to discuss various alliance and security concerns has been postponed to next year. A U.S. Pacific Command spokesperson declined to respond to specific questions regarding the conditions required for transfer but did provide a statement to Air & Space Forces Magazine. “The transition of wartime operational control (OPCON) remains a conditions-based process mutually agreed upon by the United States and the Republic of Korea,” Navy Lt. Cmdr. Chloe Morgan wrote. “Both nations remain committed to ensuring that the necessary conditions are met before any transition occurs. We will not prejudge decisions or outcomes of this bilateral process.” While the OPCON process continues and Korean leaders push to move forward, not all American experts agree that it’s a good idea. During an Oct. 27 symposium hosted by the Institute for Korean-American Studies, former USFK commanders Walter Sharp and Paul LaCamera, both Army four-stars, critiqued the weakening of the U.S.-Korea alliance, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported. “That whole combined nature goes away and … [I] really do see it as a doorway to greatly reducing the alliance, greatly reducing our work with Korea,” Sharp said. LaCamera was even more pointed. “It will be suboptimal when the fighting starts, and then we will quickly get to optimization because it is adapt or perish,” he said. As the debate continues, South Korea is leading combined missions during a two-week, biannual, air-focused Freedom Flag exercise. The top ROK air commander, Col. Lee Seung-hwan, emphasized his airmen’s role and its ultimate goal. “While using this as an opportunity to build teamwork among South Korean and U.S. pilots and polish combat skills, we will also cultivate capabilities in preparation for the OPCON transfer,” Seung-hwan said. To Transfer or No t The idea behind transferring OPCON to South Korea dates back to the 1980s when President Roh Tae-woo made it a campaign promise in 1987, driven by a desire to strengthen South Korean sovereignty. The United States didn’t transfer peacetime control to Seoul until 1994. Wartime control was expected to soon follow but was derailed during the 1993-1994 North Korean nuclear crisis. The South Korean push renewed under President Roh Moo-hyun in 2003. Then-U.S. Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld championed the idea, calling it “pushing on an open door” to free up U.S. forces on the peninsula and give the Pentagon more strategic flexibility. The pair formalized an agreement in 2006 to begin the wartime OPCON transfer. But getting to the point where the transfer makes sense for both sides isn’t so simple, multiple retired commanders with deep experience on the peninsula told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “Conditions should determine the timeline,” retired U.S. Army Special Forces Col. David S. Maxwell told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “The timeline should never determine the conditions .” Maxwell explained that target dates help drive budgets, procurement, training, and accountability, but can’t substitute for demonstrated combat capability. “If political leaders want to accelerate transition, they must accelerate the fielding of equipment, development of personnel, and combined exercises required to meet the agreed conditions,” Maxwell said. “Political authority cannot manufacture readiness.” Retired Lt. Gen. David Deptula, Dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, also emphasized the importance of not rushing the transfer. “My principal concern would be any arrangement that sacrifices combat effectiveness to satisfy an arbitrary political timeline or the symbolism of transferring command,” Deptula said. “We cannot afford to discover deficiencies in command and control after a conflict begins.” Still, Maxwell, now vice president of the Center for Asia Pacific Strategy , said changing conditions “cannot become an unexplained justification for indefinite delay.” “Both allies must identify what has changed, which operational requirements it affects, and what capabilities will close the resulting gaps. We should distinguish the agreed conditions from the evolving military capabilities required to satisfy them,” Maxwell said. “The objective is a successful transition that strengthens deterrence and combined defense. Most importantly, political leaders cannot base decisions on threat assessments from five, 10, or 20 years ago.” Maxwell and Deptula highlight several critical conditions before OPCON transfer should go through: South Korea should demonstrate the capability to lead a combined defense and coordinate offensive actions at scale. There should be comprehensive alliance capabilities to respond to North Korean nuclear and missile threats. A stable security environment Integrated architecture for intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and early warning for near-real-time actionable data Integrated air and missile defenses across U.S. and ROK forces Secure, resilient command and control in the face of cyber and electronic attacks. Sufficient munitions, logistics, infrastructure protection, and sustainment capabilities. Certified initial operational capability, full operational capability, and full mission capability assessment results for readiness. While wartime control of the entire combined U.S.-ROK force is in question, more complex considerations apply to the use of the 7th Air Force, USFK’s air component based at Kunsan and Osan Air Bases in South Korea. Airmen assigned to the 36th Fighter Generation Squadron install a missile during exercise Freedom Shield 26 at Osan Air Base, Republic of Korea. (Air Force photo by Senior Airman Rome Bowermaster) The Air Side If conflict were to break out today, U.S. and ROK forces would be controlled by a Combined Forces Command that has existed since 1978. The commander of U.S. Forces Korea is dual-hatted as the head of the CFC and has a Korean deputy. Once the OPCON transfer occurs, that arrangement would flip: a South Korean four-star commander with a U.S. four-star deputy. But even with that combined arrangement, the Pentagon doesn’t cede control of its forces entirely, and it does not give the Korean commander authority over U.S. aircraft in the Pacific. Retired Lt. Gen. Jeffrey A. Remington, who commanded the 7th Air Force from 2008 to 2012, explained that under the new arrangement, the 7th Air Force commander would still oversee the air component for the Korean general in charge, informing the general on the status of air forces, personnel, and wartime options. “[The 7th Air Force commander] would continue to be the air component commander, not a Korean, … a U.S. Air Force three-star general,” Remington said. The commander would then come to the Korean four-star and say, ““Here’s the options, here’s what I can do for you. Here’s the implications of those options,’ and we’ll come to an agreement,” he said. Even in that arrangement, Remington said Washington likely wouldn’t be involved directly in any major decision involving U.S. forces, especially major airpower assets. Deptula stressed that in hammering out the details of this arrangement, “the issue is not whether a South Korean general is capable of commanding American airpower. It’s whether the command structure provides the authority, experience, capabilities, and operational flexibility necessary to employ airpower effectively.” The ROK military is highly professional and capable and a solid U.S. ally in the region, Deptula added. But such a transfer requires more. “Commanding a modern, integrated air campaign involving hundreds of aircraft, sophisticated intelligence and surveillance capabilities, electronic warfare, space-based systems, and long-range strike assets requires far more than flying airplanes or managing individual missions,” Deptula said. Day-to-day operations running an Air Operations Center and delivering air tasking orders already happen in a combined way through the AOC at Osan Air Base, Deptula said. “The real issue is creating a master air attack plan,” he said. “That is the mechanism through which an air campaign translates strategic and operational objectives into coordinated tactical actions. It integrates offensive counterair, defensive counterair, strategic attack, interdiction, close air support, intelligence collection, electronic warfare, air refueling, and other capabilities into a coherent campaign.” While the U.S. has participated in combined forces operations in World War II and with NATO in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo, it has never been in a combined force operation without being the ultimate authority for wartime OPCON. Most U.S. operations during the Global War on Terror and since have been in coalitions. Those typically operate with separate militaries covering different areas, such as the British contribution to the invasion of and early stages of the Iraq War, where their forces were concentrated near Basra and controlled the southeastern section of the war effort near Kuwait. Combined warfare is different. “Combined warfare means you’re there together. You’re executing together. You’re mixed and making things happen,” Remington said. “Whereas in a coalition it’s not all that combined, especially from a command-and-control perspective.” In a very technical sense, for U.S. aviators that might mean being controlled through another nation’s airborne early warning or air battle management systems. That has been somewhat common with NATO combined forces arrangements in past operations and exercises and with South Korea via their ROKAF Master Control and Reporting Centers. Those two MCRCs serve as nerve centers for all air ops on the peninsula and have operated since the mid-1980s, preceded by a Tactical Air Control Center that ran from the early 1980s until the advent of MCRC. One MCRC, call sign Watchman, is at Osan. The other, call sign Acacia, is at Daegu Air Base and serves as a reserve aerospace operations center. Air Force Staff Sgt. Cameron Russell, left, and Staff Sgt. John Gegato, both 36th Fighter Generation Squadron F-16 avionics craftsmen, perform maintenance on an F-16 Fighting Falcon during exercise Freedom Shield 26. (Air Force photo by Senior Airman Rome Bowermaster) Beyond the Peninsula While 7th Air Force is the USFK air component with primary duties to defend South Korea, it also relies on Pacific Air Forces for support and contributes to PACAF’s needs to support U.S. Pacific Command. U.S. Forces Korea are not on a proverbial island, focused solely on local security concerns. Should a conflict with China or other regional problems erupt, USAF may need to draw upon 7th Air Force. “The U.S. military is operating with declining force structure and must meet growing global requirements,” Deptula said. “Aircraft, aircrews, munitions, tankers, intelligence platforms, and other assets cannot be committed to two different campaigns simultaneously without accepting significant operational risk.” That fact means that contingency planning, force allocation, and command relationships take on even more significance when looking to transfer operational control, Deptula said “Both nations must understand in advance what capabilities are committed, what reinforcements may be available, and under what circumstances U.S. forces might be required elsewhere,” he said. Any such transfer “must preserve” U.S. commanders’ ability to employ their capabilities where they can achieve the greatest strategic effect, he said. “Any future defense of South Korea must begin with an appreciation for the fact that air superiority provides the freedom to attack and the freedom from attack,” Deptula said. “It enables all other military operations. The campaign must be designed to achieve the degree of air superiority necessary to permit the joint force to operate effectively, rather than simply contest the airspace.” The post When Will US Transfer Operational Control to South Korea? Debate Rages appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: ‘X-Men,’ ‘Star Trek’ Star Patrick Stewart Dies At 86
body: Patrick Stewart, the British Shakespearean actor who became a Hollywood megastar through roles in the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises, has died at the age of 86, an official statement said Thursday. “We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” the statement said. The actor, who hailed from the northern English region of Yorkshire, trod the boards in Britain with the Royal Shakespeare Company before crossing the Atlantic to enjoy an acclaimed career on the US stage and screen. His best known Hollywood roles were as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and Professor Charles Xavier in multiple “X-Men” and related Marvel films. “His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre,” the statement said. “He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction’s most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise.” AFP The post ‘X-Men,’ ‘Star Trek’ Star Patrick Stewart Dies At 86 appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Russia, Africa call for reform of global financial institutions
body:
MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Russia and African countries consider reform of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Trade Organization and the World Bank necessary, according to the Declaration of the Third Russia-Africa Summit.
The parties agreed to advocate comprehensive reform of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank in order to ensure that the institutions operate based on the principles of depoliticization, equality and respect for the interests of all parties. They also called for greater African representation in the IMF and World Bank leadership, as well as a greater role for African countries in decision-making.
Russia and African nations also agreed to promote reform of the World Trade Organization to ensure an open, transparent, inclusive, non-discriminatory and rules-based trading system.
The parties emphasized the need to preserve the central role of the World Trade Organization and uphold fundamental principles, including consensus-based decision-making, most-favoured-nation treatment, and special and differential treatment for developing and least-developed countries.
