title: Record deployment for destroyer USS Spruance casts doubt over US Navy maintenance
body: The Arleigh-Burke class destroyer USS Spruance has set a post-World War II record for a U.S. Navy destroyer deployment and is raising questions about the maintenance work that could follow its eventual return. The ship left Naval Base San Diego on Nov. 21, 2025, as part of the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group. It remained at sea even after the carrier group moved on and the Lincoln returned to its home port. As of Oct. 29, the ship has been deployed for 342 days, a time period that far exceeds the Navy’s commonly cited seven-month deployment benchmark for ships based in the United States. It also comes as the service contends with a persistent surface-ship maintenance backlog, delays at private shipyards and warnings from senior Navy leaders that extended operations could create years of additional pressure on the fleet. For families waiting at home, the uncertainty has become its own burden. Marie Bailey, whose husband serves aboard Spruance, told Military Times that families have repeatedly been told the ship would return soon, only to see that expectation pushed back. “We are hearing they’re supposed to come home sometime next month, but we’ve been hearing about ‘next month’ for several months,” Bailey said. Extended deployments are not new to the Navy, but that offers little comfort to families counting down the days until a homecoming that continues to appear just out of reach. For them, another extension is not simply a change to an operational schedule, but yet another period of uncertainty. “We don’t know what to expect anymore, but it’s hard getting your hopes up time and time again,” Bailey added. “Most of the families are just worried about their sailors, knowing how long they’ve been gone.” Some Spruance sailors also say they feel their experience has been overlooked compared with the sweeping national attention given to the USS Abraham Lincoln. Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln sails in the Arabian Sea on May 8, 2026. (U.S. Navy) Two of those sailors, who were granted anonymity due to fear of reprisal, noted that life aboard a destroyer brings its own challenges, even when the ship receives less public attention. “It’s tight, cramped and just as challenging on the destroyers, if not more than bigger ships,” one sailor said. The other sailor pointed to the families waiting at home, arguing that the size of a ship should not determine how much attention its crew receives. “Our boat isn’t as big as an aircraft carrier, but our 300+ families matter to us just as much as anyone else’s,” the sailor said. The frustration reflects a basic reality of carrier strike groups: Destroyers may operate in the shadow of the aircraft carriers they accompany, but their crews endure the same prolonged separation from home. For families waiting on a return date, the distinction between a carrier and a smaller warship offers little consolation. Spruance is not the only Navy destroyer facing an unusually long deployment. The USS John Finn, USS Mustin and USS Rafael Peralta have also had expected return dates pushed from 2026 into 2027, with some planned to stretch over 14 months, according to Defense One . The extensions illustrate the demands facing the surface fleet, although the Navy has not publicly provided a comprehensive count of destroyers that have had deployments extended. A fleet under sustained pressure The Navy’s Optimized Fleet Response Plan organizes a 36-month cycle for ships homeported in the United States. The Government Accountability Office describes the cycle as allocating eight months to depot-level maintenance, 10 months to training and 18 months to deployment and sustainment operations. Extended deployments can disrupt that sequence, pushing scheduled maintenance later and compressing the time available for repairs, training and preparation before a ship is needed again. GAO has documented longstanding maintenance challenges across the Navy’s surface fleet. Private ship repair companies took nearly 10,000 days longer than planned, cumulatively, to repair destroyers between fiscal years 2015 and 2022, according to a February 2025 GAO report . The Navy’s surface-ship maintenance backlog reached $2.3 billion in deferred work by August 2022, GAO reported. In a May 2022 report , GAO found a nearly $1.8 billion backlog in depot-level maintenance for Navy ships, including approximately $1.7 billion for surface ships. About $1.2 billion of the backlog was associated with ships the Navy had proposed for early decommissioning. GAO found that maintenance backlogs contributed to decisions to retire nine ships. A separate GAO analysis of 10 surface-ship classes between fiscal years 2011 and 2021 found increases in maintenance cannibalizations, casualty reports and delays in depot-level maintenance. Steaming hours declined and costs per steaming hour rose for most of the classes examined. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle warned Oct. 26 that the effects of extended deployments could reverberate through the fleet’s maintenance schedule for years. Speaking at the United States Navy Memorial, Caudle said maintenance availabilities, particularly for destroyers, could snowball as ships return from deployments exceeding 300 days. “You’re talking hundreds of availabilities and millions of dollars. Hundreds of millions of dollars have to be applied to that problem as we start retrograding these destroyers back into their maintenance period,” Caudle said. “But this is a years-long recovery,” he added. “There is no workaround on that.” Rear Adm. Kavon Hakimzadeh, commander of Norfolk Naval Shipyard, also warned of capacity constraints as destroyers return from the Middle East. Speaking at a September roundtable hosted by the Center for Maritime Strategy, Hakimzadeh said shipyards would have to manage the volume of returning ships. “There’s some choke points just based on capacity out there for all the destroyers that are going to be coming back,” Hakimzadeh said. “We’re running the destroyers really hard out there, and I suspect they’re all going to need to go into the same dry dock, and we’re going to have to sequence them in.” The remarks highlight a constraint beyond identifying the repairs each ship needs: Shipyards must also have the capacity and workforce to complete the work. An MH-60S Sea Hawk helicopter takes off from the flight deck of USS Spruance in support of Operation Epic Fury, Mar. 5, 2026. (U.S. Navy) The Navy’s maintenance challenges have persisted despite billions of dollars in repair funding. A December 2025 Congressional Budget Office analysis found that maintenance for Navy destroyers and amphibious ships takes 20% to 100% longer than the service plans for. The cumulative burden for destroyers is substantial: Roughly nine years of a ship’s planned service life is expected to be spent in maintenance, or about one year out of every four. GAO found that the Navy received nearly $25.9 billion for combat surface-ship maintenance from fiscal years 2020 through 2023, roughly $1 billion more than it had requested. The service reported obligating 99.7% of those funds by the end of fiscal 2023. GAO has also identified shortages of spare parts and qualified maintenance personnel, along with deferred work, among the constraints affecting maintenance schedules. What Spruance’s schedule shows Navy budget documents show that the planned timing of Spruance’s next maintenance period has shifted. The Navy’s fiscal 2025 operations and maintenance budget listed a scheduled restricted availability for the destroyer from July 3, 2026, through Feb. 21, 2027. A restricted availability is a period when a ship is taken out of normal operations for maintenance and repairs. In the fiscal 2027 budget , the planned period had shifted to Jan. 19 through April 28, 2027. Based on those dates, the scheduled start moved 200 days later, while the planned completion was bumped to 66 days later. The availability of sailors to perform maintenance at sea is another factor in the Navy’s efforts to keep ships ready for operations. In a September 2024 report , GAO surveyed personnel aboard 232 Navy ships about their ability to carry out maintenance while underway. The survey received a 91% response rate. Sixty-three percent of responding executive officers said it was moderately to extremely difficult for their crews to complete repairs underway with their assigned sailors; 64% said it was similarly difficult to conduct sailor-led maintenance while also meeting classroom training requirements; and 75% reported that it was moderately to extremely difficult for sailors to complete repairs. GAO also found that the Navy did not track how many sailors assigned to ships were unavailable for duty. What comes next for Spruance GAO has recommended that the Navy compare planned depot-maintenance durations with typical availabilities for ships of the same type, while accounting for factors such as age, condition and maintenance requirements. Such comparisons, according to GAO, could help establish whether a ship’s maintenance period is unusually long. Spruance’s post-deployment assessment and actual maintenance schedule will show what work the Navy identifies as necessary and how long the destroyer remains unavailable for operations. Until those details are established, the effect of its record deployment on its future readiness remains uncertain. The Navy did not respond to Navy Times’ request for comment by publication.

The frustration reflects a basic reality of carrier strike groups: Destroyers may operate in the shadow of the aircraft carriers they accompany, but their crews endure the same prolonged separation from home. For families waiting on a return date, the distinction between a carrier and a smaller warship offers little consolation. Spruance is not the only Navy destroyer facing an unusually long deployment. The USS John Finn, USS Mustin and USS Rafael Peralta have also had expected return dates pushed from 2026 into 2027, with some planned to stretch over 14 months, according to Defense One . The extensions illustrate the demands facing the surface fleet, although the Navy has not publicly provided a comprehensive count of destroyers that have had deployments extended. A fleet under sustained pressure The Navy’s Optimized Fleet Response Plan organizes a 36-month cycle for ships homeported in the United States. The Government Accountability Office describes the cycle as allocating eight months to depot-level maintenance, 10 months to training and 18 months to deployment and sustainment operations. Extended deployments can disrupt that sequence, pushing scheduled maintenance later and compressing the time available for repairs, training and preparation before a ship is needed again. GAO has documented longstanding maintenance challenges across the Navy’s surface fleet. Private ship repair companies took nearly 10,000 days longer than planned, cumulatively, to repair destroyers between fiscal years 2015 and 2022, according to a February 2025 GAO report . The Navy’s surface-ship maintenance backlog reached $2.3 billion in deferred work by August 2022, GAO reported. In a May 2022 report , GAO found a nearly $1.8 billion backlog in depot-level maintenance for Navy ships, including approximately $1.7 billion for surface ships. About $1.2 billion of the backlog was associated with ships the Navy had proposed for early decommissioning. GAO found that maintenance backlogs contributed to decisions to retire nine ships. A separate GAO analysis of 10 surface-ship classes between fiscal years 2011 and 2021 found increases in maintenance cannibalizations, casualty reports and delays in depot-level maintenance. Steaming hours declined and costs per steaming hour rose for most of the classes examined. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle warned Oct. 26 that the effects of extended deployments could reverberate through the fleet’s maintenance schedule for years. Speaking at the United States Navy Memorial, Caudle said maintenance availabilities, particularly for destroyers, could snowball as ships return from deployments exceeding 300 days. “You’re talking hundreds of availabilities and millions of dollars. Hundreds of millions of dollars have to be applied to that problem as we start retrograding these destroyers back into their maintenance period,” Caudle said. “But this is a years-long recovery,” he added. “There is no workaround on that.” Rear Adm. Kavon Hakimzadeh, commander of Norfolk Naval Shipyard, also warned of capacity constraints as destroyers return from the Middle East. Speaking at a September roundtable hosted by the Center for Maritime Strategy, Hakimzadeh said shipyards would have to manage the volume of returning ships. “There’s some choke points just based on capacity out there for all the destroyers that are going to be coming back,” Hakimzadeh said. “We’re running the destroyers really hard out there, and I suspect they’re all going to need to go into the same dry dock, and we’re going to have to sequence them in.” The remarks highlight a constraint beyond identifying the repairs each ship needs: Shipyards must also have the capacity and workforce to complete the work. An MH-60S Sea Hawk helicopter takes off from the flight deck of USS Spruance in support of Operation Epic Fury, Mar. 5, 2026. (U.S. Navy) The Navy’s maintenance challenges have persisted despite billions of dollars in repair funding. A December 2025 Congressional Budget Office analysis found that maintenance for Navy destroyers and amphibious ships takes 20% to 100% longer than the service plans for. The cumulative burden for destroyers is substantial: Roughly nine years of a ship’s planned service life is expected to be spent in maintenance, or about one year out of every four. GAO found that the Navy received nearly $25.9 billion for combat surface-ship maintenance from fiscal years 2020 through 2023, roughly $1 billion more than it had requested. The service reported obligating 99.7% of those funds by the end of fiscal 2023. GAO has also identified shortages of spare parts and qualified maintenance personnel, along with deferred work, among the constraints affecting maintenance schedules. What Spruance’s schedule shows Navy budget documents show that the planned timing of Spruance’s next maintenance period has shifted. The Navy’s fiscal 2025 operations and maintenance budget listed a scheduled restricted availability for the destroyer from July 3, 2026, through Feb. 21, 2027. A restricted availability is a period when a ship is taken out of normal operations for maintenance and repairs. In the fiscal 2027 budget , the planned period had shifted to Jan. 19 through April 28, 2027. Based on those dates, the scheduled start moved 200 days later, while the planned completion was bumped to 66 days later. The availability of sailors to perform maintenance at sea is another factor in the Navy’s efforts to keep ships ready for operations. In a September 2024 report , GAO surveyed personnel aboard 232 Navy ships about their ability to carry out maintenance while underway. The survey received a 91% response rate. Sixty-three percent of responding executive officers said it was moderately to extremely difficult for their crews to complete repairs underway with their assigned sailors; 64% said it was similarly difficult to conduct sailor-led maintenance while also meeting classroom training requirements; and 75% reported that it was moderately to extremely difficult for sailors to complete repairs. GAO also found that the Navy did not track how many sailors assigned to ships were unavailable for duty. What comes next for Spruance GAO has recommended that the Navy compare planned depot-maintenance durations with typical availabilities for ships of the same type, while accounting for factors such as age, condition and maintenance requirements. Such comparisons, according to GAO, could help establish whether a ship’s maintenance period is unusually long. Spruance’s post-deployment assessment and actual maintenance schedule will show what work the Navy identifies as necessary and how long the destroyer remains unavailable for operations. Until those details are established, the effect of its record deployment on its future readiness remains uncertain. The Navy did not respond to Navy Times’ request for comment by publication.

title: Record deployment for destroyer USS Spruance casts doubt over US Navy maintenance
body: The Arleigh-Burke class destroyer USS Spruance has set a post-World War II record for a U.S. Navy destroyer deployment and is raising questions about the maintenance work that could follow its eventual return. The ship left Naval Base San Diego on Nov. 21, 2025, as part of the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group. It remained at sea even after the carrier group moved on and the Lincoln returned to its home port. As of Oct. 29, the ship has been deployed for 342 days, a time period that far exceeds the Navy’s commonly cited seven-month deployment benchmark for ships based in the United States. It also comes as the service contends with a persistent surface-ship maintenance backlog, delays at private shipyards and warnings from senior Navy leaders that extended operations could create years of additional pressure on the fleet. For families waiting at home, the uncertainty has become its own burden. Marie Bailey, whose husband serves aboard Spruance, told Military Times that families have repeatedly been told the ship would return soon, only to see that expectation pushed back. “We are hearing they’re supposed to come home sometime next month, but we’ve been hearing about ‘next month’ for several months,” Bailey said. Extended deployments are not new to the Navy, but that offers little comfort to families counting down the days until a homecoming that continues to appear just out of reach. For them, another extension is not simply a change to an operational schedule, but yet another period of uncertainty. “We don’t know what to expect anymore, but it’s hard getting your hopes up time and time again,” Bailey added. “Most of the families are just worried about their sailors, knowing how long they’ve been gone.” Some Spruance sailors also say they feel their experience has been overlooked compared with the sweeping national attention given to the USS Abraham Lincoln. title: 2027 Elections: Oyebanji Targets 80% Of Votes For Tinubu
body: Ekiti State Governor, Mr. Biodun Oyebanji, has called on leaders and members of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the state to intensify grassroots mobilisation ahead of the January 2027 presidential election, with a target of securing 80 per cent of registered voters’ support for President Bola Tinubu. The governor urged party stakeholders to strengthen their engagement with voters, particularly those who remain undecided, as part of efforts to mobilise support for the President’s re-election bid. Oyebanji spoke on Thursday at the Ekiti Parapo Pavilion, Ado-Ekiti, during the inauguration of the Ekiti State chapter of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement and the presentation of 25 campaign vehicles by the movement to support grassroots mobilisation across the state. The movement, convened by Government Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, is seeking to expand support for President Tinubu through direct engagement with voters in communities across the country. Governor Oyebanji expressed appreciation to the convener and members of the movement for their commitment to the President’s re-election campaign, assuring them that their investment in Ekiti State would be matched by sustained mobilisation efforts. He urged APC members to work collectively and take the campaign to every community, stressing that victory at the polls would depend largely on direct engagement with voters at the grassroots. The governor also warned against voter apathy, particularly among eligible voters who possess the Permanent Voter Card (PVC) but failed to participate in previous elections. He urged campaigners to identify such voters, engage them personally and encourage them to turn out on election day. Oyebanji further challenged APC stakeholders in the state to demonstrate their appreciation for the support Ekiti had received from the Tinubu administration by mobilising support for the President in the forthcoming election. He said the Federal Government’s support had contributed to his administration’s development efforts, adding that continued cooperation between the state and federal governments remained important to sustaining ongoing projects and programmes. The governor recalled the APC’s performance in the last governorship election, urging party members to sustain their mobilisation efforts and translate their support at the state level into votes for President Tinubu in January 2027. He maintained that Ekiti should aim for at least 80 per cent of registered voters’ support for the President, describing the target as a challenge to party leaders and members in view of the Federal Government’s support for the state. “This is a big challenge to us in Ekiti State. If someone from the Niger Delta can put up this structure, and as of today, they have visited 19 states and are still going to visit other states before the end of the campaign, then I challenge all of us here to support the President with our votes in January. “I have always said that in our 30 years as a state, there has been no President who has been as fair and supportive to Ekiti as President Tinubu. “We are extremely grateful, and we assure you that your investment in Ekiti State will not be in vain. I assure you that Ekiti will perform well and record an outstanding result in January. We are grateful for your visit and support, and we assure you that the vehicles will be deployed in a manner that will also support the work we are doing here,” the governor said. Earlier, the convener of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, Government Ekpemupolo, said the donation of the 25 vehicles was intended to strengthen the movement’s grassroots mobilisation and extend its campaign message to communities across Ekiti State and other parts of the country. Represented by the Grand Patron of the PBAT Door To Door Movement, Kestin Pondi, he called on Nigerians to support Tinubu for a second term, arguing that the administration needed more time to consolidate its economic reforms and achieve its objectives. According to him, the reforms had improved the capacity of state governments to meet financial obligations, including the payment of workers’ salaries and pensions, as well as the execution of development projects. Ekpemukolo cited projects being undertaken in Ekiti State as evidence of the resources available to the government, attributing the development to the economic reforms introduced by the Tinubu administration. He added that governors in the 19 states visited by the movement had similarly highlighted the impact of the reforms on their ability to meet financial obligations and implement projects. He argued that far-reaching economic reforms required time to deliver their full benefits and called for continuity to consolidate the policies. The convener also challenged political aspirants seeking public office to explain how their programmes would improve the lives of Nigerians compared with the policies being implemented by the Tinubu administration. He urged the APC leadership at the federal, state and local government levels to foster cooperation and ensure that the donated vehicles were effectively deployed for the movement’s activities. The post 2027 Elections: Oyebanji Targets 80% Of Votes For Tinubu appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Ukraine's Neptune Missiles Destroy 2 Russian Su-34 Bombers in Volgograd Region
body:
Ukraine’s Neptunes successfully destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers, used by Moscow to launch unguided and guided aerial bombs (KABs), in Russia’s Volgograd region on Thursday, Oct. 29.
The Ukrainian Navy’s Neptune coastal missile system hit the aircraft, which can also carry missiles of various types, at the Marinovka airfield, near the settlement of Oktyabrsky. This was initially reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU).
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Several minutes later, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the report, noting that Ukraine had carried out two missile strikes during the day. In one of the strikes, a launcher for Russia’s Iskander ballistic missiles was hit as well.
The Su-34, a two-seat long-range strike derivative of the Su-27 fighter, was originally developed in the 1990s, but was only brought into service in 2014.
It is described as Russia’s main aircraft launching KABs on Ukrainian cities nationwide, capable of carrying up to 8 tons of munitions, with an estimated value of each jet at about $50 million.
Such bombs remain one of Russia’s most destructive weapons against Ukrainian cities near the front line. Earlier on Thursday, three KABs struck an apartment building in Izium, Kharkiv region, injuring at least 13 people.
Throughout the day, at least 20 people were killed and 109 wounded in Russian attacks on Ukraine nationwide, with several types of weapons used, including ballistic missiles and first-person-view (FPV) drones.
The Marinovka airfield, located about 400 kilometers (249 miles) from Ukraine, has previously been targeted by Ukrainian Defense Forces in 2025 as well, as it hosts a squadron of Su-34s.
Overnight Oct. 14-15, Ukraine struck six Russian Su-34 bombers with a Neptune missile strike, at another military airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region. The attack targeted Borisoglebsk airfield and also destroyed equipment used to support flight operations
Originally designed to destroy warships, Neptune is a domestically developed Ukrainian Cruise missile. In April 2022, its ground-based system sank Russia’s shadow fleet vessel, the Moskva.
Since then, Ukraine has upgraded the missile for strikes on land targets deep inside Russia, with the new version capable of reaching targets up to 1,000 kilometers (621 miles) away.
During the same remarks, Zelensky said Ukraine had obtained intelligence that Russia was preparing fresh ballistic missiles.
He called on partners to provide interceptor packages for Patriot air-defense systems, of which Ukraine is facing a critical shortage. “We are waiting for the relevant decisions,” Zelensky said.
The appeal follows similar warnings during his visit to the Netherlands on Wednesday, Oct. 28, where he described Patriot missiles as Ukraine’s most critical shortage, urging Washington not to delay deliveries under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) – a mechanism through which allies fund purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine.
Ahead of winter, Russia is increasingly relying on ballistic missiles to target Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, including the power grid and water supplies.
Meanwhile, Kyiv has reportedly depleted its stocks of Patriot interceptors as early as Oct. 15, due to limited deliveries from allies.
For Ukraine the PAC-3 is among the very few weapons capable of deterring Russia’s ballistic missiles. Russian Iskander-M, for example, is a ballistic missile carrying a half-ton warhead that is strong enough to tear down a quarter to half of a typical apartment block.
“Another aspect of our anti-ballistic work is the interceptor packages, primarily for Patriots, that partners can provide to us,” Zelensky said on Wednesday.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Tinubu defends borrowing plans, says investment ‘will expand opportunities for future generations’
body:
President Bola Tinubu has robustly responded to criticism, especially from opposition leaders, over new loans the country has accessed from international institutions and banks.
In an essay titled “From reforms to delivery: Our infrastructure investment and growth strategy,” to be published on Nigerian news platforms, President Tinubu wrote: “The real question is not how much we borrow, but what we build, what value we create and what future we leave behind.”
The President identified the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway, Trans-Sahara Superhighway, electricity grid upgrades and the modernisation of key commercial ports in Lagos as major projects expected to strengthen Nigeria’s productive capacity.
He said the projects, alongside investments in healthcare, education and vocational training, would connect economic regions, reduce logistics costs, unlock agricultural and industrial potential and attract private investment.
The Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway is expected to cut logistics costs along its corridor by 15 to 20 per cent. It could add up to two per cent to Nigeria’s GDP through expanded trade, tourism, and industrial activity.
The project is also projected to generate about 100,000 direct jobs in construction and engineering, alongside more than 150,000 indirect jobs in logistics, materials and related services.
“We are not simply building highways. We are opening economic corridors, connecting markets, unlocking industries and reshaping Nigeria’s economic geography,” the president said.
He said the administration’s ambition to build a $1 trillion economy by 2030 would require sustained infrastructure investment to support higher productivity, industrialisation and trade.
“We cannot build a USD 1 trillion economy with infrastructure designed for an economy a fraction of that size,” President Tinubu said.
He wrote that improving economic indicators and growing international investor confidence are creating opportunities for Nigeria to attract long-term investment and expand critical infrastructure.
The president said the economic reforms his administration introduced in May 2023 helped restore macroeconomic stability, strengthen public finances, and improve the country’s standing in international financial markets.
He said a $1 trillion economy would not emerge by declaration alone but must be built through sustained investment, higher productivity, industrialisation, and trade, stressing that infrastructure development would be critical to achieving the target by 2030.
In an article titled “From reforms to delivery: Our infrastructure investment and growth strategy,” President Tinubu said real Gross Domestic Product growth reached 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, while headline inflation fell to 14.63 per cent in September from 20.98 per cent a year earlier.
He also said gross external reserves rose to $55.1 billion as of 9 October, 2026, including about $46 billion in net reserves, while the tax-to-GDP ratio increased to 12.5 per cent from seven per cent.
President Tinubu said real Gross Domestic Product growth reached 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, while headline inflation fell to 14.63 per cent in September from 20.98 per cent a year earlier.
The president attributed the improvements to measures including petrol subsidy removal, exchange rate unification, tax reforms and coordinated efforts to tackle inflation.
“The decisions taken since 2023 were difficult but necessary,” he said, referring to the reforms.
President Tinubu said the gains have strengthened Nigeria’s ability to attract investment and finance projects that support long-term economic growth.
“Confidence has a price; our cost of borrowing is going down, and the country risk premium has drastically decreased,” he said.
The president cited positive assessments by international credit rating agencies as evidence of improved confidence in the economy.
“These are not political endorsements; they are independent assessments by global rating agencies, index providers, regulators and investors, recognising stronger external reserves, improved macroeconomic management and greater financial credibility,” President Tinubu said.
According to the president, the improved standing could help Nigeria attract more institutional investors, secure longer-term financing and reduce borrowing costs.
He said the administration was shifting public borrowing away from financing short-term fiscal pressures towards investments that would generate economic returns, create jobs and expand opportunities for future generations.
The president said the government was also pursuing longer-term financing arrangements to match the lifespan of infrastructure assets, reduce refinancing pressures and secure more competitive funding for productive investments.
President Tinubu said Nigeria must convert renewed international confidence into capital expenditure, completed infrastructure and lasting economic benefits for citizens.
He identified five priorities for the next phase of the Federal Executive Council’s economic strategy: food affordability and energy price stability; budget harmonisation and fiscal discipline; completion of high-impact projects and investment in critical infrastructure; an improved economic policy framework and regulatory efficiency; and targeted household support alongside investment in human development.
The president stressed that the success of the current administration’s economic schemes would be measured by completed projects, increased investment, employment generation and improved living standards.
“Securing financing is not the achievement. Completing the project, delivering value and improving the lives of Nigerians is the achievement,” he said.
He added that the nation’s economic ambition must be supported by responsible borrowing and investments that create lasting opportunities for future generations.

title: Pentagon investigates series of commissary freezer failures as possible cyberattack
body: The Pentagon’s criminal investigative service is leading a joint investigation into mysterious refrigeration failures at military commissaries across the country amid concerns that the incidents may have been caused by cyberattacks, a Defense Department official confirmed Thursday. “We are aware of speculation regarding a potential cyber incident,” the official said. “The Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS), the criminal investigative arm of the [Department of Defense] Office of Inspector General, is leading a joint investigation. For security reasons, we do not comment on ongoing law enforcement investigations.” The failures affected at least six military commissaries in August, with some installations temporarily unable to sell refrigerated or frozen food. Military Times previously documented outages at seven Army , Navy and Air Force installations across the country. The investigation comes after a confirmed cyberattack disrupted refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France earlier this month. CNN reported that hackers remotely activated defrost cycles , spoiling food and, in some cases, causing fires. The disruption resembles the incident at Fort Huachuca, where every commissary freezer entered defrost mode overnight, according to the installation’s Facebook page . Army Criminal Investigation Division spokesman Thomas Hamilton confirmed to Task & Purpose that Army CID is working with the Defense Commissary Agency and DCIS to determine what happened at the U.S. commissaries. “Army CID is also working with DCIS and French law enforcement in understanding the refrigeration outages in Europe,” Hamilton said. News Space Force wants to embed more guardians into the joint force By Nicholas Slayton News Nearly 50 recon and intel Marines headed to undersea cable guard duty in Europe By Matt White News US expands alcohol restrictions for troops in Japan By Nicholas Slayton The department separately confirmed that Defense Cyber Defense Command is coordinating with law enforcement and other federal agencies. Reuters reported Thursday , citing four officials familiar with the matter, that investigators are treating the incidents as suspected cyberattacks, although the Pentagon has not publicly confirmed that hackers were responsible. Wes Bryant, a former Air Force special operations member who previously served as chief of civilian harm assessments at the Pentagon’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, said service members and their families depend on commissaries for affordable groceries, and disruptions could force them to shop elsewhere at higher prices. Bryant said the military’s dependence on fresh food extends beyond domestic installations. Even overseas, he said, service members rely on regular food supplies rather than routinely eating Meals, Ready-to-Eat, or MREs. “If you take away service members’ ability to eat in the U.S., that effectively ends or deeply impacts our operations, full stop,” Bryant said. “This is our Achilles’ heel in some regards. A lot of troops won’t work with no access to food.” The post Pentagon investigates series of commissary freezer failures as possible cyberattack appeared first on Task & Purpose .

title: Polymarket probes suspicious trades around Israel election, Bloomberg News reports
body: Prediction market operator Polymarket is investigating a string of well-timed and profitable trades on Israel's election this week, according to a Bloomberg News report on Thursday.Shortly before polls closed on Tuesday, hundreds of newly created accounts placed bets on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu retaining his position and his Likud party winning the most seats, according to the report.The report said those trades quickly became profitable- and together some of the accounts already cashed out over $100,000 - after some exit polls showed that Netanyahu's party had won more seats than early reports suggested.Many wallets have significant gains that have not yet been realized, the report said.Prediction markets face growing scrutiny over potential insider trading, with platforms such as Polymarket and Kalshi reporting a surge in suspicious activity amid a sharp increase in trading volumes. Reuters reported in May that Polymarket had seen a significant uptick in trades flagged as suspicious this year.Polymarket investigates suspicious betting activity linked to Israeli electionPolymarket is reviewing dozens of newly created wallets that traded on the election, its internal investigative team told Bloomberg.Data analysis firms Polysights and Bubblemaps have also flagged the activity as suspicious and are investigating, the report said.The findings are not conclusive, and it can be difficult to distinguish potential insider trading from original research or lucky bets, Bloomberg reported.Representatives for Polymarket and Polysights did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Bubblemaps said its analysis shared with Bloomberg was recent and that it had no further updates.

title: FG Inaugurates Committee to Review National Security Strategy 2026
body: Linus Aleke in Abuja The Federal Government on Thursday inaugurated a 33 member committee to review the 2019 National Security Strategy and develop a new framework for addressing emerging security threats. Speaking at the inauguration ceremony in Abuja, the National Security Adviser, Nuhu Ribadu, urged the committee members to produce a comprehensive, realistic and actionable document that reflects the country’s changing security environment. Represented by the committee chairman, Major General Sarkin Bello (Rtd.), the NSA said Nigeria’s domestic, regional and global security landscapes had changed significantly since the last review in 2019, necessitating a reassessment of the country’s security priorities. “Our national security landscape is undergoing rapid and profound transformations. Since the last review of our strategy in 2019, the domestic, regional and global security environments have changed dramatically in intensity,” he said. Ribadu identified terrorism, banditry, kidnapping, cyber threats, misinformation, economic challenges, food insecurity and environmental problems as some of the threats the new strategy must address. Against this backdrop, he said the National Security Strategy 2026 would provide an overarching framework for coordinating national security, resilience and sustainable development. “The National Security Strategy 2026 will serve as an overarching compass for coordinating national security, resilience and sustainable development for Nigeria. It must reflect our current realities, anticipate future disruptions and directly support the realisation of our national objectives amid the President’s Renewed Hope Agenda, particularly in the areas of human security, economic transformation and national cohesion,” Ribadu said. He further urged committee members to engage relevant institutions and stakeholders in developing a strategy that could be effectively implemented. “Engage robustly with our resource institutions and strategic stakeholders to produce a comprehensive, realistic and actionable document. Nigeria demands a strategy that is realistic and implementable,” he said. To facilitate the process, Ribadu said the Office of the National Security Adviser would provide the necessary administrative, technical and logistical support to ensure the successful completion of the assignment. In his acceptance remarks, the committee’s deputy chairman, Major General Emeka Onumajuru (Rtd.), highlighted the evolving nature of security threats, stressing the need for a comprehensive strategic realignment. He noted that conventional security challenges, including terrorism, insurgency and banditry, had become increasingly intertwined with non-kinetic threats such as cyber vulnerabilities, economic challenges, food insecurity and climate change. Emphasising the need for a forward-looking approach, Onumajuru said the new strategy must go beyond reactive measures to address the country’s complex security challenges. “To address these complexities, our nation requires an overarching framework that moves beyond reactive measures. The National Security Strategy 2026 must be an inclusive, forward-looking and highly actionable blueprint,” he said. He added that the committee would consult resource institutions, private-sector representatives and traditional leaders to ensure that the strategy reflected a broad range of national security concerns. Major General Onumajuru also disclosed that the committee had four weeks to submit its final draft to the NSA, describing the timeline as demanding. “Our timeline is quite unyielding. We have exactly four weeks from today to submit our final draft copies to the National Security Adviser. So, it demands immediate, focused momentum,” he said. The committee is chaired by Major General Bello (Rtd.) and comprises representatives of government ministries, the Armed Forces, intelligence agencies, law enforcement bodies, civil society organisations and academia. Other institutions represented on the committee include the Defence Headquarters, the Nigerian Army, Navy and Air Force, the Nigeria Police Force, the Department of State Services, the National Intelligence Agency, the Defence Intelligence Agency and the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission.

title: Admiral Bauer: If Russia attacks, Alliance will fight back to break enemy
body:
Admiral Rob Bauer, former Chair of the NATO Military Committee, expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform on the sidelines of a special event organized by the Brussels office of the Kyiv Security Forum.
"Ukraine has to fight this war in a certain way because it was limited by the U.S. and other Western nations in the use of certain weapon systems or not allowed to use some of them. So NATO is not going to fight exactly the same way as Ukraine is fighting the Russians," Bauer said.
He explained that in the event of an attack, the Alliance would deploy its air force and navy and launch long-range precision strikes against Russian territory.
"This is something that Ukraine is now doing more and more with weapon systems that it has developed yourself. As you were limited at the outset, you started to work on the drones. So in a way, the drones were your answer to a limited amount of artillery ammo. The fact that you are successful in that area now is a testament to the fact that you found an answer to the fact that you were not supported as we should have supported you," the admiral said.
Even Ukraine's possession of a certain number of F-16 fighter jets cannot match the capabilities of a full fleet of strategic bombers, F-35s, F-22s, F-15s, F-16s and other assets available to the Alliance, Bauer said.
He added that the Alliance's regional plans are fully aligned with the tasks at hand.
"General Grynkewich, NATO's SACEUR, talked about this at a forum in Warsaw just a couple of weeks ago. His message was that Article 5 is ironclad and that the U.S forces in Europe will fight within NATO to first block the Russians, then blunt them if necessary, and if it takes longer, to break them. We are talking about the industrial complex and the logistics support of a longer war that we will have to break, as Ukraine is doing now with Russia, with its refineries and everything else," the admiral said.
Asked whether he believed all NATO allies would have the political will to repel an aggressor, Bauer said: "General Grynkewich would never have been able to say this in Warsaw if it hadn't been exclusively approved by the White House."
In Bauer's view, this was "a message from President Trump to NATO: America is with NATO, article 5 is ironclad, and the regional plans are in place."
He also explained that if intelligence indicated Russia was building up its forces and the Alliance knew which direction they might try to advance in, "the battle groups can be strengthened from 1,000 to 5,000, to a brigade size in different nations."
"At the political level, these plans have already been agreed, so at a certain stage, within those plans, certain things are going to happen," the admiral said.
He added that the situation had been different in the past, when many of these measures would have been debated, with questions raised about whether they were necessary.

title: First Lady Unveils N110m Empowerment Scheme For Elderly, PWDs In All 109 Senatorial Districts
body: Deji Elumoye in Abuja Wife of the President, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, on Thursday unveiled her pet project, the Renewed Hope Initiative’s (RHI’s) N110 million empowerment package for elderly citizens and persons with disabilities in all the 109 senatorial districts nationwide. She has, therefore, urged the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) senatorial candidates to oversee its implementation and ensure the funds reach vulnerable Nigerians. The initiative, comprises two programs, each with a N55 million allocation, targeting 250 beneficiaries apiece. Under the RHI Economic Empowerment Program for Persons with Disabilities, 250 beneficiaries are expected to receive N200,000 each per senatorial district. The RHI Elderly Support Scheme will follow the same funding structure, with 250 elderly beneficiaries receiving N200,000 each per senatorial district. Mrs Tinubu announced this at a stakeholders’ meeting attended by the APC National Chairman, Professor Nentawe Yilwatda; Senate President, Godswill Akpabio; other APC members of the Senate, members of the RHI Governing Board and APC senatorial candidates. The First Lady said the decision to work through the senatorial candidates followed consultations with political leaders on how best to deliver the intervention to beneficiaries, improve coordination and ensure that the program achieves its intended purpose. According to her, the initiative was designed to leverage the candidates’ familiarity with their constituencies to identify vulnerable people and facilitate the distribution of the assistance. She cautioned that the program must not be restricted to APC members. “We don’t say give it only to party members, but give it to your voters,” she emphasized to the candidates to ensure that deserving people in their districts benefit from the intervention. Mrs Tinubu said the intervention reflects her longstanding commitment to the welfare of vulnerable Nigerians, drawing on her experience in public service and empowerment initiatives during her 12 years in the Senate. “The vulnerable in society are the people we are supposed to care for”. She explained that the RHI had previously supported persons with disabilities but was expanding its empowerment efforts to give them renewed assistance, while also stating that the intervention for elderly citizens has entered it fourth edition. Mrs Tinubu said she had considered various approaches to delivering the funds, including working through state coordinators and traditional rulers, before consultations with political leaders led to the adoption of the senatorial district model. The First Lady said the arrangement would also help raise awareness of the RHI’s programs and ensure that communities across the country are reached more effectively. In his remarks, Senate President, Godswill Akpabio commended the First Lady for bringing together serving and incoming senators to coordinate the intervention, describing the meeting as an opportunity to strengthen the delivery of programs aimed at improving the lives of vulnerable Nigerians. He said President Bola Tinubu had given his nod to the arrangement, adding that the initiative is intended to extend assistance beyond party boundaries. Akpabio urged the candidates to treat the responsibility as a public trust and ensure that the support reached the elderly and persons with disabilities in their various constituencies. The Senate President cited the First Lady’s commitment to women, children and elderly citizens, noting that her Renewed Hope Initiative had provided support to displaced communities, vulnerable households and women across the country in the last three years. He also encouraged the candidates to work with other APC political office-seekers in their districts to broaden the program’s reach. Also speaking, Speaker of the House of Representatives, Rt Hon Tajudeen Abbas, commended the First Lady for her various empowerment programs and interventions across the country, saying the Renewed Hope Initiative (RHI) has reached 31 state with its monthly Food Outreach Program. Abass described the engagement as historic and praised Mrs Tinubu’s commitment to the welfare of women and vulnerable Nigerians. “On behalf of the House of Representatives, I want to say a big thank you to our mama for all the good things she is doing”. The Speaker said the decision to involve senatorial candidates in distributing assistance to elderly citizens and persons with disabilities would help them connect with their constituents better and ensure that the support reaches the intended beneficiaries. He urged the candidates to justify the confidence reposed in them by the First Lady and the party and deliver on the assignment. The House Speaker also wished the candidates success in the forthcoming elections, assuring them of continued support and engagement ahead of the polls scheduled for January 16, 2027. On his part, APC National Chairman, Prof Nentawe Yilwatda, commended the First Lady’s interventions, saying the RHI had reached vulnerable communities in states across the federation through food support, cash assistance and economic empowerment programs. He urged the senatorial candidates to involve party structures and other relevant stakeholders in implementing the program, while ensuring that beneficiaries were selected without discrimination on the basis of ethnicity, religion or political affiliation. Yilwatda said the initiative would strengthen social cohesion and improve the party’s engagement with communities, urging the candidates to deliver on the responsibility entrusted to them. For 250 beneficiaries of the Elderly Support Scheme, the initiative has provided a sum of 50 million per senatorial district with a similar fund provided for the financial support program for Persons with Disabilities The meeting brought together the APC leadership, serving and incoming senators and members of the RHI Board of Trustees to coordinate the planned interventions for vulnerable Nigerians. RHI Financial Support program for Persons with disabilities is a major highlight of the International Day of Persons with Disabilities which comes up on December 3 while the Elderly Support Scheme is scheduled for December 17, 2026.

title: Army selects Lockheed Martin for billion-dollar Future Interceptor program
body: The Army gave the nod to Lockheed Martin to further develop a new missile interceptor that’s expected to have better engagement range, altitude, velocity and maneuverability than legacy systems, the service announced Thursday. The contractor secured an Other Transaction agreement for the Future Interceptor program. The total project value is estimated to exceed $1 billion. Under a cost-sharing arrangement, Lockheed is expected to kick in $423 million while Uncle Sam provides about $660 million, according to an Army press release. The initiative comes as America’s adversaries are developing more capable missiles and unmanned aerial systems, including hypersonics, next-generation ballistic missiles and cruise missiles, and jet-powered attack drones. The Army, which provides much of the U.S. military’s ground-based air-and-missile defense systems, is pursuing new weapons that can defeat those types of threats. “Developing advanced interceptor capabilities is essential to maintaining our nation’s defensive advantage against increasingly sophisticated threats,” Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, portfolio acquisition executive for fires, said in a statement. “The Future Interceptor program reflects the Army’s commitment to accelerating innovation, leveraging proven technologies and strengthening the layered defenses that protect our forces and national interests at home and abroad.” Brent Ingraham, the Army’s acquisition chief, said in a statement that the contract award announced Thursday was an important step in the service’s push to deliver new systems for integrated air-and-missile defense. “Under the agreement, the Army will work with Lockheed Martin to advance prototype development and conduct testing and evaluation to assess system performance against established operational requirements,” officials wrote in an Army press release. “Future development and production decisions will be informed by prototype performance, operational requirements, available resources and applicable acquisition processes,” per the release. Lockheed Martin previously announced that it was offering its new PAC-3 Edge system for the Future Interceptor program, saying in a press release issued earlier this month that the company planned to begin testing the weapon in 2027 with the aim of having it ready for deployment by 2031. The contractor’s Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) family of systems has been a cornerstone of the Army’s and international partners’ air-and-missile defense architectures for many years. Most recently, they’ve played a significant role in conflicts with Iran in the Middle East and the war in Ukraine. According to a Lockheed Martin press release issued Oct. 9, the PAC-3 Edge is a next-generation system that will provide greater maneuverability, power, velocity and precision, and come with an advanced seeker, multi-pulse solid rocket motor, and control system upgrades. “PAC-3 Edge is designed to be integrated with existing and future IAMD capabilities including the Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS), the M903 launcher, containerized launchers and HIMARS Flex,” per the Lockheed press release. The post Army selects Lockheed Martin for billion-dollar Future Interceptor program appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: Democrats' Golan meets Eisenkot, opposition heads as leaders weigh path to coalition
body: The Democrats chairman Yair Golan met with members of the opposition bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday.After the meetings, they expressed their commitment to “working swiftly and decisively to establish a government of 'repair and rescue' for Israel, recognizing the scale of the responsibility and the opportunity created by the election results,” The Democrats said.Neither bloc secured the 61 seats needed to form a Knesset majority, leaving no clear path to forming a coalition.The meetings came after Golan called on Wednesday for the opposition to form a coalition with the Arab parties, following a record-high number of seats projected for the Joint List and Ra'am.Golan earlier met with Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, whose party won the largest number of seats in the opposition bloc.Eisenkot met separately on Thursday with B'Yachad chairman Naftali Bennett and said they had “discussed ways to establish a good government in Israel as quickly as possible.”Earlier, Golan had met with opposition leader Yair Lapid, No. 2 on the B'Yachad list.Eisenkot and Golan discussed the election results and their “shared commitment to implementing the voters' will as quickly as possible,” Yashar said.Golan determined to do 'whatever is necessary'Golan said he was determined to do “whatever is necessary, with courage and responsibility, to seize this historic opportunity for change and secure Israel's future as a Jewish and democratic state.”The other opposition party leaders – Eisenkot, Bennett, and Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman – had drawn a redline to Arab parties being part of the government, saying they are not viable coalition partners after the October 7 massacre in 2023.The political deadlock could ultimately lead to another election, although the parties may still reach an agreement through coalition negotiations. Other possible outcomes include a unity government among Netanyahu and members of Eisenkot's bloc, or the formation of a minority government.After his meeting with Eisenkot, Golan said they had both “dedicated many years to Israel's security, and we both understand the immense responsibility that now rests on our shoulders. Israel's future is at stake. We share a common path and a commitment to ensuring a better future for Israel.”Lapid said he and Golan had met to “coordinate their next steps.”Notably, Bennett was not part of the meeting, according to the statement and picture that were published after the meeting.Golan said he was “determined to make every effort, turn over every stone, and act with all our partners to save Israel.”“We will continue to work in coordination,” he said. “We will not give up on the opportunity for change.”Liberman restates will not join with coalition with Arab partiesLiberman on Thursday reiterated that he would not sit with the Arab parties or Netanyahu."The only coalition we would consider is one made up exclusively of Zionist parties, including Likud without Bibi [Benjamin Netanyahu],” he said.According to the final vote count, Netanyahu's bloc maintained its lead with 53 seats in the next Knesset, while the opposition bloc won 48, and the Arab parties 19, the Central Elections Committee reported Thursday.Likud received 27 seats, making it once again the largest party in the Knesset.

title: Sunbeth’s N150bn Commercial Paper Offer Oversubscribed by 46.7%
body: * Investors subscribe N220bn as cocoa trader strengthens procurement and processing expansion plans Sunbeth Global Concept Limited has secured subscriptions exceeding N220 billion for its N150 billion commercial paper offer, surpassing its target by more than N70 billion and recording an oversubscription of over 46.7 per cent. The strong investor response underscores confidence in the company’s business strategy and growth prospects as it expands its cocoa sourcing, trading and processing operations. Sunbeth said proceeds from the issuance would be used to support cocoa procurement for the new season, as well as meet its trading and working capital requirements. The successful offer comes amid the company’s efforts to strengthen its position in the cocoa value chain through an expanded sourcing network, increased trading capacity and investments in local processing. A key component of the strategy is a planned cocoa processing plant in Nigeria with a capacity of 70,000 metric tonnes. The facility is expected to support the company’s ambition to deepen local value addition and supply cocoa products to customers in domestic, regional and international markets. Commenting on the outcome of the issuance, Sunbeth’s Chief Financial Officer, Adeyemi Aduwo, said the level of subscriptions reflected investors’ confidence in the company and its growth strategy. “The strong response reflects investors’ confidence in Sunbeth and our growth strategy. We thank our investors and transaction partners for their support. This funding strengthens our cocoa procurement capacity as we continue building an integrated business spanning sourcing, trading and processing,” Aduwo said. The commercial paper proceeds are expected to provide additional funding flexibility for seasonal cocoa purchases, a critical requirement in the company’s trading operations, while supporting its broader expansion objectives. Sunbeth also acknowledged the contributions of Chapel Hill Denham, the lead arranger, alongside the participating dealers, advisers and professional partners involved in the transaction. The partners included AVA Capital Plc, Cordros Advisory Services Limited, Coronation Merchant Bank Limited, FSL Advisory Limited, Meristem Capital Limited, Norrenberger Advisory Partners Limited, PAC Capital Limited, Rand Merchant Bank, CFG Manyard, Absa Nigeria, Zedcrest and KPMG. The New Practice served as legal counsel to the transaction. The successful issuance provides Sunbeth with additional resources to strengthen its procurement capacity at the start of the new cocoa season while advancing its plans to build a more integrated business. The company said it remained focused on expanding its global customer base, strengthening its sourcing network and developing its processing capacity, supported by disciplined financial management. With the planned processing investment complementing its existing sourcing and trading activities, Sunbeth is positioning itself to capture greater value from Nigeria’s cocoa sector and participate more actively in regional and international cocoa markets.
