Now, the draft joint document for the ongoing summit has removed this language, speaking instead of an “ever-closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself.” Canada is choosing not to get caught up in the war of terminology, with Politico quoting Carney as saying that “the good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature.” Two key unifiers have driven Europe and Canada closer together: Russia’s war against Ukraine, and U.S. President Donald Trump. Canada launched Operation Reassurance in 2014 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and has led NATO’s multinational battle group in Latvia since 2017. Cooperation and coordination deepened further after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Trump’s threats against NATO, Europe and Canadian sovereignty alike have accelerated the integration process. Particularly the Arctic has emerged as an area of interest. In February, Canada and Denmark signed a memorandum on defense cooperation amid Trump’s insistence that Greenland become a part of the United States, having threatened military force. Pointedly, the agreement with Ottawa was signed with Danish, Greenlandic and Faroese delegates present. It covered innovation, industrial cooperation, mutual logistics support, personnel, training and exercises. And in March, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden held a summit in Oslo that laid the cornerstone for an Arctic-centric, security-focused format and concrete actions to secure an area that these countries increasingly perceive as a zone of joint security interests, especially vis-à-vis Russia and, to a lesser extent, China. Finland and Norway also separately signed Arctic security-themed agreements with Canada in April and March, respectively, covering intelligence sharing, interoperability, logistics and maritime topics like the building of icebreakers, among other topics. In July, Canada announced its intention to buy up to twelve new German-Norwegian submarines, preferring the European boats over a South Korean offer, just a few weeks after Ottawa singled out Sweden’s Saab as the preferred candidate to supply it with six new airborne early warning and control aircraft. Around the same time, Canada secured preferential access to procurement under the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defense-financing program, allowing Canadian-origin components to account for up to 80% of the procurement value of equipment purchased with its loans.

title: Nigeria poised to tackle women’s barriers in cross-border trade
body:
The Nigerian government and development partners have launched the Making Trade Work for Women (MTWW) initiative to address barriers facing women in cross-border trade.
The initiative aims to address limited access to finance and markets, unclear trade procedures, harassment, and inadequate border facilities.
Implemented by the Centre for International Studies and Cooperation (CECI) and TradeMark Africa (TMA), and funded by Global Affairs Canada, the initiative covers Nigeria, Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana and Togo.
Speaking at the launch in Lagos on Thursday, Dayo Okewole, representing the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment, said the project would help address the challenges preventing women from benefiting fully from cross-border trade.
Mr Okewole said women account for more than 70 per cent of informal cross-border traders and make up a substantial share of small and medium-sized enterprises.
Despite this, women still face limited access to trade finance, border security concerns, and gaps in digital and trade literacy, according to Mr Okewole.
“Women are the bedrock of our economic architecture in Nigeria,” he said, adding that the project would support efforts to make trade more inclusive and accessible.
He said the ministry is committed to improving the regulatory environment, reducing bureaucratic bottlenecks, and promoting transparency in implementing trade policies.
Mr Okewole identified policy inclusivity, digital skills and access to finance and markets as key areas of intervention.
He said the initiative would help women-led businesses improve digital literacy, integrate e-commerce into their operations, and build the skills needed to expand their markets.
He also highlighted proposals to improve facilities for women traders in border communities, including a mini-market where traders could exchange goods without making repeated journeys across the border.
According to him, a visit to the Seme border revealed that some facilities for women traders were unused, partly because of inadequate awareness.
“We are happy to see some of the steps that have already been taken by the Customs Command in addressing some of the challenges in that area,” he said, adding that better information would help women take advantage of existing facilities and procedures.
Kwamina Ekremet, TMA’s Country Director for Ghana and Anglophone West Africa, said the initiative was intended to make trade more efficient, inclusive and responsive to women’s needs.
Citing the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Sahel and West Africa Club, Mr Ekremet said West Africa’s intra-regional food trade goes unrecorded in official statistics, at about $10 billion annually.
He said women play a central role in this trade but often face barriers that make their businesses more costly, difficult and sometimes unsafe to operate.
“Our challenge, therefore, is not simply to encourage women to trade formally. It is to make formal trade accessible, affordable, predictable and worthwhile,” he said.
Mr Ekremet said the programme, which runs from 2024 to 2028, aims to directly benefit 80,000 people, at least 70 per cent of whom will be women traders.
It also seeks to benefit about 20,000 additional traders indirectly and reach more than 50,000 people through sensitisation.
The programme aims to increase participating women’s incomes by 40 per cent and raise the number of women traders using sustainable practices by 50 per cent.
Mr Ekremet said engagements with border officials, customs officers and small-scale traders at the Seme border had highlighted multiple checkpoints along the Badagry-Seme corridor, unclear procedures, identification challenges, harassment, intimidation, poor road conditions and inadequate access to essential facilities.
He cited a trader, Madam Iyabo, who said a journey that previously took one day now takes three to five days.
“Every additional day increases her costs, reduces her profit and places greater pressure on her business and family,” he said.
Mr Ekremet said the findings underscored the need for improved trader education, simpler documentation, better coordination among border agencies and more accessible facilities for women.
He added that the initiative would work with government and regional partners to promote safer border practices, strengthen women’s associations and establish effective channels for reporting harassment.
While speaking to the PREMIUM TIMES after the launch, Sand Mba, Executive Director of the Africa International Trade and Commerce Research, which he described as the lead implementing consortium for the project, said the initiative would help address gender-based barriers, improve access to trade information and enable women to benefit from existing regional trade agreements.
He said several policies and protocols already support cross-border trade, including the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), its Protocol on Women and Youth in Trade, and the Economic Community of West African States’ (ECOWAS) Trade Liberalisation Scheme.
However, Mr Mba said implementation and access to information remained significant gaps.
“There are fantastic policies on the ground that will make women trade, but it is the implementation that we have the gap, and accessing information to make this information work. That is where we have the gap,” Mr Mba said.
He called for stronger cooperation between the government and project partners to ensure women traders understood and could access available trade facilitation mechanisms.
A representative of the Bank of Industry’s Gender Inclusion Unit, Jelilat Ismaila-Ayinde, also highlighted financing opportunities available to women-owned businesses through the bank’s Guaranteed GLOW for Women product.
She said the initiative was designed to support Nigerian women in light manufacturing, agro-processing, healthcare, and other sectors the bank supports, particularly those operating micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises.
Ms Ismaila-Ayinde said the product offered financing of up to ₦50 million, required one guarantor, and that the bank planned to digitise the application process to improve nationwide access.
She, however, noted that the product did not cover trading, while encouraging women entrepreneurs in eligible sectors to explore the bank’s online application platform.
At the event, the president of the Lagos State Association of Pineapple Sellers, Omotola Durotola, also spoke on the challenges facing traders, saying women in cross-border agricultural trade struggled to access producers, secure adequate capital, and find suitable markets.
She said many traders bought goods on credit because they lacked the funds to buy them outright, while some sellers operated under bridges in Lagos because market facilities were inadequate.
The association called for support to improve access to agricultural producers in the Republic of Benin, provide financing for traders, and build suitable market infrastructure in Lagos.

title: Adesokan: 92% of Taxpayers Pay Zero or Lower Taxes Under New Act
body: *Declares 21 states have adopted harmonised tax, levy legislation as authorities seek to dismantle multiple charges amid 27% rise in revenue *FG, states plan joint audits to cut compliance costs, disruption to businesses, seeks to end roadside tax collection, others James Emejo in Abuja Executive Secretary, Joint Revenue Board (JRB), Mr. Olusegun Adesokan, has said disclosed that the implementation of the new tax regime has yielded early fruits with a 27 per cent increase in tax revenue from 23 states in the First Half of the year (H1 2026) compared to the corresponding period of 2025. He said the performance reflected a shift towards bringing more high-income earners into the tax net while reducing the burden on lower-income taxpayers. The JRB boss spoke during an engagement with journalists in Abuja. He said the reform was also beginning to improve revenue administration through the harmonisation of taxes and levies, the introduction of a National Tax Identification system and closer coordination among federal and state tax authorities. Adesokan said 21 states had adopted the harmonised taxes and levies legislation as of October 27, with the National Economic Council (NEC) identifying the initiative as one of its priorities for implementation within a 90-day action plan. The figures provide an early indication of the reform’s potential to improve domestic revenue mobilisation without imposing additional tax burdens on low-income households and businesses. However, the board acknowledged that multiple taxation, unauthorised collections and confusion over legitimate government charges remain widespread challenges. 21 states move to harmonise levies Adesokan said the harmonisation initiative was designed to consolidate numerous taxes, levies and charges imposed by subnational authorities into nine broad categories, reducing duplication and making compliance more predictable for businesses and individuals. He said the board developed the framework in collaboration with the Presidential Committee on Fiscal Policy and Tax Reforms and had circulated it to states for adoption. He acknowledged that unauthorised roadside collections remained a problem, including demands by individuals and groups claiming to represent government authorities. He said the JRB was working with the police and state revenue authorities on a coordinated enforcement mechanism to address the practice. According to him, the board also planned to intensify efforts to eliminate illegal collections affecting transport operators and traders, although Adesokan did not give a definitive commencement date for the proposed enforcement measures. He urged businesses to verify suspicious demands with the relevant tax authorities and ensure that payments were made into authorised government accounts rather than accounts belonging to private consultants or collectors. The listed the states to include Kebbi, Niger, Kaduna, Plateau, Ekiti, Benue, Zamfara, Enugu, Kogi, Abia and Kwara. Others are Nasarawa, Anambra, Gombe, Akwa Ibom, Adamawa, Bayelsa, Delta, Yobe, Ondo and Borno. Low-income earners get tax relief Furthermore, Adesokan said data obtained from 23 states showed that an average of 92 per cent of income earners covered by the assessment now paid lower or zero personal income tax under the new framework. He said the changes were intended to leave more money in the hands of lower-income earners while ensuring that individuals with greater financial capacity contributed a fairer share. Under the revised personal income tax structure, the first N800,000 of annual taxable income is taxed at zero per cent, while higher income bands attract progressively higher rates, reaching 25 per cent for the top band. Adesokan stressed that the reform was guided by the principle of taxing prosperity rather than poverty, adding that the government had not introduced new taxes through the framework. He acknowledged concerns about traders and small businesses who continued to complain about tax demands despite the exemptions provided under the new rules. According to him, inadequate public awareness and the persistence of unauthorised collectors had contributed to the confusion. He said the board would continue its public education campaign to clarify which taxpayers were exempt from personal income tax and distinguish legitimate taxes from other authorised charges. However, the 92 per cent figure relates to the personal income tax assessment presented by the board and does not qualify as an exemption from every form of taxation, including applicable consumption taxes. National tax ID to curb multiple taxation Adesokan said the National Tax Identification system was another major component of the reform, providing a common means of identifying taxpayers across federal and state jurisdictions. The system is expected to link existing taxpayer records and enable authorities to verify tax compliance without requiring individuals and businesses to repeatedly establish their status in different states. He said the arrangement would reduce administrative bottlenecks, particularly for individuals conducting business or property transactions outside their state of residence. He stated that JRB was also promoting uniform tax administration guidelines and information-sharing arrangements to improve transparency and voluntary compliance. Joint audits planned for businesses In a further measure to reduce the cost of compliance, Adesokan said the JRB was preparing to facilitate joint tax audits involving NRS and state internal revenue services. He said the arrangement would enable relevant authorities to coordinate their examinations of businesses rather than visiting the same companies separately at different times. Under the proposed approach, state authorities could examine personal income tax compliance, including employers’ obligations, while the federal revenue service would address the company’s relevant federal tax obligations. Adesokan said coordinated audits would reduce disruption to business operations, paperwork and the time companies spend responding to separate tax assessments. He added that the JRB’s mandate was to coordinate and harmonise revenue administration rather than collect taxes directly. Implementation challenges remain Meanwhile, despite the early progress, there were concerns about continued roadside collections, conflicting demands from federal and state tax authorities, and the limited visibility of public benefits from taxes paid. Adesokan said the board was working to improve collaboration between revenue agencies, including through joint audits and more consistent administration of tax laws. He also acknowledged complaints about levies imposed on pensioners and residents in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), adding that the relevant legal provisions would be examined. The JRB chief maintained that the ultimate test of the reform would not be the volume of taxes collected alone, but whether businesses could expand, create jobs and contribute to economic growth without being weighed down by multiple and unpredictable charges. No more roadblocks, cash collection Adesokan added that JRB at its 158th meeting banned the sales of stickers and emblems nationwide. He said, “This means motorists will no longer be subjected to the purchase of irrelevant documents before transporting goods from one part of the country to another. Thereby reducing the cost of farm produce.” He explained that the prohibition was supported by the model Harmonised Taxes & Levies Law and the Presumptive Tax Regulations, 2026.

title: Iran targeted Israeli election, US midterms with cyber, recruitment plans – report
body: Iran is preparing to interfere in the US midterm elections on November 3 after attempting to disrupt Israel's general election on Tuesday, with Iranian officials describing plans to infiltrate electoral processes and hack voting systems, The Telegraph reported on Thursday.Several Iranian officials told the British newspaper that Tehran views the two elections as an opportunity to weaken its principal adversaries politically, as the conflict involving Iran, Israel, and the US continues.One Iranian official said Tehran had been examining ways to recruit individuals involved in the electoral processes of both countries, while cyber groups had been established to target their election systems.Another official said Iran regarded the operations as an extension of its military confrontation with Washington and Jerusalem, with the objective of destabilizing both countries rather than securing victory for particular candidates.The officials indicated that Tehran hopes political divisions in Israel and the US will constrain their governments' ability to conduct further military operations against Iran.The claims come after Israeli authorities raised concerns about Iranian attempts to influence the election. Ahead of the vote, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Iran and its regional proxies were considering ways to interfere in the electoral process, including cyber operations and possible attacks.The Telegraph's report did not establish that Iranian operatives had successfully penetrated voting systems in either country.Tehran sees Israeli political deadlock as an opportunityIranian officials have been closely following the results of Israel's election, particularly the possibility that neither Netanyahu nor opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot will be able to establish a governing coalition.According to results released by the Central Elections Committee on Wednesday, Netanyahu's bloc was projected to secure 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for Eisenkot's opposition bloc.Arab parties were projected to win a combined 19 seats, potentially making their support decisive in determining the composition of the next government.Fadahossein Maleki, a member of the Iranian parliament's national security and foreign policy committee, told The Telegraph that the Arab parties were seeking to prevent Netanyahu from forming another government while increasing their influence over coalition negotiations.He argued that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot would find it straightforward to secure their support, raising the possibility of prolonged coalition negotiations or another election.Such an outcome could benefit Tehran by limiting Israel's ability to make major strategic decisions while Iran rebuilds military capabilities damaged during the conflict, according to the report.Dr. Steven Wagner, a senior lecturer in international security at Brunel University of London, said Iran had reason to avoid significant military action while awaiting the political consequences of the elections.Wagner assessed that Tehran would prefer Netanyahu to lose power but could also benefit from a prolonged political stalemate.He said Iran could use the intervening period to strengthen its defenses and consolidate military assets that survived Israeli and American strikes.The possibility of another election or an alternative governing coalition has emerged as a central issue in Israeli politics, with opposition parties divided over whether they could rely on Arab parties to secure a parliamentary majority.Iran hopes US midterms will constrain TrumpIranian officials expressed particular optimism about the US midterm elections, which will determine control of the House of Representatives and approximately one-third of the Senate.According to The Telegraph, Tehran hopes that Democratic gains in Congress will restrict President Donald Trump's ability to continue military operations against Iran and provide support for additional Israeli attacks.Wagner said Iranian officials would be watching for indications that Congress might seek to limit White House spending on the conflict and military assistance to Israel.Amir Ali Abolfath, an Iranian analyst specializing in American affairs, told The Telegraph that historical midterm voting patterns, public opinion polls, and betting markets suggested Democrats had a significant opportunity to gain control of the House.He cautioned, however, that a Democratic congressional majority would not necessarily prevent further military action.Abolfath noted that the US president retains substantial authority as commander-in-chief, meaning opposition control of Congress could complicate military operations without necessarily stopping them.He also raised the possibility that the Trump administration could consider additional strikes against Iran before the election if it believed a rapid military victory would improve Republican electoral prospects.Conversely, he said, Washington might avoid an operation that risked developing into a prolonged conflict with wider regional consequences.Iranian officials threaten broader retaliationIranian officials also warned that further Israeli or American strikes could provoke retaliation extending beyond the targets attacked in previous exchanges.One senior Iranian official told The Telegraph that Tehran was prepared for a diplomatic settlement but was also ready to respond forcefully if hostilities resumed.The official indicated that a future Iranian response would not necessarily be confined to American military assets.Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, meanwhile, publicly dismissed the significance of Israel's election during remarks to reporters in Tehran on Monday.He portrayed the vote as a contest between rival political factions that, in Tehran's view, would continue pursuing hostile policies toward Iran regardless of the outcome.The distinction between Iran's public dismissal of the electoral process and its reported covert preparations highlights the importance Iranian officials attach to political developments in both countries.Israel had previously been warned about vulnerabilities to foreign electoral interference. In December 2025, State Comptroller Matanyahu Englman said Israel faced significant shortcomings in its preparedness for foreign digital interference, warning that Iranian cyberattacks and espionage attempts were intensifying ahead of the 2026 election.For Tehran, the potential advantages of political paralysis in Jerusalem and congressional opposition in Washington appear to form part of a wider strategy aimed at weakening its adversaries without relying exclusively on military confrontation.Nevertheless, the Iranian officials who spoke to The Telegraph emphasized that Tehran was not depending on either election to end the conflict and remained prepared for further fighting.

title: Current level of Russia-Africa trade turnover is not limit — Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The current level of the trade turnover between Russia and Africa totaling $27 bln is not the limit, President Vladimir Putin said at the press conference after the Russia-Africa summit.
"We are confident the current level of the Russian-African trade turnover, and it stands at $27 bln, is far from being the limit. It can be said we are at the start of the journey," the Russian leader said.
The action plan of the Russia-Africa partnership forum for 2027-2028 contains such task in the economic sphere as building up mutual export and import exchanges and improvement of their structure, Putin added.

title: Let’s Talk About The U.S. Target Drone Iran Claims To Have Recovered Intact
body: Iran claims to have brought down what looks to be a U.S.-made MQM-170C Outlaw G2 drone largely intact. A video shows it has a notable feature on top of its nose. In U.S. military use today, Outlaw-series drones are best known as an aerial target for use in training and testing . The footage in question, and the accompanying claims, should be treated with caution given that the regime in Tehran and the country’s media outlets do routinely make exaggerated and unverified claims . That being said, so far, the footage looks to be credible. Furthermore, the U.S. military has pushed back on Iran’s version of events, but has not explicitly denied having lost one of these drones in the region recently. For its part, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it captured the MQM-170-series drone following what it described as an “offensive electronic warfare operation” somewhere to the “west of the Strait of Hormuz.” The IRGC also claims that the uncrewed aircraft was conducting reconnaissance on Iranian air defenses positioned along the country’s Persian Gulf coast. At the time of writing, no firm evidence has been provided to support either of these assertions. The IRGC has released the aforementioned video, seen below, which it says shows the drone being tracked via an infrared camera, as well as after its recovery. #Iran / #USA : Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps ( #IRGC ) Navy captured a US Drone after intercepting it with EW Systems. The Drone captured by the IRGC Navy appears to be Griffon Aerospace Outlaw G2 “MQM-170C” UAV. pic.twitter.com/Xw6JYOu1s6 — War Noir (@war_noir) October 29, 2026 “In the past weeks and months, the IRGC has repeatedly lied out of desperation, and today is no different,” U.S. Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins, spokesperson for U.S. Central Command, told TWZ when asked about the specific Iranian claims. “We’re not going to waste our time. U.S. forces remain vigilant and laser-focused on our assigned missions,” Hawkins said in response to a follow-up question about whether CENTCOM could confirm or deny the loss of an MQM-170-series drone for any reason. As an aside, Iran recovered an Anduril Dive-LD uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV) largely intact last month in what the IRGC claimed had been a “complex intelligence and operational action.” U.S. authorities ultimately confirmed the loss of the advanced UUV, but said it was the result of a malfunction . As mentioned, the drone seen in the IRGC video does look to be an MQM-170C, or at least a closely-related variant thereof. It has an interesting feature on top of its nose: a single forward-looking aperture. This is something that is commonly associated with staring-type optics, which drones often use to aid with navigation. There is a possibility that it could be a seeker, if the drone were to be configured as a one-way-attack munition, but this seems unlikely. Additional views of the nose end of the drone Iran says it captured, with the ‘staring’ aperture plainly visible. Iranian media captures via X A stock picture of an MQM-170C drone in U.S. military service in its typical configuration as an aerial target. USN Another picture of U.S. MQM-170C target drones offering additional views of their noses. USAF MQM-170C’s manufacturer, Griffon Aerospace , which refers to this design internally as the Outlaw Gen 2 (G2), does say on its website that it can be configured as “an inexpensive payload development platform offering great endurance, payload size, weight, and power.” The company’s website also says that the target configuration of the G2 has a gross weight of 150 pounds, but that this can grow to 225 pounds when used as a more general-purpose drone. The drone, which is nearly 11 feet long and has a wingspan of 16 feet, otherwise has a stated maximum endurance of eight hours, top speed of 126 knots, and the ability to reach altitudes of more than 16,000 feet. The design is propelled by a 2-cylinder, 2-stroke combustion engine driving a single pusher propeller. The G2 gets into the air via a catapult-type launcher and can be recovered, either after a glide-in landing on suitable terrain or via parachute. An MQM-170C target drone seen being launched via catapult. USN Griffon Aerospace also offers an ‘expanded’ G2E version with fixed tricycle landing gear as an “open and customizable platform for ISR [intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance] missions, subsystem testing, and R&D [research and development].” This version has a lower maximum takeoff weight and total endurance compared to the baseline G2, according to the company’s website. The IRGC video does not show any evidence of landing gear, but it could have broken away when the drone came down. The landing-gear-equipped Outlaw G2E. Griffon Aerospace The larger Outlaw family, which traces back to the early 2000s, also includes the Gen 1 MQM-170A , which has a completely different design from the subsequent G2 drone. Griffon also developed a derivative of the Gen 1 design with a twin-boom tail, called the Outlaw Boomer, which the U.S. military designated the MQM-170B . There is also a twin-engine, twin-boom derivative of the Outlaw G2 that the U.S. military has at least tested in the past. A twin-engine, twin-boom derivative of the Outlaw G2, seen here in U.S. Army markings. Griffon Aerospace This brings us to the additional matter of a contract the U.S. Army awarded to Griffon Aerospace , valued at nearly $68 million, for the procurement of a Gen 3 version of the Outlaw on June 3. When the Pentagon first announced this deal, it was explicitly said to be “in support of Operation Epic Fury” against Iran. That portion of the announcement was quietly deleted sometime thereafter. “A company official declined to provide details about the Gen 3 design,” Breaking Defense reported in a story published on June 5. On August 25, Griffon received an additional contract from the Army, valued at just under $133 million, “to procure Griffon Outlaw systems, support equipment and field service representatives for system use and employment.” That announcement made no mention of operations against Iran. At the time of writing, Griffon Aerospace’s website does not appear to make any mention of the Gen 3 Outlaw. TWZ has reached out for more information about this drone. Given the known breadth of Outlaw designs to date, it is possible that the Gen 3 drone is substantially, if not entirely, different from any of the existing types. At the same time, the June contract announcement does establish a link between the Outlaw family and U.S. military use outside of training and testing, and specifically as part of real-world operations aimed at Iran. There remains the potential that Iran simply captured an Outlaw target drone that U.S. forces lost control of during training or testing in the region. The drone seen in the IRGC video lacks the high-visibility orange markings typically seen on aerial targets, though these could easily have been painted over. Iranian authorities could have still fabricated the recovery, in part or in whole, though there is no firm evidence of that at present, either. An MQM-170C target drone belonging to the U.S. Marine Corps, seen here in use during an exercise in Saudi Arabia in 2023. USMC Another non-U.S. operator region could also be employing versions of the Outlaw, including in non-target drone roles, such as for surveillance and reconnaissance, or as decoys. All of this does now come amid growing signs that the United States, as well as Israel, are preparing to launch a new major campaign against Iran. As TWZ reported recently , stimulating Iranian air defenses to glean key intelligence about their current capabilities and positions would be critical in the lead-up to any such operation. “Stimulating Iran’s air defenses is critical,” our own Tyler Rogoway wrote on X earlier this month following unconfirmed reports of unusual Israeli air activity. “By Iran operating as if a full scale attack could be coming, their air defenses can be detected, categorized and geolocated. This is absolutely critical prior to a major air operation. Surveilling them during times of lower alert does not provide the same fidelity of actionable intelligence. Knowing where those threats are and how they are operating can mean the difference of life and death and/or will help standoff munitions make their way to their targets as those defenses can be suppressed, destroyed, or avoided entirely via careful mission planning.” In September, claims had emerged that Iran had shot down a U.S.-made ADM-160 Miniature Air-Launched Decoy (MALD), but that remains unconfirmed. There were also reports of unusual, UAP-like objects flying over Iran, which have similarly not been confirmed. 15090 is the CAGE code for Raytheon, which is visible on the tail fins and other remnants. Source for images: https://t.co/weIo1Hh6RR pic.twitter.com/4LoBMChKZG — Trevor Ball (@Easybakeovensz) September 20, 2026 I don’t know what this is, or if it’s legit BUT remember we are in a new age of misdirection, decoy and guile. Specifically using low end drone technology. There are more ways to stimulate an enemy air defense system, distract a populous, assess the flow of public info from a… https://t.co/wW7YVlbayB — Tyler Rogoway (@Aviation_Intel) September 21, 2026 As we wrote at that time: “Such reports come amid an increasingly sophisticated use of low-end drones , decoys, and other forms of deception. These kinds of systems can be employed not only to stimulate adversary air defenses, but also to distract populations and probe how information moves out of a denied area. In such an environment, unusual aerial sightings should be viewed with caution — but not necessarily dismissed as irrelevant. We have been talking about how new forms of misdirection and guile will leverage relatively low-end technologies in future conflicts for many years now. While it isn’t clear if this light show in the sky over Iran was such an activity, it is certainly a reminder to keep that possibility in mind.” It would certainly be plausible for suitably configured Outlaw drones to be in use now as another means of simulating Iranian air defenses. There is precedent even for ostensible target drones to be used operationally to deploy countermeasures and just as decoys in support of major strikes. U.S. BQM-34 Firebee target drones were notably used to spread radar-confusing chaff over the Iraqi capital Baghdad as part of the opening phase of Operation Iraqi Freedom in 2003. It is also worth noting that the conflict with Iran this year has seen the first U.S. combat use of longer-range one-way attack drones , as well as explosive-laden kamikaze uncrewed surface vessels (USV). However, there is no evidence at present that drones in the Outlaw family have been configured in this way in any context. Altogether, though still not definitively confirmed, Iran’s claimed recovery of an MQM-170C drone is an interesting development as the prospect that major hostilities in the region could resume soon continues to grow. Contact the author: joe@twz.com The post Let’s Talk About The U.S. Target Drone Iran Claims To Have Recovered Intact appeared first on TWZ .

title: From donor to buyer. Germany eyes Ukrainian missiles
body:
Berlin plans to test Ukraine’s Bars cruise missile as it seeks cheaper long-range firepower to strengthen deterrence against Russia.
Berlin could sign an initial deal within weeks and begin Bundeswehr trials in early 2027, the Financial Times reports. Successful testing could lead to an order for several hundred missiles, which would mark Germany’s first known acquisition of a Ukrainian-developed offensive weapon for its own military.
The jet-powered Bars has a reported range of up to 1,000km and is already being used against targets in Russia. Although a German official confirmed the procurement talks to the Kyiv Independent on 24 October, the manufacturer remains unnamed for security reasons, and Berlin has not disclosed which variant it intends to buy.
A July agreement funded by Berlin already provides for joint production in Germany, initially to supply Ukraine’s forces. That arrangement falls under Kyiv’s Build with Ukraine initiative, which establishes manufacturing abroad using Ukrainian technology. The model gives Ukrainian producers access to allied defence supply chains, while partner countries provide funding and industrial capacity. According to the Financial Times, the first German-made batch reached Ukraine this month, and the same venture would supply the Bundeswehr.
Germany is looking to expand its long-range arsenal amid lengthy waits for US Tomahawk missiles, which the German defence outlet Hartpunkt reports may not arrive before the early 2030s. Hartpunkt also identifies Covenant’s Anthem as another candidate for Germany’s cheaper missile programme.
Army chief Christian Freuding explained the underlying logic on 7 October, noting that mass launches are meant to overwhelm enemy air defences while high-end missiles strike strategic targets. Two systems still need to qualify for Bundeswehr service, he said, with initial deliveries possible from 2027.

title: How Shevchenko became a symbol of Ukraine’s resistance: A report from Kaniv
body: Taras Shevchenko museum A banner bearing an image of Taras Shevchenko on Kyiv’s Lukianivka Street, burned by Russian missiles. October 2026. Photograph: Olga Musafirova A report by Novaya Gazeta Europe . By Olga Musafirova Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine has finally dismantled the Soviet myth of Taras Shevchenko as a rural poet of sorrow and lament. His poetic prophecies are taking on an almost mystical resonance on billboards as Ukrainian forces liberate occupied territories in the east, while the Russian army shoots at his statues as if he were a living person. Olga Musafirova traveled to Kaniv, to the hill overlooking the Dnipro River where, as Shevchenko wished, his remains lie buried, and visited the Taras Shevchenko Museum. Its most valuable exhibits have been hidden away to protect them from Russian bombing. She explores how different political regimes tried to tame Shevchenko – and how he became a symbol of Ukrainian resistance. Who was Taras Shevchenko? Taras Hryhorovych Shevchenko (born March 9, 1814; died March 10, 1861) was a Ukrainian poet, prose writer, artist and thinker. His work laid the foundations of modern Ukrainian literature and language. Born into a family of serfs, he was orphaned at an early age. His owner, Pavel Engelhardt, took the talented young artist to St. Petersburg to serve as a personal attendant, known as a “kazachok.” Seven years later, in 1838, the painter Karl Bryullov, the poet Vasily Zhukovsky and the Ukrainian artist and educator Ivan Soshenko bought Shevchenko’s freedom for 2,500 rubles. He became a student at the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts. His 1840 collection, Kobzar , established his reputation as a poet of the Ukrainian people. In 1847, Shevchenko joined the secret Cyril and Methodius Brotherhood, which advocated the abolition of serfdom, the overthrow of autocracy and a confederation of free Slavic republics. He was arrested and exiled for 10 years to the Orenburg region and the Kazakh steppes, under strict orders not to write or draw. Released in 1857, he died in St. Petersburg. Two months later, his remains were transferred to Ukraine and buried on Chernecha Hill near Kaniv. Among Shevchenko’s best-known works are Zapovit ( Testament ), The Dnipro Roars and Groans , The Dream , Haidamaky , Kateryna and the poem The Caucasus . In the latter, Shevchenko condemns the Russian Empire’s war of conquest in the Caucasus and celebrates the struggle of peoples for freedom. A line from the poem, “Fight on – and you will prevail. God is with you,” has become an enduring rallying cry for Ukraine’s revolutions. Shevchenko wrote prose, including the novellas The Artist and The Musician , in Russian while in exile. As an artist, he produced more than 1,000 works. Icons of the revolution In mid-February 2014, Kyiv’s Maidan protests entered a phase defined by the choice between “freedom or death.” Around that time, graffiti appeared on the facade of the Institute of Linguistics in central Kyiv, on Hrushevsky Street, to the right of the main barricade. The images were styled as portraits set inside frames. They seemed to have emerged overnight through the soot left by the protest bonfires. They were immediately dubbed the icons of the revolution. Their creator, an artist known by the pseudonym “Sociopath,” was in no hurry to reveal his identity. The first image showed Taras Shevchenko wearing a bandana that covered the lower half of his face. Many Maidan protesters dressed that way to avoid being identified. The police had lists and photographs of activists; they were being hunted down, abducted and killed. Beneath the portrait was a line from Shevchenko: “The fire cannot burn the resolute.” Georgia joins joint statement in support of Ukraine at UN “Four members of my family are fighting: my mother, two brothers and me” – story of Ukrainian Olha Bihari, known by call sign “Witch” Georgian ‘delegation’ delivers gifts to Russian unit fighting against Ukraine “Saturday march” in Tbilisi: “Abkhazia is Georgia” and solidarity with Ukraine. Video podcast “Protests in Georgia” Lesya Ukrainka was depicted wearing a respirator as protesters were being doused with tear gas. Her words read: “Those who liberate themselves will be free.” Ivan Franko appeared in an orange hard hat bearing the slogans “I am an extremist” and “Down with the gang!” Construction helmets and bicycle helmets offered some protection from the batons wielded by the Berkut riot police. But they could not protect protesters from bullets when Yanukovych’s regime, following Putin’s advice, began drowning the protests in blood, seeking to crush them as a dangerous example for others to follow. The Ukrainians did not scatter. Several years later, the icons of the revolution were targeted for destruction by businesspeople renting space in a neighboring boutique. Vandals smeared paint over the images and scrawled “Fake!” across them. The murals were designated a local historical monument, and their restoration was undertaken by the same artist, “Sociopath,” with support from the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory and the Maidan Museum. Today, the graffiti still gaze out from the institute’s wall onto Hrushevsky Street. But the ground-floor windows have been boarded up with particleboard panels since a Russian strike hit the building. The poetic prophecy inscribed beneath Franko’s portrait could hardly be more fitting: “Our whole life is a war.” A 2014 mural of Taras Shevchenko on the wall of the Institute of Linguistics. Photograph: Olga Musafirova Shevchenko in street art Since then, Shevchenko has become the most sought-after figure in street art. On Kyiv’s Shevchenko Boulevard alone, I counted three murals bearing the inscription: “Poet, artist, prophet or superhero?” A QR code offered a crash course on the man who “told us about our nation back when it wasn’t mainstream,” along with a gallery of contemporary interpretations. Traditional Ukrainian literature teachers would have fainted at the sight. In place of the stern genius of humble origins stands “Sheva”: a tattooed rocker in red trousers holding a bandura, a reconnaissance soldier in winter camouflage with bunny ears, a serviceman with a “Demining” patch on his tactical vest, and a young man who looks as if he has stepped out of a Renoir painting. Taras really did wear many masks: young gentleman, intellectual, traveler, fixture of St. Petersburg’s bohemian circles. He was no canonical old man in a sheepskin coat, but a fiercely defiant lover of freedom. By today’s standards, is 47 really that old? The niche media outlet Osvitoria (“education” in Ukrainian) pointed out that no government has ever accepted the poet without editing out parts it found inconvenient. The Soviet secret services were particularly thorough. Some archival materials on the life and work of the Kobzar , as Shevchenko is affectionately known, are still being declassified today. ▇ No government has ever accepted the poet without editing out parts it found inconvenient. Shevchenko: street art’s most sought-after contemporary figure. Photograph: Olga Musafirova Shevchenko as a target of the Russian army Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has made Taras Shevchenko, however strange it may sound, the Russian army’s foremost mystical enemy as well. Destroying his images has become a matter of principle. In April 2022, I visited Borodianka, in the Kyiv region, shortly after it was liberated. Near the blackened shells of apartment blocks and piles of concrete on Tsentralna Street, survivors were waiting. Rescuers were pulling bodies and body parts from the rubble, which had become mass graves. The remains had lain there for a month: the occupying forces had prevented the debris from being cleared while the dead were still inside. The Russians had also shot up a bust of Shevchenko in the main square. Three times: once in the forehead, once in the temple, and then a finishing shot to the back of the head with a larger-caliber weapon. The day after the town’s liberation, someone brought Taras the first tulips, wrapped in cellophane – yellow, greenhouse-grown flowers. Where they managed to find them remains a mystery. The border village of Hlyboke, in the Kharkiv region, was cleared of Russian forces in September 2022. Russian soldiers had turned the Ukrainian language and literature classroom at the local school into a shooting range. The portrait of Shevchenko above the blackboard served as the target. With one hand, they shot at his head; with the other, they tried to draw Ukrainians into the “Russian world.” There is a term for this phenomenon: appropriation – the act of claiming elements of another culture as one’s own. In October 2022, the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor’s Office released physical evidence showing how the occupying forces had set about imposing a Russian-style education system. At a secondary school in the village of Hlushkivka, in the Kupiansk district, investigators found not only Russian textbooks and tricolor flags but also posters featuring Russian literary figures. Among them were Gogol and Shevchenko. The caption beneath Shevchenko read: “Poet, prose writer, artist. Bought out of serfdom by Russians. Kept his diary in Russian.” Shevchenko’s monuments in Melitopol and Balakliia In January 2023, Russian occupying forces removed a monument to Taras Shevchenko from the center of occupied Melitopol, in the Zaporizhzhia region. The dismantling took place late in the evening. The city’s mayor, Ivan Fedorov, reported the removal, adding: “They probably took him to the basement. That’s the only way they know how to deal with those they don’t like.” He knew about basements from personal experience. In March 2022, he was abducted from his office, a bag was pulled over his head, and a week later he was exchanged for nine very young Russian conscripts captured by Ukrainian forces. By May 9, 2025, a bust of Stalin had been installed on the pedestal in Melitopol where Shevchenko’s monument had stood. Shevchenko has repeatedly reappeared in Ukrainian territories soon after Russian forces were driven out. A short video , filmed by Ukrainian Air Force assault troops in the liberated city of Balakliia, in the Kharkiv region, during the autumn 2023 counteroffensive, was shown on what seemed like every television channel in the country. In the footage, soldiers tear down a Russian tricolor banner from a roadside billboard. It bears the words “We are one people with Russia.” Beneath it, a portrait of the Kobzar is revealed, along with a famous stanza from his poem The Caucasus . The banner had been put up in the last year before the invasion that could still be described as relatively peaceful, to mark another anniversary of Ukraine’s independence. One soldier reacts in disbelief: “Holy f—!” Another orders him: “Read it!” And he reads the stanza aloud: “Fight on – and you will prevail! God is with you! For you are truth, for you are glory, and holy freedom!” Serhiy Nihoyan, a student who became one of the first people killed during the Maidan protests, had recited the same passage aloud against a backdrop of barricades. Today, in Kyiv’s Lukianivka district, where little remains untouched, a banner bearing Shevchenko’s portrait and the words “We are fighting. We will prevail” covers the facade of a damaged building. Ukrainians immediately recognize the reference: the call to “Fight on – and you will prevail!” is etched into their collective memory. Shevchenko’s lines are continually adapted to the moment. At Barbara, a coffee shop near the author’s home, one version reads: “Get out of our home. We are free forever. There will be no Muscovy here. Glory to Ukraine!” Chernecha hill under the tsars The hill near Kaniv, overlooking the Dnipro River and its green slopes, became a place of pilgrimage almost immediately after Shevchenko’s remains were transferred there from St. Petersburg in May 1861, in accordance with his Testament . In 1884, local residents raised funds to erect a cast-iron cross. Nearby, at the edge of the woods, they built a simple hut. One half became an improvised folk museum called Tarasova Svitlytsia (“Taras’s Chamber”); the other served as the home of a caretaker. The exhibits included a copy of Kobzar , an oil portrait of the poet with a halo above his head, brushes belonging to an unknown artist, a kobza, a traditional Ukrainian stringed instrument, and an old visitors’ book lying on a table. Embroidered Ukrainian towels, known as rushnyky , hung on the walls, including some bearing Shevchenko’s image. Many of those who brought them could neither read nor write, yet knew his poems by heart. Secret reports from the Kaniv gendarmerie on visitors to the site have survived in the State Archives of the Kyiv Region. People came to Chernecha Hill not only from neighboring villages but from far away. Surveillance intensified ahead of major anniversaries. The authorities refused to permit either accommodation for pilgrims or the establishment of an association to maintain and protect the grave. A document dated April 8, 1910, from the Kyiv provincial authority responsible for public associations explained why. Such an association, it warned, “would provide a convenient means of bringing together activists and adherents of the Ukrainophile party, allowing them to gather in an isolated place, difficult for the administration to observe and monitor.” The association’s activities, officials cautioned, “would be directed toward strengthening propaganda for the cultural and political autonomy of Little Russia.” They even found evidence of suspicious intentions in the application’s failure to specify the language to be used for official business. The implication was clear: the language in question might not be Russian. The Moscow art theatre at Shevchenko’s grave The warnings from the gendarmerie and the authorities’ fears of “advocates of autonomy” did not deter prominent figures in Russia’s artistic and intellectual circles. Zinaida Tarakhan-Bereza, the oldest living staff member of the Shevchenko National Reserve, cites historical accounts in her scholarly chronicle The Shrine (Kyiv, 1998). In May 1912, a steamer decorated with Shevchenko’s portrait, embroidered towels and flowers arrived at the Kaniv landing. “No speeches, politically charged songs or other demonstrative performances!” the “tourists” were reminded once again as they came ashore. Only two wreaths were permitted at the poet’s grave. One came from the Ukrainian Club, a national and cultural association headed by the composer Mykola Lysenko. The other was an elaborate wrought-metal wreath decorated with oak leaves, symbolizing eternity, a laurel branch and a bronze plaque bearing the inscription: “A bow to the ground before the genius Shevchenko from the Moscow Art Theatre.” The Moscow Art Theatre was touring Kyiv at the time. From then on, its actors spent every summer living communally at a nearby hamlet beside Taras Hill, drawing inspiration from the place. Among them were Ivan Moskvin, Yevgeny Vakhtangov and Mikhail Chekhov. The Ukrainian Club was shut down in 1912. I examined the leaves from the theatre’s wreath in a museum display case. They have survived two world wars and are now enduring Russia’s invasion. The Museum in a bomb shelter Few original exhibits remain on display at the museum. The most valuable surviving objects have been moved to a secure location to protect them from bombing. “Kaniv, and particularly the Kaniv Hydroelectric Power Plant, has come under fire more than once. But our academic council collectively decided not to evacuate anything outside the country,” says Hanna Manzhara, the museum’s senior collections curator. She is 80 and cannot imagine her life apart from the museum. “We resumed work in July 2022 because the number of visitors kept growing. That was such an incentive! We moved the exhibition to the basement, which had been converted into a bomb shelter. At the beginning of this year, we returned to the surface, to the galleries.” Unlike monuments in Kyiv, Shevchenko’s memorial in Kaniv has not been covered with sandbags. It is not simply a sculpture but a burial mound with a crypt inside, a place where people come to pay their respects. Yet Russian forces have also struck cemeteries: in Cherkasy in July 2025, in Odesa in October 2024 and in Kramatorsk in April 2023. Hanna Ivanivna Manzhara, senior collections curator. Photograph: Olga Musafirova Ukrainian Culture Days in Moscow The conversation naturally turns to Russia. The Moscow and St. Petersburg periods of Shevchenko’s life and work cannot simply be erased from his story. Hanna Manzhara recalls taking part in Ukrainian Culture Days in Moscow in 2003, together with Vita Dzyma, a senior researcher. “The Ukrainian Center on Arbat Street asked us to take part. “We brought an exhibition featuring lifetime editions of individual poems, as well as publications from 1911 and 1914, marking the 50th anniversaries of his birth and death. We added woven Ukrainian folk towels made by Marуsia Vasylashchuk, a traditional craftswoman. The response was fantastic! Teachers from Moscow came, along with members of the Ukrainian diaspora. Our fellow museum professionals were particularly remarkable in the attention they gave us.” “And, of course, there were collectors,” Dzyma continues. “I won’t name them; we lost contact a long time ago. But copies of Moscow newspapers reporting on Taras Shevchenko’s funeral found their way to Kaniv through antique shops on Arbat Street. “The museum was preparing for reconstruction, and we were trying to build up our collection.” Manzhara adds: “You see, the life and work of the Kobzar are far broader than anything we ourselves could convey to an audience.” Dzyma has a similar story. In the family of the St. Petersburg literary scholar Ieremiya Aizenshtok, a self-portrait of 16-year-old Taras was discovered, dating from the time he served as Engelhardt’s personal attendant, or kazachok . Research and evidence suggested it was the earliest portrait of the Kobzar . “But Aizenshtok’s relatives asked for a very high price. The Kaniv museum simply couldn’t afford it. What happened to the portrait, and who owns it now, is unknown.” At that moment, the author’s phone begins to vibrate: an air-raid alert has been issued in Kyiv. On social media, Russian military personnel who have spent nearly five years launching missiles, including at Ukrainian museums, are sarcastically dubbed “Pushkinists.” Among the institutions hit have been the Hryhorii Skovoroda Museum in Skovorodynivka, the Kupiansk Museum of Local History and the Odesa Fine Arts Museum . A Shrine to an Icon: The Museum Under Soviet Rule “Now the working people of Ukraine and the Soviet Union will be able to become more familiar with the great legacy of the poet-revolutionary, a fighter against the social and national oppression that weighed so heavily on the peoples of the former tsarist Russia,” the republican newspaper Kommunist wrote in 1936. The newspaper recalled that in 1923, a temporary monument had been erected over Shevchenko’s grave “in place of the cross so hated by the poet and all working people,” and that a temporary exhibition had been set up nearby in 1934. At the same time, construction of a museum was underway on Taras Hill. Visitors often ask why the Soviet authorities invested so heavily in the project during the Holodomor, the famine that devastated Ukraine. It was the first building in Ukraine designed specifically to house a museum. Until then, museums had generally occupied historic aristocratic or manor houses. Vita Dzyma offers an explanation: “Look around: every home had a portrait of Shevchenko – embroidered, painted, burned into wood or assembled from straw. Kobzar lay beside the Bible, or took its place when the campaign against religion began. “The villages at the foot of Taras Hill were being starved to death. People hired themselves out to work on the construction site for a piece of bread. They carried stones by hand, as in ancient Egypt. Yet they were proud of their work. The Shevchenko Museum was no less than a temple. “Arguing with Ukrainians about this is a losing battle. Taras is both a father and a prophet!” Vita Dzyma, senior researcher at the museum. Photograph: Olga Musafirova A sculptural composition of Lenin and Stalin was installed in the entrance hall, while Shevchenko’s bust was moved to the second floor so that it would not compete with them. According to Dzyma, whose account is supported by research, Soviet propagandists in the 1930s seriously pursued the idea of finding a physical resemblance between Lenin and Shevchenko. The burial mound was given an upgrade, too. Behind a granite balustrade at the base of the monument, a platform was built resembling the speaker’s tribune at Lenin’s Mausoleum, intended for members of the Ukrainian Communist Party’s Politburo. In 1939, marking the 125th anniversary of the Kobzar’s birth, Nikita Khrushchev, the first secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine, spoke at the opening of the museum and the unveiling of the new monument. “The tradition of placing microphones beside Shevchenko and addressing the community as if speaking on his behalf, from his elevated position, has survived to this day,” Hanna Manzhara explains. The museum under nazi occupation: Director Dmytro Lebedko In mid-August 1941, the last train carrying mobilized troops left Kaniv across the bridge over the Dnipro. The bridge was bombed, and its ruins can still be seen from Taras Hill. There was no time to evacuate the museum before the Nazi occupation. Its staff scattered. The women I spoke to avoid going into detail about what happened next. “It would be disrespectful to the local residents,” they say. Dmytro Lebedko, a former librarian at the reserve who had been mobilized into the Red Army and survived the bombing of his train, found himself in two roles at once: collaborator, having agreed to work with the occupying forces, and preserver of the museum’s collection. The Nazis did not close the museum. Instead, they ordered it to be put in order and kept open. Visitors, mostly German soldiers, were brought through in formation. For the first time, not a single entry appeared in the visitors’ book. The local population was afraid to visit Taras Hill, even though in the nearby district center of Horodyshche, the Nazis had toppled a statue of Karl Marx and replaced it with one of Shevchenko. Archival documents preserve Lebedko’s testimony: “In 1941, I managed to recover from the village of Pekari 15 chairs, about 2,000 books, two carpets embroidered with portraits of Shevchenko, six silk curtains and a number of other valuables.” After becoming director, he carried out a full inventory of the museum’s collection, cataloguing 4,000 items. He was not afraid to compile a list of paintings and drawings that the local Nazi district commissioner had supposedly taken for “temporary use.” He also recorded every vase and carpet appropriated by yet another official with an interest in “Slavic exoticism.” Then he took a risk that could have cost him his life: he moved the most valuable objects into a hiding place, sealed it behind a wall and went into hiding himself. After Soviet troops arrived, Lebedko still managed to help restore the museum, which the Nazis had ransacked shortly before retreating. He voluntarily admitted in court to having been involved in a “Ukrainian nationalist Bandera organization.” The authorities demanded that he strengthen his self-incriminating statement. “I thought Soviet rule would no longer exist in Ukraine and that Ukraine would become independent. I now understand the serious political error in my views,” he was made to say. He was convicted of treason and sentenced to the maximum term. Three years later, he died in the Norilsk labor camps from a perforated stomach ulcer. Dmytro Lebedko was 47, the same age as Taras Shevchenko. His name was erased from the history of the reserve for decades. Museum staff emphasize that only 10 exhibits from the prewar collection have survived to this day. Yanukovych’s makeover Toward the end of Leonid Kuchma’s presidency, plans emerged for a major restoration project in Kaniv. A nationwide fund was established specifically to restore historical and architectural heritage sites, and UkrNDIproektrestavratsiya, a Ukrainian research and design institute specializing in restoration, was selected to develop the project. Its specialists proposed returning the building to its original appearance, based on the drawings of architect Vasyl Krychevsky. In the 1930s, Krychevsky had been unable to realize his full vision. His design was deemed “too Ukrainian,” and both he and his closest student, Petro Kostyrko, were removed from the project. The construction was completed by more compliant hands. As a result, museum staff, whose building had received no major restoration since World War II, were afraid even to express their hopes aloud. The project stalled, then resumed under President Viktor Yanukovych. According to those involved, the massive, even pompous building made a strong impression on him. If the museum was to host the annual Shevchenko National Prize ceremony, Ukraine’s highest state award for achievements in culture and the arts, it had to meet the president’s aesthetic standards. Few understood Yanukovych’s tastes better than Hanna Herman, one of his closest allies, a member of parliament from the Party of Regions and head of its humanitarian policy team, and her protégé, architect Larysa Skoryk. “History repeated itself,” Vita Dzyma says. “At the final stage, UkrNDIproektrestavratsiya was removed from the project, and the national character of the design was discarded. ‘No painted decoration on the exterior – this isn’t some village hut!’ they said. But the preparatory work for the majolica facade had already been completed. The same was true of the alfresco work – the decorative painting in relief. “The Ministry of Culture’s scientific and methodological council convened and decided: whitewash it!” Hanna Manzhara adds: “Even the surviving fragments of Krychevsky’s original work, which had miraculously survived the previous war and were rediscovered during the restoration, were covered up again.” Skoryk developed a stripped-down design concept. The polychrome landscape inspired by the poem Haidamaky was replaced with a monochrome version. The original coffered ceiling was concealed behind a stretch ceiling. Red lines of Shevchenko’s poetry ran across the gray fabric like information scrolling through a subway station. Glass replaced the wooden mosaic partitions in the entrance hall, while granite slabs took the place of parquet flooring. “We wanted at least to restore the unique botanical and floral patterns on the columns. “Both museum staff and Krychevsky’s relatives wrote to Yanukovych. It made no difference. What we got was a gray-and-white renovation,” Dzyma concludes. She asks whether the author noticed the granite boulder at the entrance, in the center of the lobby. The author is puzzled. Surely this is not a geological museum. ▇ “Shevchenko is the cornerstone of the national idea. It’s a metaphor!” Photographs From 1944 and a Forced-Labor Camp in the Museum The author’s attention was drawn to two framed photographs on the wall, dated the last day of January 1944. Yakov Davidzon, a frontline correspondent, arrived at Taras Hill immediately after Kaniv was liberated. He found the museum surrounded by barbed wire, with burned books, torn paintings and shattered sculptures. Sixteen shrapnel wounds had been counted on the pedestal of Shevchenko’s monument. “We learned only in 1981 that a forced-labor camp had operated inside the museum during the final months of the occupation,” says Valentyna Avramenko, head of the Tarasova Svitlytsia section. She recalls a visitor from Moscow who wandered through the galleries as if he knew every corner of the building. It turned out that he was a native of the area who, as a teenager, had been caught in a roundup. Young people were deported to the Reich for forced labor, while children as young as 13 or 14 were made to dig trenches and build fortifications. Several hundred schoolchildren were held inside the building, half-starved, sleeping on damp, rotting straw alongside horses. A toilet had been hacked directly into the parquet floor. Armed guards marched the children to the banks of the Dnipro with shovels and forced them to work under gunpoint. If one escaped, the others were beaten almost to death. Staff at the reserve began tracking down the former child prisoners and recording their testimonies. Those who had survived long enough were later helped to submit applications for compensation from Germany. Why had no one spoken about the camp sooner? The author found the answer herself in an archival leaflet issued by the Taras Shevchenko partisan unit, which operated in the forests of the Cherkasy region: “We will find and kill everyone who helps the Germans build defensive lines along the Dnipro!” Makohon’s bust: From Kaniv to Volodarka In Davidzon’s second photograph, Shevchenko’s bust has a bullet hole in its forehead. The resemblance to the monument in Borodianka, shot up by Russian forces in 2022, is chilling . The author was told that Ivan Makohon, a prominent Soviet Ukrainian sculptor, had created the plaster bust in 1937 specifically for the opening of the museum in Kaniv. But the work’s fate after World War II remains unknown. It is held neither in the museum’s exhibition nor in the collection of Ukraine’s National Art Museum. The sculptor’s son, Ihor Makohon, himself a painter, sculptor and graphic artist, is now 90 and lives in Italy. He was surprised to hear the story of the wounded, missing Kobzar . “There must be some misunderstanding! I visited Kaniv in the mid-1950s and took photographs. The bust was on the second-floor balcony, completely undamaged. “In 1961, my father decided to modify the composition slightly, adding shoulders. The new version was more monumental. Two plaster casts were made in the workshop at the Kyiv Art Institute, where Professor Makohon taught, and the mold was preserved.” More than 60 years passed. In 2024, Ihor Makohon received a request from Volodarka, a district center in the Kyiv region. Local residents wanted to install a “historic” Shevchenko monument by Makohon and asked for his permission. Ihor Ivanovych not only found the original mold but also arranged for the bust to be produced. “We cast the bust in concrete with the lads and took it to Volodarka. There was enormous interest, and a lot of people gathered,” he recalls. The unveiling took place on the Feast of the Intercession of the Holy Mother of God, which Ukraine also celebrates as the Day of Defenders and Defendresses. The project fulfilled an idea conceived by Oleksandr Ushynskyi, a local resident, environmentalist, researcher of the Holodomor, Maidan protester and war veteran. In 2014, Ushynskyi volunteered for the front, defended Donetsk airport and later established a community museum dedicated to the Russian-Ukrainian war in his hometown. The monument in Volodarka became the 1,385th monument to Shevchenko in Ukraine and around the world. The nazis, the communists and Russian propaganda “Both the Nazis during World War II and the Soviets used Shevchenko to manipulate Ukrainians’ minds for propaganda purposes,” says Ihor Solovey, head of the Center for Strategic Communications and Information Security under Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture. “The Nazis tried to exploit our national sentiments under the guise of ‘friendship.’ “They took passages from Kobzar and amplified them to turn people against Soviet rule. The message was supposedly about resistance to Russian oppression, mixed with all sorts of vile nonsense about ‘Jewish Bolshevism.’ They even put Taras’s words on posters – the familiar line: ‘Muscovites are strangers; they bring you harm.’ “To present themselves as benefactors, the Nazis deliberately published his poetry and prose during the occupation and ran articles about Shevchenko that served their purposes. They wanted people to believe that Ukrainian culture was free and flourishing under the Reich.” “The Communists did exactly the same thing. They just dressed it up differently to persuade Ukrainians to fight the Germans. Think of the famous rallying cry: ‘Drench freedom in the enemy’s blood!’” Solovey continues. Eighty years have passed. In June 2026, Ukraine’s Security Service announced that a 57-year-old woman from Kaniv had been formally notified of suspicion over the dissemination of “materials justifying and denying the Russian Federation’s armed aggression against Ukraine.” The woman reportedly referred to the invasion as a “special military operation,” urged support for the Russian army and openly promoted pro-Kremlin narratives among acquaintances and colleagues. According to investigators, she was one of the deputy heads of the Shevchenko National Reserve. Modern Russian propaganda reproduces methods first used under the Russian Empire and later adopted by the Soviet Union. One is to present Shevchenko primarily as part of Russian culture, pointing to the fact that he wrote his diaries and prose in Russian. Another is to portray him as a “pan-Russian poet,” downplaying the importance of his work in shaping Ukrainian national identity. But those carrying out Russia’s full-scale war on Ukrainian soil increasingly see Shevchenko, his monuments and his museums not as shared cultural heritage, but as an adversary and a source of resistance. exchange

title: Even birds get jet lagged, study shows
body:
Manx shearwaters race back to their nests after spending weeks hunting at sea. New research suggests they get jet lagged on their journey home. birdsonline/Getty images hide caption
New research shows that humans are not the only species to get jet lag: Some birds appear to experience it too.
A study published in the journal Science found that a type of seabird known as the Manx shearwater appears to become slightly disoriented during long flights across the Atlantic Ocean. That disorientation, the authors say, is due to the bird's internal clock falling out of sync with the sun's position in the sky.
Manx shearwaters are a common bird in the British Isles. They look a little like seagulls, but "they're actually very closely related to an albatross," said Patrick Lewin, a behavioral ecologist at the University of Oxford.
Shearwaters mate for life, and when they breed, a couple lays just one egg.
Then they take turns incubating it: "One partner will sit on the egg nonstop while the other one goes out to sea," Lewin said.
For up to two weeks the hunting partners scour the North Atlantic for fish and squid, often travelling hundreds of miles from their nests.
Once these birds' bellies are full "they absolutely bomb it back to their colony," Lewin said. Often they make the long journey home in just a day or so.
Which raised an interesting question: Do Manx shearwaters feel jet lag (or perhaps more aptly, flap lag)?
To see if these little birds really did feel the effects of flying through time zones like humans do, Lewin used a remarkable tool – for 20 years, his colleagues had been tagging birds with GPS trackers and collecting data on their flights out to the Atlantic and back.
He figured he could see the jet lag in their flights. That's because the Manx shearwaters are believed to use the sun to navigate.
"To use the sun as a compass you have to know what time of day it is," Lewin said.
In the morning, the sun is in the east, at midday it's slightly to the south (if you're in the northern hemisphere) and then in the evening it's in the west. If the shearwaters had the wrong time of day, they would fly the wrong way.
That's exactly what Lewin and his colleagues saw. As the birds rushed back to their partners and eggs, they veered ever-so-slightly off course. It wasn't much: A seven-degree error, the maximum deviation observed, only took a bird out of its way by about three miles on a 600-mile journey. "It's a really small addition," he said.
"This paper is so cool," said Alice Boyle, a biologist at the Centre for Animals on the Move at Western University in Ontario, Canada who was not part of the study.
Boyle said pretty much every creature on the planet, from corals to chipmunks, has to navigate its environment, yet it's rare to see a study showing navigation decisions in action. That's what makes this type of GPS work so valuable.
"It's using these wild birds that travel to completely remote places and we're able to learn so much about how they do that," she said.
