title: Ukraine should not agree to limits on size of its armed forces – Admiral Bauer
body:
He made the remarks in an interview with Ukrinform on the sidelines of a special event hosted by the Brussels office of the Kyiv Security Forum.
"I think there's two elements that are extremely important when it comes to a just peace. One is that Ukraine remains a truly sovereign state, which can decide its own future and its alliances. And that means credible Armed Forces. That means the ability to run the country as the people of Ukraine want. All these demands from Russia that there shouldn't be credible Armed Forces in Ukraine are unacceptable," Bauer said.
He added that, second, there must be credible means of deterring the aggressor from invading again.
"People often talk about security guarantees, but there should be credible deterrents to make sure that Russia understands that, if they try again, they will fail," the Dutch admiral said.
In his opinion, unless these two conditions are met, it is highly unlikely that Ukraine will be able to accept any peace settlement proposal.
He believes that even territorial concessions could form part of a settlement, but only if the two conditions outlined above are met.
"Also, it's not about giving away lands. You could say that you are accepting that you have no control over these territories, but you're not accepting that they are Russian. No de jure recognition. It's only accepting the situation only to end the war," he said.
At the same time, drawing on the experience of the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Bauer believes it is unlikely that anything short of a mechanism as close as possible to Article 5 of the NATO Treaty would be an acceptable option.
Speaking about the security of the entire European continent, the admiral also said that Ukraine must genuinely become "part of our security in the larger sense, when it comes to Europe."

title: Modi'in Mayor Haim Bibas calls for Netanyahu-Eisenkot unity government, warns against new elections
body: Modi'in-Maccabim-Reut Mayor Haim Bibas called for a broad national unity government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot following inconclusive election results, warning against another round of elections and calling for a thorough investigation into allegations of Qatari funding in Israel's Arab sector, he told 103FM.The election results failed to produce a clear victory for either political bloc. Will politicians seek to form a unity government? Bibas, who also serves as chairman of the Federation of Local Authorities in Israel, spoke with Eli Ohana and Barak Seri on 103FM about the election results and addressed allegations of foreign Qatari funding within the Arab sector.Bibas addressed the controversy surrounding alleged Qatari funding within Arab society on election day and drew his conclusions."Justice Solberg made a very correct decision, especially in light of what the Shin Bet said. This needs to be investigated thoroughly. Any foreign money entering the country with the aim of creating chaos within the State of Israel requires us to address the problem at its root," he said."We must not give up or stop. Qatar is active not only in Israel but also in the US, and everywhere it is working to create chaos. We do not want to become Paris. We see what is happening in Paris and what is happening in Barcelona. We must not reach that point. All these warning signs should alert everyone. Even if we hold another election, we will end up in the same place. This is the time for broad national unity, with shared goals concerning the economy, security and military enlistment. We are not living on some Riviera. We live in the Middle East."Bibas went on to call for unity between the two political blocs, arguing that a government should have a Zionist majority and reflect the will of the people."There is no outright right-wing victory here, and there is no outright left-wing victory. The government must be built first and foremost on the two central pillars, Likud and Yashar! Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot. Under that framework, we need to bring in all the Zionist forces, B'Yachad, Religious Zionism, and also parts of the haredi community that understand the need to build a foundation of trust and formulate a military draft law. We need to build that structure, including the haredi parties, unequivocally."'Build a foundation of trust'Regarding the more extreme parties on both the Right and Left, Bibas explained:"They always say that extremists in a broad government look for a way out. Either they understand that they need to come in and fall into line, or they will ultimately remain outside. Extremism is not what should lead us. It has brought us to where we are. Do you think Arab society turned out to vote in such large numbers for no reason? Someone made them understand that they were in a state of emergency."Bibas then outlined his interpretation of the election results and what he believed should happen next."Ultimately, the number of seats won in the Arab sector leaves us with one of two possibilities: a unity government or new elections. In the end, something happened here that made it clear to everyone that there is no outright right-wing victory and no outright left-wing victory. Either we have a broad national government, or we go to another round of elections. Those are the implications of the results.""If I were making the decision now, I would sit down with Likud representatives and Eisenkot's people to build trust and establish a joint framework, with the aim of creating a broad, national, Zionist government that would ultimately address the issues that most Israeli citizens expect us to address."Bibas also discussed the common ground that Netanyahu and Eisenkot would need to establish."We need to build a foundation of trust, without a doubt. We need to establish trust with the necessary guarantees. If there is no foundation of trust, then it is new elections and goodbye to everyone. I think the interest of the other side, at this moment, before everything settles, is to build a framework with a very clear process: establishing trust, building the necessary structures and defining the central goals, and examining the issues.""There cannot be a situation in which any segment of the public is not sharing the burden. Ultimately, that is what the entire public expects: that those who contribute and serve are placed at the top of the pyramid. It does not matter which sector they come from. When they are there, they receive the benefits, and then you build the incentive."

title: Apple’s new laptop supports one of the coolest features for color pros
body:
The new MacBook Pro brings with it a bunch of firsts for Apple laptops, the two flashiest being an OLED display and touchscreen functionality. But as an image-accuracy enthusiast, trained calibrator, and resident display expert, what excites me most about the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is the technology it uses to display an accurate picture. It’s the first laptop, and only the second product overall, to support Apple CMF 2026 color modes. It could be the future for displays.
CMFs, or color-matching functions, mathematically represent how we perceive color, and there are a few different variations. The specification that’s been the standard for years is CIE 1931 (CIE stands for Commission Internationale de l’Éclairage, or International Commission on Illumination). For nearly a century, CIE 1931 has been a reliable calibration target, and most of the reference modes on the new MacBook use it.
But with the development of new display technologies over the past 20 years that have ultra-narrow band spectra — such as OLED, LEDs with KSF phosphors, and quantum dots — CIE 1931’s shortcomings are increasingly apparent. Even when calibrated to the same D65 white point, the same image on an OLED and quantum dot LED can look identical to one person, but different to another because of biological variations in our eyes. We all have small discrepancies in our eyes — such as the sensitivity of the cones in our eyes, which allow us to see color — and those can change as we age. CIE 1931 doesn’t properly handle that and was created based on only 17 test subjects. It’s not ideal in a professional setting where content needs to look the same regardless of the screen technology it’s on or who’s viewing it. Apple CMF 2026 addresses that, so that displays look the same regardless of the technology they use.
Apple first included its new CMF on the Studio Display XDR, which I reviewed earlier this year and found to be an excellent, albeit expensive, monitor for color professionals because of Apple CMF 2026 and the reference color modes. But the fact that this technology is now on a laptop that’s portable and not just a standalone monitor living on a desk is a big help for professionals on the move.
As on the Studio Display XDR, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has two Apple CMF 2026 reference modes — one for P3 color primaries and one that includes both P3 and Adobe RGB color primaries for more flexibility. Peak brightness with both HDR and SDR content is 2,000 nits (on the XDR monitor peak SDR luminance is up to 1,000 nits), and the True Tone setting automatically adjusts HDR tone mapping, brightness, and white point based on ambient lighting. (An option to disable True Tone is in Displays preferences.)
The MacBook doesn’t require using Apple CMF 2026, as there are 14 more reference color modes that use the CIE 1931 color space — it is still the standard, after all — including DICOM for medical imaging (which is cool, but only useful to those in the medical field). The MacBook also supports Apple Pro Display Calibrator, which includes three calibration methods to adjust the reference color modes, or a custom mode, if necessary. There are options for a full calibration or to fine-tune a calibration with the proper measurement gear, or to visually fine-tune the display.
Color science and display technologies have come a long way since 1931, when the CIE 1931 color space was established. Apple’s development of the Apple CMF 2026 and its standardization efforts — the company is currently working with a CIE technical committee on a proposed standard — is an important step to make sure current display technologies look the same to as many people as possible.
Extending support to the new MacBook expands the user base considerably (let’s face it, more people are buying a touchscreen MacBook, even at $2,900, than a $3,300 professional monitor). And more importantly, it gives professionals that can get the most out of it easier, portable access.

title: Melania Trump hopes humanitarian operation in Alyoshki will help resolve Ukraine conflict
body:
WASHINGTON, October 29. /TASS/. US First Lady Melania Trump hopes the humanitarian operation in the town of Alyoshki, in the Kherson Region, will help resolve the Ukraine conflict.
"Humanitarian leaders en route to Alyoshki. Let’s remain united in support and wish them safety as they approach Alyoshki. May this humanitarian mission end the suffering and begin a new chapter of durable peace between Russia and Ukraine," she wrote on X.
The Russian Defense Ministry reported that, as of 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27, the Russian Armed Forces had ceased fire on the Kherson front and established a "regime of silence" in preparation for a humanitarian operation near Alyoshki.
Earlier, Russia and Ukraine, with the assistance of US First Lady Melania Trump, agreed to a ceasefire in Alyoshki to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid and prepare for the evacuation of civilians through a designated safe corridor.
Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki critical on September 21. Shelling and drone attacks by Kiev have rendered the delivery of food and medicine to the town impossible. Just over 1,000 of Alyoshki’s former 20,000 residents remain in the town.

title: Asene farmers demand compensation for farms destroyed by Accra-Kumasi expressway
body: More than 200 farmers at Akyem Asene, near Oda in the Eastern Region, have appealed to the government to pay them adequate compensation for their farms and plantations destroyed to make way for the construction of the new Accra-Kumasi expressway. The affected properties include cocoa farms, food crop farms and oil palm plantations, which the farmers say were their main sources of livelihood. The farmers, some of whom wore red pieces of cloth around their heads, necks and arms, staged a demonstration through some principal streets of Asene before gathering at the Asene durbar ground to address the media. Leaders of the affected farmers, including Kofi Koranteng Sarpong, Yaw Peprah, Da Costa Asamoah and Yaw Ampomah Asiedu, took turns to describe the economic hardships they have endured since their farms were destroyed more than eight months ago. They said the loss of their farms had made it difficult to meet their daily needs and pay the school fees of their children in tertiary institutions. Mr Asamoah said he had struggled financially since his eight-acre cocoa farm was destroyed in February 2026. He said the farm had previously earned him an average annual income of about GH¢40,000. Mr Koranteng Sarpong, meanwhile, expressed concern that the farms of more than 20 affected farmers, including his own, had not been measured by surveyors to determine the extent of the damage and the compensation due to them. When contacted by the Daily Graphic , the Head of the Ghana Highway Authority (GHA) survey team for the project, Samuel Tieku, confirmed that some of the destroyed farms had not been measured to assess the extent of the damage. He explained that the original width of the expressway was 120 metres but had been increased to 150 metres, a change that had affected additional farmers.

title: Divided by Party, United in Suffering: Ghana’s dilemma of blind partisan loyalty
body: There is something deeply troubling about the way politics has come to occupy Ghana’s public space. Every morning, from television and radio programmes to conversations in taxis, offices and homes, we encounter the same political theatre. The government of the day says one thing, the opposition holds press conference to say another, their supporters then rush to defend, accuse and counter-accuse one another over who has mismanaged the country more. And somewhere in the middle of all this noise is the ordinary citizen, struggling with unemployment, rising living costs, inadequate public services and the daily uncertainty of making ends meet. The concern is not simply that Ghana is politically divided. It is that partisan loyalty increasingly shapes our understanding of right and wrong, our tolerance for poor governance and our willingness to demand accountability from those entrusted with public office. This is where I juxtapose Karl Marx’s famous description of religion as the “opium of the masses” to offer an interesting lens through which to examine Ghanaian partisan politics. Marx, the German philosopher and economist, used opium as a metaphor for something that provides comfort amid suffering while potentially distracting people from the conditions responsible for that suffering. The argument was not merely that religion was harmful, but that it could through its teachings make suffering more bearable without necessarily changing its underlying causes. A similar argument can be made about partisan politics and the particular version of democracy we practice here in Ghana. It is no doubt that political parties (the NDC and the NPP) are essential to representative democracy. They represent competing ideas, offer alternatives to voters, mobilise citizens and create opportunities for peaceful changes in government. But there is an issue when political loyalty consistently interferes with independent judgement. In Ghana, partisan identification provides many people with a sense of belonging, identity and emotional reassurance. It gives supporters a political community and the feeling that their preferred party represents their interests. But when that attachment becomes unconditional, it can numb their response to wrongdoing. Imagine a scenario where a former or serving government official is facing allegations of corruption, mismanagement or questionable conduct. Party communicators and supporters rush to defend the individual, question the credibility of the investigating institutions or redirect attention to the conduct of a previous or opposing administration. An allegation involving a member of one party quickly becomes an opportunity for the other to revisit controversies from its own time in office. The familiar questions follow; Who started the problem? Which government borrowed more? Which administration built more roads? Who was more corrupt? I mean, these are legitimate questions in a functioning democracy. Historical context matters, and governments should be assessed against their predecessors where appropriate. However, comparisons should clarify responsibility, not erase it. The fact that a previous government committed similar mistakes does not absolve the current government. Likewise, criticism of an incumbent administration should not automatically become a defence of its predecessor. A country cannot make meaningful progress if every demand for accountability is met with a counter-accusation. The Ghanaian political scene also interestingly operates through the psychology of the divide trap. This is the tendency for citizens to become so invested in political groups that the success or failure of their side influences how they interpret reality. When political identity becomes deeply embedded in one’s sense of self, criticism the party can feel like criticism of one’s own community or identity. This creates an “us versus them” mentality. When our side succeeds, we celebrate it as evidence of competence. When the opposing side succeeds, we search for reasons to diminish its achievements. When our party faces allegations of wrongdoing, we demand evidence and caution. When the opposing party faces similar allegations, we demand immediate punishment. The same action can therefore be interpreted differently depending on who performs it. This is the divide trap, reinforced by partisan motivated reasoning. People tend to accept information that confirms their political beliefs while dismissing information that challenges them. Over time, the question becomes less about whether something is true and more about whether it benefits their political side. Instead of political parties being accountable to citizens, citizens begin to feel accountable to political parties. Instead of asking, “Is this government doing the right thing?” we ask, “What will this mean for our party?” Instead of asking whether an allegation is credible, we ask who is being accused. Rather than asking how the country can improve, we focus on how our side can defeat the other in the next election. That is where partisan politics begins to resemble a drug to which we have become addicted. Political arguments become emotionally satisfying while the material problems generating our frustrations remain unresolved. A young person struggling to find employment may spend hours defending a political party online. A family facing rising living costs may spend an evening arguing about which government is responsible. A citizen frustrated by poor public services may defend an official simply because that official belongs to the party they support. The irony is difficult to ignore. We can be fiercely committed to defending political leaders while complaining about the very conditions their decisions, or those of their predecessors, helped create. One of the most troubling consequences of the divide trap is the transformation of accountability into a political weapon. An investigation involving political opponents is celebrated as evidence that the rule of law is working. A similar investigation involving political allies is described as persecution, witch-hunting or political victimisation. Political influence can exist within investigations, and not every allegation proves wrongdoing. Due process, credible evidence and the presumption of innocence are fundamental principles of justice. But these principles must apply consistently, regardless of political affiliation. If we believe in due process, we must believe in it when our opponents and our allies are investigated. If we believe corruption should be punished, we must demand accountability regardless of the political colours of those involved. If public officials should be held accountable, we cannot suspend that principle whenever an official belongs to our preferred party. Otherwise, we are not defending principles. We are defending our side. Public officials are not private representatives of party supporters. They exercise public authority and use public resources. Their primary obligation is to the Ghanaian people and the laws of the Republic, not to political parties. Political disagreement is a natural and necessary part of democracy. But democracy should be more than a competition between two political camps. A government initiative should not automatically be considered good because our party introduced it, nor should it automatically be condemned because the opposing party introduced it. Policies must be judged on their merits, politicians on their conduct, institutions on their performance and governments on whether their decisions improve people’s lives. Yet political discussion increasingly seems less concerned with these judgements and more concerned with winning arguments for one’s preferred party. From morning radio programmes to television discussions and social media, we debate who said what, who insulted whom, which party is responsible and which administration performed worse. Then tomorrow, we begin again. Meanwhile, the unemployed graduate remains unemployed. The struggling farmer continues to face production challenges. Families confronting rising costs continue to struggle, while citizens waiting for better healthcare, education, roads and public services continue to wait. The political argument has been won, but the problem remains. The contradiction becomes even clearer when a party moves from opposition into government. While in opposition, its supporters demand transparency, accountability, respect for the rule of law and freedom of expression. Yet when that same party assumes power, some of those demands suddenly lose their urgency. The standards used to criticise political opponents are not always applied to political allies. This inconsistency undermines the very democratic principles citizens claim to defend. The problem is not that citizens support political parties. They have every right to believe that one party offers better policies, leadership or vision. The distinction is in whether that support remains open to evidence, criticism and reconsideration. There is a difference between political loyalty and political blindness. There is a difference between defending a policy because one believes it is right and defending it simply because one’s party introduced it. There is also a difference between challenging an allegation because the evidence is inadequate and dismissing it because the accused belongs to one’s political camp. Democracy requires the former, not the latter. Breaking out of the divide trap does not mean abandoning our political parties. It means putting them in their proper place. Parties exist to serve democracy. Democracy does not exist to serve political parties. Our allegiance to Ghana must therefore be greater than our allegiance to any political party. We should be able to admit when our party is wrong, acknowledge when an opposing party introduces a good policy and criticise our preferred government without being accused of working for the opposition. Equally, praising an opposing government should not amount to a betrayal of our political identity. These are not signs of political weakness. They are signs of democratic maturity. The responsibility also extends to the media and political actors. Radio and television discussions should create room for evidence-based debate, meaningful policy analysis and scrutiny of all political parties. Political communicators must recognise that defending a party does not require defending every action taken by its members. Journalists and media platforms must also avoid turning political conflict into entertainment simply because confrontation attracts attention. Citizens deserve discussions that help them understand policies, assess performance and hold public officials accountable, not endless exchanges that deepen political divisions without addressing national problems. Citizens, too, must play their part. We cannot continuously complain about bad governance while rewarding those in realm of affairs with unconditional loyalty. We cannot demand accountability from the government we oppose and excuse the government we support. Our political consciousness should be measured not by how fiercely we defend the NDC or the NPP, but by how consistently we demand honesty, transparency and accountability from whoever holds political power. Regardless of who occupies the presidency, certain questions should remain central to our political conversations. Are young Ghanaians finding meaningful employment? Can families afford a decent standard of living? Can citizens trust public institutions? Can public officials be held accountable? Can the country move beyond the familiar cycle of promises, disappointments, blame and political retaliation? These are questions that should unite us. Yet the divide trap encourages us to see those on the other side of the political divide as enemies rather than fellow citizens who may be experiencing the same frustrations. The NDC supporter and the NPP supporter may disagree passionately because of party identity, yet both may be struggling with the same economic pressures. Both may have children seeking employment. Both may complain about the same roads, schools, hospitals and public services. Their political identities divide them, but their lived realities often unite them. If we fail to recognise this, we risk becoming participants in a political cycle that continually demands our emotional loyalty while offering too little in return. I’m not saying Ghanaians should stop caring about politics. But can we care about politics without allowing politics to control our judgement. Can we support a party without surrendering our conscience? Can we oppose a government without romanticising its predecessor? Can we demand accountability from our own side with the same energy with which we demand it from the other? And can we recognise that the greatest victory in a democracy is not the triumph of one political party over another, but the triumph of citizens over bad governance? Until we do, partisan politics risks remaining “the opium of the us” keeping us emotionally occupied, politically divided and perpetually arguing while the deeper problems of our society remain largely untouched. The question, therefore, is not simply, “Whose side are you on?” It is, “Whose interests are being served?”

title: Ukrainian FM on appointment of Russian national as Assistant Secretary-General: Moscow has ‘mined’ the UN
body:
Heorhiy Tykhy, spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine, has criticized the appointment of a Russian representative to lead the UN’s mine action efforts.
"Moscow has 'mined' the United Nations. Fact 1: After more than a decade of Russian aggression, Ukraine has become the most heavily mined country in the world. Fact 2: A serving Russian ambassador, who has represented the regime throughout the entire full-scale war against Ukraine, has been appointed to lead the UN’s mine action activities. Two facts. One reality," Tykhy wrote on Instagram on Thursday.
The Foreign Ministry questioned how the UN Secretariat "reconciles these two facts, or what results it expects from such a combination."
"Entrusting this responsibility to a representative of an aggressor state is deeply alarming and undermines trust in the United Nations. This appointment confirms what has been known for many years: Russia’s illegal occupation of the Soviet Union’s permanent seat on the UN Security Council is poisoning the entire UN system," the message reads.
Earlier, UN Secretary General António Guterres announced the appointment of Russian ambassador Gleb Desyatnikov as Assistant Secretary-General for Mine Action and Police in the Department of Peacekeeping Operations.

title: Obi To Tinubu: Go Round And Tell Nigerians What You Have Done Or Go Home
body: Gideon Arinze in Enugu The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Mr. Peter Obi, has challenged President Bola Tinubu to tour the country and account for his performance in office before seeking another term in 2027. Obi spoke Thursday in Enugu at the Obi-Kwankwaso Town Hall Meeting, attended by the party’s vice-presidential candidate, Rabiu Kwankwaso. Obi said Nigerians deserved to know what the president had achieved with the funds borrowed and revenue generated by his administration. “Let other candidates move around and tell Nigerians what they will do for them. Your president said he will not campaign across Nigeria. He must come and campaign and tell the people what he has to offer,” he said. Speaking further, he said: “He has been travelling outside the country. Let him take 36 days and go round and say what he has done with billions of dollars borrowed and the ones we earned. “Whoever wants to be president must go round and account for his time. The job requires energy and time. Let him say what he has done before we give him another one.” He added that Nigeria was grappling with hunger, unemployment and insecurity, insisting that the country needed a leader committed to addressing the challenges. Obi further stated that his administration, if elected in 2027, would prioritise national unity, security, employment, healthcare and accountability in the management of public funds. “I will unite Nigeria as president. I will secure Nigeria. I will not be president and someone will kidnap our children, and we will not enter the bush together,” he said. Obi urged Nigerians not to support him because of his ethnic background, but on the basis of his qualifications and commitment to national development while also calling on supporters to mobilise voters ahead of the 2027 general election, urging them to sustain their efforts in promoting the party. In his remarks, a former presidential adviser, Pat Utomi, said Nigeria could become one of the best places to live if genuine change was achieved. “The time is now for genuine change to happen. We need to ensure that people come out massively, vote and defend their votes,” Utomi said. The senator representing Anambra Central, Victor Umeh, described Obi and Kwankwaso as leaders ready to serve the country, urging supporters to mobilise for the election. He said supporters would resist attempts to intimidate them and called on Nigerians to use their votes to express their choices in 2027 while also commending Kwankwaso for his role in strengthening the party’s support in northern Nigeria, expressing confidence in the ticket’s appeal across the country.

title: IMF sets December target to clear Egypt's last programme review
body: The International Monetary Fund said on Thursday a mission has been in Egypt this week to hold talks aimed at reaching a staff-level agreement on the country's economic programme. A draft is to be presented to the IMF's executive board for approval by mid-December. Cairo entered into a 46-month Extended Fund Facility (EFF) programme with the IMF in December 2022. It was supposed to expire in October but has been extended until December 15, 2026. Egypt embarked on its Resilience and Sustainability Framework (RSF) with the fund in 2025. IMF communications director Julie Kozack said the purpose of the visit was to reach a staff-level agreement for the executive board's approval before the EFF expires. “We have a mission in the field right now discussing the reviews, the programme,” she told a news conference. Ms Kozack said the final disbursement would be roughly $2.3 billion. The fund in July completed the seventh review of Egypt's EFF and the second of its RSF programme , which allowed authorities to unlock roughly $1.8 billion in funding at the time. That brought total purchases and disbursements under the two arrangements to about $7.3 billion. Ms Kozack said discussions this week were focused on maintaining a tight monetary policy and a fiscal consolidation plan with the overall aim of preserving Egypt's macroeconomic stability. Beyond the macroeconomic measures, structural reforms will remain a central topic of discussion with the intention of reducing the state's economic footprint, she said. “The goal of these reforms is to ⁠support ​stronger, more private ​sector-led growth in Egypt,” Ms Kozack said. Ms Kozack said priorities remain to accelerate Egypt's divestment programme, implement state ownership policy, level the playing field between public and private sector companies, and improve the business climate. The fund has previously pointed to Egypt as a positive example of how countries can undertake reforms. The IMF said its strong macroeconomic buffers, flexible exchange rate and swift policy response had helped it absorb the effects of the Iran war. The IMF expects Egypt's economy to pick up from 4.4 per cent last year to 5.1 per cent this year, before easing to 4.7 per cent in 2027, according to its World Economic Outlook released this month. Consumer prices are forecast to east from 12.1 per cent in 2025 to 9.4 per cent in 2026, before climbing to 11 per cent next year.

title: Putin talks about upcoming meetings with African leaders
body:
MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin said that tonight and tomorrow he will continue meetings with the heads of African states who arrived for the summit.
The third Russia-Africa summit is taking place in Moscow now. The main multilateral program has already come to an end, and a number of bilateral contacts have already taken place.
"In addition to the plenary sessions of the summit and the Economic and Humanitarian Forum, we had several useful bilateral meetings. Such contacts will continue tonight and tomorrow. Conversations are planned with most of the African leaders who came to our summit," Putin said.

title: Prisons Council explores legal aid for inmates over challenges with appeals
body: The Chairman of the Ghana Prisons Service Council, Apostle Ing. Alexander Nana Yaw Kumi-Larbi, has disclosed plans to explore legal assistance for inmates, following concerns over difficulties in accessing court proceedings and securing legal representation for appeals. He made the disclosure during a familiarisation visit to the Ankaful Prison Complex in the Central Region, where inmates appealed for support in navigating legal processes. Apostle Kumi-Larbi said he was in discussions with more than 100 lawyers who are members of The Church of Pentecost to explore ways of providing legal support to inmates. The visit involved a tour of the various prison establishments and engagements with officers and inmates on welfare, rehabilitation, and operational challenges. During the interaction, inmates expressed gratitude to President John Mahama for the recent presidential amnesty but highlighted difficulties in obtaining court proceedings needed to pursue appeals and accessing legal assistance. Drawing inspiration from the biblical story of Joseph, the Council Chairman encouraged the inmates to remain hopeful and focused on building a better future. He also prayed for both officers and inmates. The delegation visited the prison infirmaries, where Prof. Ernest Yorke, President of the Ghana Medical Association and a member of the Prisons Service Council, offered recommendations on managing available healthcare resources. Prof. Yorke also assured the delegation of his commitment to exploring avenues for additional support to improve healthcare delivery within the facilities. The visit forms part of the Council’s efforts to engage stakeholders, address operational challenges and strengthen rehabilitation and reintegration programmes within the Ghana Prisons Service.

title: Nigeria’s health insurance enrolment rises to 23 million — NHIA
body:
Nigeria’s health insurance enrolment increased to 23.06 million people in the second quarter of 2026, up from 16.2 million in late 2023, the Director-General of the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA), Kelechi Ohiri, has said.
Mr Ohiri disclosed this on Thursday while delivering the keynote address at the 11th Future of Health Conference organised by Nigeria Health Watch in Abuja.
He said enrolment across federal, state and private health insurance schemes grew by 42.35 per cent over the period.
However, Mr Ohiri said increasing enrolment alone would not guarantee access to healthcare or protect Nigerians from financial hardship.
“We constantly face the reality of a difference between an insurance coverage record and genuine financial risk protection,” he said.
“An insurance card in a citizen’s pocket is meaningless if it does not grant immediate access to a functional facility, guarantee essential medicines, protect against catastrophic out-of-pocket expenses, and deliver dignity during medical emergencies.”
Mr Ohiri said the NHIA had introduced measures to help enrollees understand their benefits, access support and hold healthcare providers accountable.
These include the MyNHIA mobile application and an online self-enrolment portal. He said the authority also distributed enrollee charters and benefit package details through interactive QR codes at accredited health facilities nationwide.
According to him, the codes enable enrollees to check the consultations, diagnostic services and medicines covered by their insurance packages.
Mr Ohiri said the NHIA also strengthened its complaints management system to address grievances involving enrollees, healthcare facilities and health maintenance organisations (HMOs).
Mr Ohiri said the NHIA received and tracked 2,209 complaints through social media, telephone calls, walk-in desks, call centres and letters.
He said 82 per cent of the complaints were resolved within 48 hours, adding that the authority secured direct refunds for enrollees who had been improperly charged by healthcare facilities.
The NHIA also issued formal warnings to facilities and delisted providers for persistent non-compliance, he said.
“That is how regulation converts coverage into genuine financial protection,” Mr Ohiri said.
The NHIA boss said the authority was expanding insurance access for vulnerable Nigerians through targeted programmes supported by public subsidies, grants and public-private partnerships.
He said under the Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) Gateway, enrolment increased from 2.6 million people in the second quarter of 2026 to 3.2 million in the third quarter, representing a 20.5 per cent increase.
He added that all the enrollees under the gateway had been biometrically verified using their National Identification Numbers (NINs).
Mr Ohiri also highlighted a programme established in partnership with the Global Fund to provide health insurance coverage for key population groups living with or affected by major infectious diseases in Gombe, Anambra, Ebonyi and Kwara states.
He said enrolment under the programme increased from 25,815 beneficiaries in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 58,447 in the third quarter of 2026.
He said women accounted for 68 per cent of the enrollees, while all beneficiaries had been biometrically verified using their NINs.
The conference, themed “From Innovation to Impact: The Future of Health is Now”, brought together stakeholders to discuss how innovations, investments, research and policies can translate into measurable improvements in healthcare delivery.
Mr Ohiri said health innovations must solve practical problems, generate evidence, remain financially sustainable and become integrated into existing systems to achieve impact at scale.
He said the NHIA’s reforms were intended to build a health financing system that protects Nigerians from financial hardship while improving access to healthcare.
“The future of health is not a distant vision,” he said.
“Through strategic purchasing, rigorous evidence, and commitment to equity, the future of health is happening right now.”
In her remarks, the Managing Director of Nigeria Health Watch, Vivianne Ihekweazu, said Nigeria must look beyond the development of health innovations to the financing, policies, procurement processes and data systems needed to sustain them and expand their reach.
Mrs Ihekweazu said the 11th edition of the conference provided an opportunity to reflect on lessons from more than a decade of discussions on universal health coverage, healthcare financing, technology and the role of the private sector in strengthening Nigeria’s health system.
She said innovations would only deliver meaningful health outcomes if policymakers prioritised scale and sustainability from the outset.
Citing a review of digital innovations in maternal and newborn health in Nigeria, she said none of the 10 interventions examined had achieved sustained scale, largely because they lacked clear ownership within the health system and a pathway into routine service delivery.

title: AAP to INEC: Obey court order on party registration
body: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA – The African Alliance Party (AAP) has urged the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to comply with a court order directing its registration, saying time is running out ahead of the 2027 general election. The party made the demand in a communiqué issued in Abuja on Thursday after a meeting of its National Executive Committee (NEC). Commending the Court of Appeal, Makurdi Division, for its June 11, 2026, judgment, AAP also praised the Supreme Court for striking out INEC’s application for a stay of execution. “NEC commends the Court of Appeal, Makurdi Division, for its judgement of 11th June 2026, which ordered the Independent National Electoral Commission to register the African Alliance Party as a political party, and the Supreme Court for striking out INEC’s frivolous stay of execution paving the way for the registration of AAP,” the communiqué stated. The party urged INEC to expedite the process, stressing that time was running out. “NEC urged INEC to expedite action for the formal registration of AAP as ordered by the appellate court as time is of the essence,” it added. AAP reaffirmed its readiness to participate in the 2027 general election and urged its members nationwide to remain calm and focus on the polls. The party also called on Nigerians to participate actively in the electoral process, vote for candidates of their choice and ensure their votes count in the final results, rather than relying solely on INEC’s Results Viewing Portal (IReV). The post AAP to INEC: Obey court order on party registration appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Russia and Africa to hold exercises to counteract outbreaks of infections — Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Moscow and African countries intend to deepen their health partnership and conduct joint exercises to combat outbreaks of infections, President Vladimir Putin said at a press conference after the Russia-Africa summit.
"I want to emphasize that we also took into account everything said by our African friends about the importance of cooperation with Russia in areas such as healthcare and epidemic control," he said. "We will increase the supply of effective medicines, transfer mobile laboratories, and conduct joint exercises to respond to outbreaks of infections.
"I will mention, in particular, the decision taken to extend the Russian program of assistance to African countries to combat infections until 2029."

Utah has filed criminal charges against Kalshi and its executives, accusing the prediction market of breaking anti-gambling laws, as reported by The Salt Lake Tribune and the Associated Press . The state has filed 14 charges against Kalshi, as well as CEO Tarek Mansour and COO Luana Lopes Lara, including 12 counts of illegally promoting online gambling.
The move marks an escalation in a nationwide battle against prediction market platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket. Utah has already sued Kalshi over claims that it’s operating illegally in the state, joining several other states, including New York , Nevada , New Mexico , Washington , Connecticut , and others, in taking legal action against the company. New York and Kentucky have sued Polymarket as well. In March, Arizona became the first state to file criminal charges against Kalshi, but a federal judge later blocked its case .
In the backdrop of these legal battles, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) is fighting state-level attempts to regulate prediction markets, arguing that it has “exclusive jurisdiction” over the platforms. States recently netted wins with two federal appeals courts ruling against Kalshi and Polymarket’s bid to fight state-level oversight. However, the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in April that the CFTC has the exclusive authority to regulate prediction markets in New Jersey, which recently asked the Supreme Court to take up its case .
Kalshi says Utah’s charges are a “crazy overreach” in a statement provided to the Associated Press , adding: “We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona.”

title: Experts call for wider adoption of proven health innovations in Nigeria
body:
Health experts have called for effective health innovations to be scaled up and integrated into existing health systems to improve healthcare delivery and expand access to essential services in Nigeria.
They made the call on Thursday in Abuja at the 11th edition of the Future of Health Conference, organised by Nigeria Health Watch , where speakers highlighted the importance of evidence, political leadership, community participation and sustainable financing in translating innovations into measurable health outcomes.
The conference, themed “From Innovation to Impact: The Future of Health is Now”, brought together policymakers, health professionals, researchers, innovators and development partners to examine how research, technology, investment and policy can address persistent challenges in the country’s health system.
In her remarks, the Managing Director of Nigeria Health Watch, Vivianne Ihekweazu, said the focus must shift from developing promising solutions to ensuring they reach more people and produce lasting improvements in healthcare.
Mrs Ihekweazu said the conference, established in 2015, had provided a platform for discussions on universal health coverage, health financing, private-sector participation, technology and health workforce challenges.
She said the current edition was an opportunity to examine the barriers preventing effective innovations from being adopted at scale and how partnerships could help overcome them.
According to her, innovations must move beyond discussions and isolated interventions to deliver practical benefits to the population.
In his keynote address, the Director-General of the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA), Kelechi Ohiri, said health innovations must address practical problems, generate evidence, remain financially sustainable and become integrated into existing systems to achieve impact at scale.
Mr Ohiri said the authority’s reforms were aimed at building a health financing system that protects Nigerians from financial hardship while improving access to healthcare.
“The future of health is not a distant vision. Through strategic purchasing, rigorous evidence, and commitment to equity, the future of health is happening right now,” he said.
Also speaking, Erasmus Morah, a senior adviser at the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), said scientific breakthroughs alone would not transform healthcare without political commitment, effective leadership and the involvement of affected communities.
Drawing on his experience in Nigeria and other African countries, Mr Morah said the successful implementation of health interventions depended on the ability to translate evidence into policies and practices that respond to people’s needs.
He illustrated this with Nigeria’s progress in HIV treatment coverage, recalling that coverage was about 33 per cent in 2017 before a national survey helped revise estimates of the number of people living with HIV.
According to him, the Nigerian AIDS Indicator Survey showed that the estimated population of people living with HIV was about 1.8 million, rather than the previously projected 3.2 million.
He said the revised estimates helped reveal gaps in the country’s response and contributed to a change in reported treatment coverage.
Mr Morah argued that reliable data could improve decision-making, but that achieving results also required people willing to challenge established assumptions and ensure that evidence informed policy.
He also recounted his experience in Malawi, where efforts to expand HIV testing required a shift from voluntary testing and counselling to provider-initiated testing and counselling.
The experience, he said, demonstrated the importance of changing policies and delivery approaches when existing methods were failing to reach enough people.
“Science without politics, it’s powerless. Politics without science, dangerous,” he said, urging governments, researchers and communities to work together to implement effective health interventions.
He called for major health innovations to be supported by locally accountable implementation coalitions led by committed champions and shaped by the communities they serve.
Meanwhile, Ifeyinwa Rhodes-Vivour, founder of AfroScientric, highlighted the potential of malaria genomics to help Nigeria develop more targeted interventions against the disease.
She said conventional epidemiological approaches alone might not provide sufficient information about the genetic characteristics of malaria parasites, particularly as drug resistance threatens the effectiveness of existing treatments.
According to her, genomic sequencing can help researchers identify resistance patterns, track parasites and provide policymakers with evidence to guide interventions suited to different locations.
Mrs Rhodes-Vivour said research conducted by her team had identified differences in drug-resistance profiles between malaria parasites in northern and southern Nigeria, underscoring the limitations of applying a uniform approach across the country.
She said the work included a pilot study in Lagos State in 2017 and subsequent national surveys, including a second survey in 2025.
According to her, the team has collected about 32,000 parasite samples through its research, providing data to support the development of targeted malaria interventions.
She also highlighted efforts to reduce the cost of genomic sequencing and make the resulting information more accessible to policymakers through digital tools.
Mrs Rhodes-Vivour said the cost of sequencing had been reduced from about $150 per sample to approximately $20–$24 through laboratory innovations.
She said the team had also developed a dashboard and an artificial intelligence-powered WhatsApp interface to help policymakers access information about malaria drug resistance and make more informed decisions.
The work, she added, demonstrated how research and technology could be adapted to local conditions and made more useful to decision-makers.

title: Russia still hasn’t found an effective way to curb VPNs. Now officials are considering limits on all foreign internet traffic.
body: What happened? On October 27, Forbes reported that Russia’s Digital Development Ministry is considering routing all foreign internet traffic through TSPU filtering equipment (TSPU is the Russian acronym for “technical means of countering threats”), effectively separating the Russian internet from the global internet at a technical level. The measure could primarily affect people who use VPN services to bypass blocks. The plan is to cap the amount of foreign data each user can consume. The proposed limit is not yet known. Several sources told Forbes about the proposals, which will likely be included in a bill to overhaul the telecommunications industry. The authorities have been preparing changes to telecommunications laws since the spring and are discussing specific proposals with major industry players. The Digital Development Ministry stressed that all the proposed measures “are being examined, but it is premature to say which will make it into the final amendments or in what form.” Haven’t there been proposals like this before? Not quite. First, in the spring, the Digital Development Ministry wanted to limit foreign traffic only on mobile networks. Now, the proposal apparently also covers home internet connections. Second, the earlier plan called for telecommunications providers themselves to identify and limit foreign traffic. The ministry asked them to charge users extra if they used more than 15 gigabytes of foreign data a month. BBC News Russian reported that each additional gigabyte would have cost 150 rubles. Now, the ministry plans to impose the restrictions itself using TSPU equipment. What would the authorities gain from this? The Digital Development Ministry intends to use this approach to combat VPNs that allow users to bypass Russian internet blocks. These services are generally based abroad, as are most of their servers. So when users connect to one of these VPNs, all their traffic becomes foreign traffic, even when they visit Russian websites. VPN services could try to rent servers inside Russia to get around the data cap. But this summer, the authorities banned Russian hosting providers from serving them. There are also plans to create a register of violators who have used servers in Russia to run VPNs. If caught bypassing blocks, they will be barred from signing contracts with hosting providers in Russia for a full year. In other words, using Russian hosting infrastructure will become even harder in the future. But for now, too much about the proposal remains unknown, Sarkis Darbinyan , a digital rights lawyer and expert at RKS.global, told Meduza: It’s unclear what exactly the ministry will consider a foreign domain, whether there will be exemption allowlists, and what will happen once the quota runs out: disconnection, slower speeds, or an extra charge. These details will determine whether the measure specifically targets VPNs or affects everyone. How does the ministry plan to identify foreign traffic? We don’t know. Most likely, by IP address. Since 2019, Russia’s communications regulator, Roskomnadzor, has required Russian holders of autonomous system numbers , which identify networks, to report their network addresses and notify the agency of any changes within three business days. Roskomnadzor can use those addresses to determine whether a given data packet came from Russia or abroad. But under this approach, even people who don’t use VPNs could find that some traffic from Russian websites is technically classified as foreign . Much depends on whether individual components of a webpage — fonts, images, or videos — load from foreign sources and exactly how the data is routed. Even traffic from a site with an IP address registered in Russia can pass through nodes abroad. This could happen, for example, because of the particular terms of traffic-exchange agreements between telecommunications providers or because traffic takes alternative routes during network outages. Russia’s internet restrictions Russia has spent a decade trying to stop people from bypassing internet censorship. Now it plans to spend nearly 60 billion rubles over three years on traffic filtering. The Kremlin’s crackdown on VPNs is escalating. Here’s what Meduza readers in Russia have to say about it. Meduza asked four experts to sketch three likely futures for VPNs in Russia. The best possible scenario may be the one Russians are already living in. How would TSPU equipment limit an individual user’s foreign traffic? We don’t know this for certain, either. The difficulty is that TSPU equipment filters data packets that don’t explicitly identify the user they belong to. Only the source and destination IP addresses are visible. That information is not enough to limit a particular person’s foreign traffic: Different subscribers can use the same IP address at different times. Telecommunications providers, however, have the missing information. In the spring of 2025, they were required to give Roskomnadzor comprehensive information about their subscribers, including their assigned IP addresses and the number identifying the specific TSPU device through which each user’s traffic passes. Since December 2025, telecommunications providers have been subject to fines of 300,000 to 500,000 rubles for each failure to provide this information. If the ministry’s proposal is adopted, how will it affect ordinary Russians? For now, we can only speculate. But requiring all foreign traffic to pass through a filter that tracks quotas would clearly make it easier to slow and ration that traffic. This would be another major step in the authorities’ campaign against independent VPNs, and users of those services would be hit hardest, Darbinyan said. Besides finding a working VPN, they would have to decide how best to use their allotted gigabytes of foreign data, choosing between videos, games, social media, and other sites and services unavailable in Russia. Darbinyan said there could be several other consequences: There will be problems with updates. Updates for iOS, Windows, and games can run to tens of gigabytes. A single file could eat up a month’s allowance. “And then,” Darbinyan said, “if you can’t afford an extra international data package, you’re stuck without up-to-date software.” That creates an additional risk: Devices without updates are more vulnerable to scammers and malware, both of which are proliferating with the AI boom. Developers, IT workers, and remote workers will suffer. Using GitHub, Docker Hub, cloud services, Zoom, and Microsoft 365, or working with foreign clients, means using lots of foreign data. “For freelancers, students taking international online courses, and scientists, the restrictions will become an obstacle to their work. Online gaming will probably become a pastime only for the wealthy, who can afford to pay for extra gigabytes, since gaming requires enormous amounts of data,” Darbinyan told Meduza. Still, Darbinyan believes the authorities are unlikely to impose a strict, very low cap on everyone at once: Technically, it’s very difficult, and politically, it’s costly — because it would upset users opposed to the government as well as businesses, the IT industry, and gamers. Most likely, they’ll start with mobile networks, a generous cap, and extensive allowlists, then gradually tighten the restrictions. This measure is also unlikely to make foreign services disappear entirely. The aim, apparently, is to make access to foreign services inconvenient, slow, and expensive so that people switch to Russian alternatives on their own, rather than to cut off access to everything abroad. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. title: Competition Bureau chief urges limits on non-compete clauses for workers
body:
The Competition Bureau of Canada is calling on provincial and territorial governments to limit the use of non-compete agreements in an effort to “foster more competitive labour markets.”
In a letter dated Oct. 29, Interim Commissioner of Competition Jeanne Pratt said the breadth of use of non-compete clauses in Canada is “concerning.”
Non-compete clauses can restrict workers from joining a rival company or starting a competing business for a set period of time after leaving a job.
According to a survey from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Canada has one of the highest prevalence rates of non-compete clauses with employers reporting that between 29 and 39 per cent of private-sector employees fall under them.
Non-compete clauses were designed to target high-level executives, Jon Pinkus, an employment lawyer and partner at Samfiru Tumarkin LLP in Toronto, told Global News.
He said ideally the clauses should only be used for employees who have a “real fiduciary duty” and who “can do real damage if they go to a competitor.”
But the data tells a different story. Among Canadian firms that use non-competes, 30 per cent reportedly apply them to every employee regardless of their role or seniority, according to the OECD.
Pratt argued that widespread use of non-compete clauses can reduce job wages, mobility and entrepreneurship.
According to the OECD, 23 per cent of Canadian workers who report having a non-compete agreement say it has prevented them from changing jobs. Approximately 12 per cent self reported that the agreement prevented them from starting a business.
Despite the prevalence of non-compete agreements, Pinkus said many of them are not enforceable.
“The courts may determine that they are an unreasonable, what we call restraint of trade, and invalidate them on that basis,” he said, adding that the responsibility is on the employer to prove a non-compete is necessary.
But more than 40 per cent of employees operating under a non-compete said they would turn down a competing job even if the agreement was unlikely to be upheld in court, according to the OECD.
The Government of Canada committed in its 2025 budget to restricting the use of non-compete agreements which it said will “protect workers’ rights, promote labour mobility, strengthen competition, and empower workers to move to a higher-paying job or start their own business.”
Ontario was the first and only province to enact a statutory ban on the use of non-compete clauses which it did so in 2021.
The province’s Employment Standards Act prohibits most new employment non-competes, with a few limited exceptions including certain agreements associated with the sale of a business and agreements involving senior executives.

title: Shas officials blame hardline draft stance for one of party’s worst-ever election defeats
body: Shas is facing one of the worst electoral defeats in its history, with party officials blaming its increasingly hardline stance on haredi military enlistment and calling for a fundamental overhaul of the party, as the scale of its losses became clear on Thursday, two days after the election.The party is currently slated to receive six seats in the 26th Knesset.The party, which had grown accustomed to maintaining its political strength and even increasing its support over the years, has suffered a particularly painful electoral blow. In the 2022 election, Shas received 392,964 votes, representing 8.25% of valid ballots, and secured 11 Knesset seats. In the latest election, according to the vote count excluding double-envelope ballots, the party has received only around 275,000 votes, or approximately 5.3% of valid ballots.This represents a loss of roughly 118,000 votes, a decline of about 30% in the number of voters supporting the party. According to estimates within Shas, once the vote count and allocation of seats are completed, the party could fall to as few as six Knesset seats.For Shas, the defeat is especially severe. A party whose electoral base has a high birth rate might reasonably have expected its support to grow naturally, potentially increasing its representation to 12 or even 13 seats. Instead, Shas finds itself facing the prospect of securing barely half the parliamentary representation it had hoped for.The recriminations and soul-searching have now begun. In internal party discussions, sharp criticism is being directed at the political course Shas has pursued in recent years, particularly during the war, regarding haredi (ultra-Orthodox) enlistment and its attitude toward the IDF and the state."Extremist elements have taken control of us," a Shas official said. "Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef led a very hardline and extreme approach on the draft issue, and other rabbis pulled the party in the same direction. We've reached a point where there's no difference between us and the Jerusalem Faction. Is this the Shas we want to be?"The criticism is not directed solely at the rabbis. Some within the party believe the political leadership went along with the growing extremism rather than attempting to restrain it.During the war, Shas MKs were sent to visit haredi men held in military prison after being arrested over draft evasion. There are allegations that the visits were imposed on the MKs and carried out against their wishes.One of the most prominent examples of the approach that drew criticism was a series of statements by Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef opposing military enlistment. Among other things, he called on haredi men not to enlist even if they were not studying Torah and urged them to flush military draft notices down the toilet.His remarks sparked public controversy at a time when IDF soldiers were fighting on multiple fronts, and hundreds of families had lost loved ones.Shas 'revolution'Meanwhile, despite the severe electoral result and reports suggesting he might step down, associates of Shas chairman Arye Deri insist that he has no intention of going anywhere.On the contrary, following one of the worst defeats in Shas's history, Deri intends to lead the party's recovery process himself."We're going to carry out a revolution, a restart of the party," a Shas official said. "We were dragged into extremism, and we're going to shake it off. We'll bring Shas back to what it always was, a party of the Sephardi, haredi and traditional public. It will be a long process, but we're setting out on that path. We've been through difficult times before and recovered. We'll manage to put things right, with God's help."

title: Bauchi governor signs law establishing Alkaleri Mining Institute
body: By Christopher Ameh, Bauchi Bauchi State Governor, Senator Bala Mohammed, has signed into law a bill establishing the Mining Institute Alkaleri, Bauchi State (MIABAS), to promote mining education, develop technical skills and help tackle illegal mining. The development followed the passage of the bill by the Bauchi State House of Assembly, paving the way for the establishment of a specialised institution dedicated to mining education and technical skills development. A statement by the Information Officer of the Ministry of Natural Resources Development, Fatima AbdulKarim, said the governor had also approved the conversion of the Kaura Mineral Processing and Buying Centre at Gwaram village, Alkaleri Local Government Area, into the institute’s temporary site to facilitate its take-off. According to the statement, Mohammed also directed the relocation of the mineral processing and buying centre to Toro Local Government Area. AbdulKarim said the initiative was designed to develop local expertise, equip young people with industry-relevant skills and maximise the economic benefits of the state’s solid mineral resources. She said the institute would offer specialised training in mining, mineral processing, geology and related disciplines, creating opportunities for employment, entrepreneurship and greater local participation in the solid minerals value chain. The statement added that the establishment of MIABAS reflected the state government’s commitment to harnessing its mineral resources for sustainable economic growth and expanding opportunities for residents. Details of the institute’s administrative take-off, academic programmes and admission procedures, it said, would be announced through official channels. The post Bauchi governor signs law establishing Alkaleri Mining Institute appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Odessa rejects ban on Russian-language content
body:
MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The Odessa City Council in southern Ukraine has voted against a moratorium on the public use of Russian-language cultural content, the Strana news outlet reported.
Authorities in several Ukrainian cities, particularly in the west of the country, have already introduced similar bans. However, according to the news outlet, only 18 of the 64 members of the Odessa City Council voted in favor of the proposal. Two abstained, another 21 did not take part in the vote, and the remaining members were absent.
Since 2014, Ukraine has pursued a policy of openly pushing out the Russian language. In 2019, the country adopted a law "On ensuring the functioning of Ukrainian as the state language," which significantly restricted the use of Russian and minority languages in the country. Local authorities have imposed blanket bans on Russian-language works of art, books, films, theater productions and songs. They have also banned the study of Russian in schools and universities and required schoolchildren to speak only Ukrainian during breaks. At the same time, Ukrainians continue to use Russian widely in everyday life, which regularly becomes a source of conflict.
