title: Former Shas minister blames Deri for alienating voters as party drops to six seats
body: Former Shas minister Shlomo Benizri criticized party leader Arye Deri over Shas's disappointing election results, saying the party had lost nearly half its Knesset seats and failed to address the issue of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) military conscription, in an interview with 103FM on Thursday.With 97.3% of the votes counted, Shas had secured just six Knesset seats, prompting widespread disappointment within the party.According to Benizri, "Shas itself was not clear. On the one hand, they went to a Knesset committee with a decision by the Council of Torah Sages to proceed with enlistment through an agreed-upon law. On the other hand, some of the rabbis spoke out sharply against enlistment."Addressing Deri's responsibility for Shas's dismal election performance, Benizri said, "We lost almost 50% of our seats. This is something that is truly traumatic, a shock and a tremendous blow to our entire community.""We need to do some soul-searching. I am against immediately calling for heads to roll because of an election result. The leader should have identified the problem as soon as it emerged. In other words, the conscription issue did not arise today. This was a process that should have been stopped. He lost the haredi public because the haredi public holds him responsible for failing to pass a conscription law or prevent all the decrees against the haredi community."Benizri also criticized Shas's close political alignment with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu."I have always argued that Shas's disaster is that we are to Netanyahu's right. As for Netanyahu, I don't see him solving any problems. He is going to solve more of his own problems than those of Shas. In my opinion, it hasn't dawned on him that the haredim are no longer so firmly in his pocket, and under certain circumstances now, with the left-wing parties, they might go with them.""The Likud doesn't understand that Shas is not a satellite party of Likud. We are a party with our own principles, and the most important of them is the yeshiva students and the Torah world. The moment that is not accepted, Likud is simply pushing them toward the left and toward making different decisions."He also took a swipe at the prime minister, saying, "I can say one thing about the left: When they make promises, they keep them. With them, a word is a word."'Deri is a millstone around Shas's neck'Meanwhile, media commentator Barak Seri wrote on X that Deri bore responsibility for Shas's electoral losses."From what appears to be emerging at this moment, Shas is dropping to six seats, and this is a complete, disgraceful, enormous failure by one man: Arye Deri. He drove all the traditional voters away from Shas because of his statements that he is proud of his three draft-dodging grandsons; because of bizarre interviews in which he said that in the next government he would demand 'tens of billions for the haredim and ten government ministries that would serve the haredi public'; his statements to haredim after the horrific massacre that 'you must not even think about enlisting in the IDF'; and statements such as 'conscription is the IDF's problem, let them deal with it themselves.'""In the previous elections in 2022, Shas won 11 seats, five and a half of which came from the traditional public, people who served in the IDF and whose children enlist in the military. For these people, the IDF is a sacred value. All those seats went to Likud. Shas has remained a Lithuanian haredi party that lost many votes even in haredi cities and neighborhoods because of their anger that it failed to secure the passage of a conscription law."Seri concluded with a sharp attack on Deri and those close to him."Deri failed. Deri is a millstone around Shas's neck, and all those associates who are now saying he is considering resigning are bluffing. These are threats in the style of former Egyptian president Nasser, who, after the defeat by Israel in the Six Day War, threatened to resign but was actually saying: I don't want to resign, please hold me back."

title: Northrop Grumman’s FMU-139D/B electronic bomb fuze contract ceiling increased by U.S. Navy
body: Northrop Grumman manufactures the electronic fuze at the Naval Industrial Reserve Ordnance Plant at Allegany Ballistics Laboratory in Rocket Center, West Virginia. Investments in automation and advanced manufacturing have raised the site’s capacity to as many as 85,000 fuzes annually. The FMU-139D/B controls when and how a munition functions, providing safety and timing capabilities for air-delivered weapons. It is used with multiple munitions and aircraft operated by U.S. and allied forces. The company delivered its 200,000th FMU-139D/B earlier this year. It said manufacturing improvements had increased efficiency, supported shorter delivery timelines and strengthened its ability to respond to surges in demand. The US$97 million increase raises the maximum potential value of the existing contract. The announcement did not disclose the revised ceiling, additional production quantities or delivery dates.

title: Kaduna deputy gov swears in three commissioners, 18 special advisers
body:
The Deputy Governor of Kaduna State, Dr Hadiza Balarabe, has counseled political appointees to serve the administration faithfully and act without fear or favor. She reminded them of the import of taking the Oath of Allegiance and Oath of Office, as prescribed by the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.
Balarabe made this known after swearing-in three Commissioners, the Deputy Chief of Staff Administration and Counselor of Infrastructure, as well as 18 Special Advisers on Thursday.
According to her, the oath of allegiance and oath of office are not mere words because ‘’they bind you before God and the people of Kaduna State , to serve faithfully.’’
She said the administration of oath is a moment of trust, a call to service, and a solemn reminder that leadership is not a privilege to be enjoyed, but a responsibility to be carried with humility, integrity, courage, and an unwavering commitment to the people.
‘’Your appointments reflect the confidence His Excellency has placed in your abilities, experience, judgment, and capacity to contribute meaningfully to the development of our dear state,’’ she added.
The deputy governor urged the appointees ‘’to receive this confidence not merely as recognition of your past achievements, but as a challenge to accomplish even greater things in the service of our people.’’
Justifying the timing of the appointments in the middle of an election season, she maintained that ‘’elections have their calendar, but the needs of our people do not wait for it.’’
According to her, Governor Uba Sani is focused on delivering on his promises to the people of Kaduna State, irrespective of party or ethno-religious affiliations.
The governor’s objective is to build a peaceful, prosperous, inclusive Kaduna State where no community is left behind, she stated.
‘’Since May 2023, Kaduna State has been steadily transformed. Communities once divided by conflict are reconciling under the Kaduna Peace Model; farmlands are reopening and markets are alive.
‘’More than 500 schools closed by insecurity have been reopened, and over 300,000 out-of-school children returned to class in 2025 alone, ‘’ she added.
Balarabe further said that hundreds of classrooms have been built while more have been renovated, and tens of thousands of teachers trained.
In the health sector, she said that 255 primary healthcare centres have been upgraded to level two, adding that ‘’our general hospitals are being improved.’’
Balarabe further said that about 160 road projects, covering some 1,335 kilometres, are opening up all 23 local government areas and that “the light rail and bus rapid transit projects point to the Kaduna of tomorrow.’’
She enjoined the newly sworn in appointees to go to their various duty posts and be the bridge between the government and the grassroots.
‘’Let your performance be the argument that convinces the skeptical and the proof that justifies the trust of the supportive,” she stressed.
The three commissioners that were sworn in are Hon Benjamin Dalhat Solomon Kure(Sports Development), Hon Amina Akilu Dalhat (Special Duties I) and Abdullahi Garba Abbas (Special Duties II) as well as 18 special advisers.
At the same event, Dr Haliru Musa Soba and Balarabe Muhammad Bello were sworn in as Deputy Chief of Staff(Administration) and Counsellor Infrastructure respectively.

title: ICPC arraigns PFIPC’s Adeyemi afresh on 22 counts
body: The Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) on Thursday arraigned Adeniyi Adeyemi afresh on 22 counts of alleged forgery, impersonation and related offences before an FCT High Court in Abuja over his purported role as director-general of the Presidential Foreign Investment Promotion Council (PFIPC). Adeyemi pleaded not guilty to all the counts. The fresh arraignment followed the striking out of an earlier eight-count charge against him by a Federal High Court in Abuja on October 12, after the Federal Government sought to terminate the proceedings following a review by the Attorney-General of the Federation (AGF). Rotimi Oyedepo, Director of Public Prosecutions of the Federation, had told the court that the review established that the alleged offences fell within the jurisdiction of the FCT High Court rather than the Federal High Court, where the police initially filed the charge. The prosecution subsequently filed the fresh charge before the FCT High Court. Forgery, impersonation allegations In the new charge, the ICPC accused Adeyemi of forging a letter dated March 8, 2024, purportedly signed by Femi Gbajabiamila, Chief of Staff to the President, appointing him director-general of the PFIPC. The commission alleged that Adeyemi used forged documents to present the purported council as a legitimate government institution and gain access to government facilities and official processes. Other counts accuse him of forging an executive order purportedly establishing the council and a legislative instrument bearing the titles of the Presidential Economic Advisory Council and PFIPC. The ICPC also alleged that he forged a document addressed to the Accountant-General of the Federation seeking approval for the purported agency to operate within the government’s financial reporting structure. Another allegation concerns documents purportedly submitted to the National Information Technology Development Agency to obtain a domain name for the council. The commission further accused Adeyemi of using forged documents presented to the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy to seek more than N27 billion for the establishment of the purported agency and N3.8 billion for personnel costs. In separate counts, the ICPC alleged that Adeyemi gave N210,000 to Aminu Abdullahi, an assistant chief technical officer in the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, to facilitate the allocation of office space without official authorisation. He was also accused of giving N300,000 to Ogaba Harry, an officer in the Office of the Chief Economic Adviser to the President, to facilitate the release of a Prado sport utility vehicle and a Land Cruiser. The commission further alleged that Adeyemi obtained N20 million from Oyekunle Gbenga, managing director of Divine Dopacy Nigeria Limited, under the pretence of a project facilitation loan for a purported N2.8 billion contract to furnish and renovate the official residence of the PFIPC director-general. The alleged offences reportedly occurred between 2024 and 2026 and are punishable under relevant provisions of the Penal Code, the Advance Fee Fraud and Other Fraud Related Offences Act, and the Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Act. Adeyemi has denied the allegations. He has separately alleged that Gbajabiamila collected N400 million through a proxy in connection with the appointment letter. The allegation against Gbajabiamila remains a claim by Adeyemi and is not established by the charges outlined in court. Court orders written bail application After Adeyemi entered his plea, ICPC counsel, Fatima Bardi, asked the court to fix a date for the commencement of trial. Defence counsel, Ibrahim Angulu, made an oral application for bail, but the presiding judge, Halilu Yusuf, directed him to file a formal written application. Angulu agreed but urged the court to schedule an early hearing, citing his client’s prolonged detention and health concerns. He told the court that Adeyemi had spent 155 days in detention and had a medical report from the police clinic where he received treatment. The judge adjourned the case until November 9 for trial and possible hearing of the bail application. The post ICPC arraigns PFIPC’s Adeyemi afresh on 22 counts appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Minerals Commission defends termination of Northern Ashanti Mines’ mineral rights over $8.3m debt
body: The Minerals Commission has defended its decision to terminate the mineral rights of Northern Ashanti Mines Limited, formerly Owere Mines, insisting that the company persistently failed to meet its statutory financial obligations despite several opportunities to settle its debts. According to the Commission, the company accumulated approximately US$8.33 million in unpaid Annual Mineral Right (AMR) fees on its mining leases as of April 2025, alongside US$49,928 owed on prospecting licences. Addressing a press conference, the Commission rejected allegations by Northern Ashanti Mines that the termination was carried out in bad faith, maintaining that the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources acted within his legal authority. The Commission explained that Owere Mines acquired a mining lease covering 595 cadastral blocks in January 2010 but subsequently failed to fulfil its annual payment obligations under Section 24 of the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703). It disclosed that the company had accumulated more than US$4 million in outstanding fees by May 2020, prompting the issuance of a notice to remedy the breach. Press Briefing On The Revocation Of Mining Leases Of Northern Ashanti Mines Limited – October 2026 Download Following the takeover of the company by BCM Investments, management proposed settling the debt in four instalments. However, the Commission said the company failed to honour the arrangement despite being given additional opportunities. By October 2022, the outstanding debt had risen to US$5.59 million, increasing to US$6.18 million by December of the same year. The Commission indicated that further notices issued in April 2025 revealed that the company’s indebtedness had reached US$8.33 million in mining lease fees, excluding outstanding prospecting licence fees. Consequently, on April 7, 2026, the Commission recommended the termination of the company’s mineral rights to the Lands Minister, citing persistent non-payment. The Minister subsequently approved the issuance of the termination notice. Responding to the company’s challenge to the debt figures, the Commission insisted that its records showed Northern Ashanti Mines had paid only US$300,000 in two instalments, contrary to the company’s claim of having paid US$1 million. “For a company that claims to have spent US$200,000,000 on the mine, what prevented it from paying the US$8,000,000 owed to the people of Ghana?” the Commission questioned. It further criticised the company’s decision to pursue legal action against the Lands Minister, the Minerals Commission and the Attorney-General while simultaneously seeking public dialogue over the matter. The Commission maintained that the company should allow the courts to determine the dispute rather than engage in what it described as litigation through the media. It stressed that the termination of the mineral rights meant the affected concessions had reverted to the State, without cancelling the company’s outstanding financial liabilities. The Commission consequently announced its intention to pursue the recovery of all outstanding payments owed by Northern Ashanti Mines. It also emphasised the State’s responsibility to protect the affected mining assets from encroachment and other illegal activities, citing Section 70 of Act 703. The Commission reaffirmed that due process had been followed throughout the termination proceedings and insisted that no mining company, whether locally or foreign-owned, would be permitted to disregard its statutory obligations. “No one is above the law in this country. If you flout the laws, there are sanctions, and those sanctions will apply,” the Commission stated. It reiterated its commitment to enforcing Ghana’s mining laws without fear or favour, stressing that the country’s mineral resources belong to the people and must be managed in accordance with the law.

title: European attempts to choose negotiator for talks with Russia descend into chaos — media
body:
LONDON, October 29. /TASS/. European countries’ attempts to agree on a negotiator for talks with Russia on Ukraine have descended into chaos, The Guardian reported, citing a senior European diplomat.
"There is an agreement overall that we need to talk to Putin, but the outreach is starting to feel like a free-for-all," the diplomat said, adding: "Too many leaders believe they can be the one to get Putin to negotiate."
Moscow has repeatedly expressed its readiness to hold talks with European countries on a continental security architecture based on mutual respect to the interests of all parties. Earlier, Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed, in a conversation with TV reporter Pavel Zarubin, with the US position that discussions on ensuring the future security of Ukraine and Russia required addressing European security architecture. Russia will monitor developments over the coming days, Putin added.

title: Ukrainian Navy says it destroyed two Su-34s in Russia with Neptune strike
body:
Two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers were destroyed as a result of a missile strike by Neptune at the aviation base at Marinovka airfield in Russia's Volgograd region, the press service of the Naval Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) said.



"As a result of the strike, two Su-34 front-line fighter-bombers were destroyed on the territory of the 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment (located in Oktyabrsky, Volgograd region) of the fourth Mixed Aviation Division of the fourth Army of the Russian Air Force and Air Defense Forces," the AFU Navy press service said on Facebook on Thursday.

The navy said the Su-34 is one of the main platforms of Russian tactical aviation for delivering guided aerial bombs on Ukrainian cities, Defense Forces positions, and frontline territories.

"The Ukrainian Navy continues to strike enemy military targets, reducing the enemy's ability to conduct combat operations against Ukraine," the press service said.

title: Umejiaku, Dunstan Fire Flamingos Into U-17 World Cup Quarter-Finals
body: Nigeria’s Flamingos have booked a place in the quarter-finals of the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco after defeating Mexico 2-1 on Thursday, extending their impressive recovery from an opening-day defeat to Poland. Oluebube Umejiaku and Mary Dunstan scored in either half to secure the Round of 16 victory, despite a late goal from Emily Delgado that threatened to set up a tense finish. The Flamingos began their campaign with a 2-1 loss to Poland but responded with a 2-0 victory over Puerto Rico before producing one of the tournament’s biggest surprises by defeating defending champions North Korea 3-1. Against Mexico, Umejiaku broke the deadlock in the 39th minute after the North Americans had resisted a barrage of Nigerian attacks. The forward capitalised on a defensive error, collected the ball inside the box and finished past goalkeeper Ania López to give Nigeria the lead. The goal was reviewed by the Video Assistant Referee (VAR) following a challenge involving Tosin Rafiu and Zoe Sánchez earlier in the move, but the referee upheld the decision. Nigeria continued to press after the break, and Dunstan doubled the advantage in the 70th minute. The midfielder reacted quickest after substitute Precious Oscar’s effort was punched away by López, collecting the rebound before lifting her shot over the goalkeeper and into the net. VAR officials reviewed the goal for a possible foul by Oscar in the build-up but ruled that it should stand. Mexico mounted a late push, with Delgado pulling one back in the second minute of added time after controlling a loose ball following a corner and firing into the net. However, the goal came too late to inspire a comeback as the Flamingos held on to secure their place in the last eight. From opening setback to statement victory The victory over Mexico continues a campaign in which the Flamingos have demonstrated their ability to recover from disappointment. After losing to Poland in their opening Group B fixture, Nigeria defeated Puerto Rico through goals from Oluwakemi Adegbuyi and Precious Oscar. Their most significant group-stage result followed against North Korea , the two-time defending champions, whom they beat 3-1. Adegbuyi opened the scoring in the 15th minute before Umejiaku doubled Nigeria’s lead in the 38th minute. Kanyinsola Rodiat Yusuf added a third with a free-kick in the 56th minute, while North Korea scored a late penalty. The result ended North Korea’s 18-match unbeaten run in regulation time at the competition and secured Nigeria’s passage to the knockout stage. The Flamingos finished second in Group B with six points, having scored six goals and conceded four across their three group matches. Their recovery from the defeat to Poland has now carried them through the Round of 16, leaving them two victories away from a place in the final. Venezuela next The Flamingos will face Venezuela in the quarter-finals on Sunday, November 1, after the South Americans eliminated Germany with a 1-0 victory in their Round of 16 encounter. Venezuela scored through Diana Bravo in the fifth minute and held on despite Germany’s efforts to find an equaliser. The fixture will present Nigeria with another test as they seek to advance to the semi-finals and improve on their third-place finish at the 2022 edition in India. With Umejiaku, Adegbuyi and Yusuf among our leading attacking contributors, the Flamingos will hope to maintain their scoring form while tightening up defensively as the competition enters its decisive stages. The post Umejiaku, Dunstan Fire Flamingos Into U-17 World Cup Quarter-Finals appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Russian Finance Ministry not supporting oil and gas sector taxation changes
body:
MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The Russian Ministry of Finance considers it inappropriate to alter the current taxation system in the oil and gas sector, as the tax burden on the industry remains one of the highest in the country, said Alexey Sazanov, the Deputy Minister of Finance, during a plenary session in the State Duma.
"Currently, our oil companies are repairing the damage caused to their refineries within very tight deadlines and are providing Russia and our consumers with petroleum products. Under these conditions, we believe that altering the taxation of the oil and gas sector makes no sense. We need to let the industry companies work in peace and perform the state function that they are currently successfully fulfilling," he said.
The level of tax burden in the oil industry already exceeds 60%, Sazanov said. "This is higher than in any other industry in the Russian Federation," he added.

title: How I paid money into ex-CCT chairman’s wife’s account, covered his children’s school fees – Contractor
body:
The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) opened its corruption case against former Code of Conduct Tribunal (CCT) chairman Danladi Umar with its first prosecuton witness at the FCT High Court in Abuja on Thursday.
Oluwatayo Solomon, owner of JTF Global Links Limited and Portal Realities, testified on how he allegedly bankrolled Mr Umar’s children’s school fees at the Baze University in Abuja and transferred money into his wife’s account after the CCT paid him for a contract.
He said he received a call to pay N6 million into the bank account of Zulaihatu Umar, Mr Umar’s wife, barely two days after he was paid by the tribunal.
According to the witness, a deputy director at the CCT at the time, Akinola Akonju, called him concerning the “request” and forwarded the account details to which the payment would be made.
“Mrs Umar also called me about the payment. The money was paid from the Portal Realities Limited Wema Bank account into her account,” the witness said.
On 9 July, the EFCC arraigned Mr Umar before the FCT High Court in Abuja on charges of receiving gratification involving about N15.6 million from CCT’s contractors between 2021 and 2024.
Mr Umar, whose tenure spanned July 2011 to November 2024, allegedly received financial inducements from contractors via deposits into his wife’s bank account and through the settlement of his children’s school fees at Baze University, Abuja.
The anti-corruption agency alleged that Kurchmives International Limited, a subcontractor under the contract awarded by the CCT to Momanaf Global Ventures Limited for the painting of the tribunal’s headquarters, sent N5 million to his wife, Zulaihatu Umar’s Zenith Bank account on 5 October 2021.
It also alleged that Portal Realities Limited, a sister company of JTF Global Links Limited, a company awarded the contract for the digitalisation of CCT’s management records, sent N6 million to Mrs Umar’s account on 25 January 2024.
The prosecution also stated in the charges that Portal Realities Limited paid over N4 million for Mr Umar’s children, Faiza and Yakubu, at Baze University.
These transactions, according to the prosecution, constituted acts of corruption, involving a public officer using his office or position to gratify or confer any corrupt or unfair advantage upon himself or any relation or associate criminalised under section 19 of the Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Act, 2000.
Mr Solomon, the first prosecution witness, explained how he made payments for the school fees of Mr Umar’s children.
The witness said Mr Akonju called him in October 2021 that Mr Umar asked that he be informed to pay the school fees of two of his children in Baze University, Abuja.
“I paid about N2 million for Yakubu Umar Danladi from the Portal Realities Limited account in Jaiz Bank to Baze University. I also paid school fees on behalf of Faiza Umar Danladi,” from the same account.
Led in evidence by EFCC’s lawyer Christopher Mshelia, the witness presented the documents regarding the contract awarded by the CCT, chaired at the time by Mr Umar, to his company, JTF Global Links Limited.
Under cross-examination by defence lawyer Edward Sunday, Mr Solomon confirmed that he had known Mr Umar for more than ten years.
He also acknowledged that he knew Mr Umar’s wife and children and could be considered as family friends.
Responding to the defence lawyer’s suggestion that the N6 million paid into Mrs Umar’s account could be considered a loan, Mr Solomon said, “There was no reason to give her a loan because I did not have that discussion with her.”
He acknowledged a transfer of N3 million from Mrs Umar into his business account with Zenith Bank on 16 February 2024 but confirmed the transaction was omitted from his statement to the EFCC.
On how he was asked to pay for Mr Umar’s school fees, Mr Solomon said he received the directive from Mr Akonji, the CCT official, but never cross-checked with Mr Umar.
“Based on the relationship I have with him and the beneficiaries sent to me are the people I am familiar with,” the prosecution witness said.
He also disclosed that Portal Realities Limited, through which he paid the fees, was not awarded any contract by the CCT.
Witness answers questions on relationship with Umar, qualification
Earlier, Mr Solomon told the court that CCT awarded a contract to JTF Global Links Limited on 22 September 2021, after submitting the company’s profile to the tribunal.
Responding to the defence lawyer’s suggestion under cross-examination that he asked to be awarded the contract, Mr Solomon said, “Based on my relationship with Mr Umar, he asked me to meet Mr Akonji, whom I submitted my company profile to. Mr Akonji called me on the 18th (no month stated) to come for a financial bid.”
The witness, who said he is registered and has all the necessary documents “for bidding according to the laws of Nigeria,” maintained that the documents he submitted for the CCT contract confirmed that “I am qualified to be awarded the contract,” pushing back a suggestion that he won the contract based on his relationship with Mr Umar.
He said he could not list other entities who bidded for the contract because, according to him, he was “not part of the tenders board.”
He also told the court that Mr Akonji served as the current procurement director for the CCT.
The witness said, before the CCT contract, he had executed contracts for the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission (RMAFC), and Katsina State Government.
Defence lawyer, who described some of Mr Solomon’s claims as an afterthought, sought to confront him with his extrajudicial statement.
But he could not proceed with that line of cross-examination after it was realised that there was no certified true copy of the witness’ extrajudicial statement in court.
The judge, Peter Kekemeke, then adjourned the matter until 20 January 2027 for the prosecution to furnish the defence with the certified true copy of the statement.
Section 19 of the Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Act, 2000, under which Mr Umar was charged criminalises the act of public officers who use their office to confer undue advantage on themselves, friends or family.
The offence attracts seven years’ imprisonment upon conviction.

title: NBU Hikes Rate to 16.5% After Forecast Turns to Recession and Higher Inflation
body:
Ukraine’s central bank raised its key policy rate by 0.5 percentage points to 16.5% on Oct. 29, after sharply worsening its macroeconomic forecast. Ukraine’s economy is now expected to shrink this year, while inflation is set to finish 2026 far above earlier projections.
The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) downgrade confirms the gloomier outlooks other analysts published earlier, which already reflected the impact of recent Russian strikes on Ukraine’s largest businesses and the effect of the port blockade.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
In the NBU’s updated forecast, the economy is expected to contract by 0.4% in 2026, against the 1.8% growth projected in the 2026 July Inflation report. Real GDP is expected to grow just 0.4% in 2027 (2.8% in the previous forecast) and 2.2% in 2028 (3.0% before).
This is also the second contraction of Ukraine’s economy since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The war caused a 28,8% drop in Ukraine’s GDP in 2022, while it grew by 5.5% in 2023, by 2.9% in 2024, and by 1.8% in 2025.
End-of-the-year inflation forecast is revised upwards to 12.5% in 2026 from 10.0% and 7.3% in 2027 from 6.9%, before returning to the 5.0% target in 2028. International reserves were cut in all three years, to $62.8 billion in 2026 ($69.7 billion before) and $57.0 billion in 2028 ($70 billion before). The current account deficit narrows to $3.6 billion in 2026 from the $16.1 billion projected in July, but widens to $49.5 billion by 2028.
Inflation was driven primarily by direct and second-round effects from the surge in fuel prices caused by the war in the Middle East, as well as the summer wave of Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s warehouses and logistics.
The NBU has also estimated the toll of Russian blockade of sea ports and attacks on production facilities and logistics, saying it subtracted 1.9 percentage points from this year’s GDP. In the third quarter this year, the NBU estimated that the real GDP decreased by 0.5% year-over-year.
“The NBU estimates that consequences of aerial attacks alone will add around 0.7 percentage points to annual inflation. Other important factors affecting the price dynamics will include effects of higher fuel prices and an expansion of fiscal stimulus,” NBU governor Andriy Pyshny said during the monetary press briefing on Thursday, where the NBU board presented the decision.
Metallurgical and ore mining enterprises suffered the greatest losses while performance also deteriorated in other industrial sectors, trade, and agriculture, he added. For 2027, the NBU assumes inflation will be restrained by the likely cooling of domestic demand and the labor market in the coming months after Russia’s attacks.
The central bank wrote that international aid in the third quarter fell short of expectations because Ukraine delayed reforms, although parliament adopted laws in October to unblock EU and IMF financing. Its forecast assumes about $50 billion in direct budget support and more than $32 billion under the defense component of the Ukraine Support Loan in 2026, and $52 billion and $37 billion respectively in 2027 .
Lending growth remained strong despite tighter policy. In September, net hryvnia corporate loans grew more than 32% year on year and net retail loans more than 38%.
The war remains the primary risk to inflation and growth, per the central bank press release , as Russian strikes on production and infrastructure raise costs and cut supply, in addition to higher oil prices from the war in the Middle East.
The NBU’s forecast envisages keeping the key rate at 16.5% until the second quarter of 2027. The NBU expects a slow recovery in 2027-28, supported by investment in the defense industry, localization of weapon production financed by the Ukraine Support Loan, and reconstruction of critical infrastructure.
Olena Hrazhdan is the Business Reporter at Kyiv Post, covering Ukraine’s markets, business, and economic policy. While she reports broadly on economic issues, her core focus is banking, finance, monetary and fiscal policy. Olena previously wrote for leading Ukrainian business media and became a Fellow of the International Monetary Fund’s Journalism Fellowship in 2024.

title: HYPE teases all-time high as NYSE owner ICE eyes US Hyperliquid perps
body:
Hyperliquid’s token pumped following news of ICE and Trade[XYZ] unveiling plans for US perpetual futures.
Hyperliquid’s native token HYPE surged about 20% Thursday after New York Stock Exchange owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) announced plans for US perpetual futures with Trade[XYZ], whose investors include billionaire Wall Street investor Stanley Druckenmiller.
HYPE traded above $96 at the time of writing, up by around 20% in the past 24 hours, according to CoinGecko , flirting with September’s all-time record of $97.96.
Perpetual futures allow traders to take positions on asset prices without an expiration date. Hyperliquid is the largest decentralized exchange in the world to trade such instruments, DefiLlama data shows.
HYPE surged about 20% on Thursday. Source: CoinGecko
The companies said Thursday they would seek regulatory approval for markets covering cryptocurrencies, stocks, indexes, commodities and currencies. The proposed market would target retail traders. ICE said it would operate separately from its institutional futures business, with a dedicated clearing structure.
More than 99% of participation in its markets is institutional, ICE said, with the separate clearing structure intended to shield existing customers from retail counterparty risks.
The proposal would give US retail traders a regulated route to Hyperliquid-based perpetual futures, and ICE a new route into retail trading. President Donald Trump said on Aug. 19 that Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chair Michael Selig was working to bring Hyperliquid into the country in a “fully compliant and legal fashion.”
Related: Wall Street wealth creation model is unsustainable for most participants: Hyperliquid CEO
“I am excited to be an investor in trade(xyz),” Druckenmiller wrote on X, adding that he looked forward to using its products.
Elon Musk also drew attention to the agreement, sharing Druckenmiller’s post with the one-word comment “Interesting.”
ICE is taking a minority stake in Trade[XYZ], but disclosed neither the investment amount nor a launch date. Cointelegraph reached out to ICE and Trade[XYZ] for comment but had not received a response by publication.
Customers would undergo identity and Anti-Money-Laundering checks and trade through participating futures brokers.
Distribution is expected through ICE’s joint venture with OKX, pending separate approvals. ICE invested in OKX at a $25 billion valuation in March.
Related: ICE, CME press US regulators to ‘rein in’ Hyperliquid energy trading: Report
Meanwhile, ICE’s separate tokenized stock venture with OKX has disclosed objections from 38 companies, up from 26 reported by Cointelegraph on Oct. 27 .
Its Oct. 28 notice adds Walmart, Eli Lilly, Carnival, Arcos Dorados and Cigna. However, those objections concern tokenized shares, while the Trade[XYZ] proposal involves perpetual futures and remains subject to separate regulatory approvals.
The regulatory opening remains conditional. The CFTC approved Kalshi’s Bitcoin perpetual contract in May , but said perpetuals referencing other asset classes should receive case-by-case review.

The US power sector could release 42 percent more planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution by 2030 than it did in 2025 as it builds out more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a new analysis by the Sierra Club . That would essentially wipe out 15 years of greenhouse gas reductions.
CO2 emissions from electricity generation would increase by 618 million tons by the end of the decade if planned AI projects are constructed. That’s roughly equivalent to carbon pollution from the electricity use of 128,788,523 homes in a year.
The Sierra Club’s estimate is higher than some previous projections
The Sierra Club’s estimate is higher than some previous projections from other groups. Another study published by academic researchers in June forecast that electricity demand from data centers and crypto mines could push up power sector emissions by 28 percent by 2030 when compared to a scenario with no data center growth. The outcome depends on how many planned data center projects actually come to fruition, as well as on what type of technology is used to power those facilities.
Net US greenhouse gas emission have fallen from a peak of about 6.58 billion metric tons in 2007 to about 5.35 billion metric tons in 2025 . But that pollution started ticking back up last year as data centers drove up electricity demand. The Trump administration is incentivising the buildout of fossil fuel infrastructure for data centers while simultaneously rolling back pollution regulations and stalling renewable energy projects.
The US is now planning to build more fossil fuel capacity than it has in a decade , according to a separate report published this month by the Environmental Defense Fund.

title: Publish details of N30bn East-West road approval, Ugolor tells Umahi
body: By Adesina Wahab An activist and publisher of The Common Good Letter, Rev. David Ugolor, has challenged the Minister of Works, Dave Umahi, to publish details of the Federal Government’s approval of N30 billion for remedial works on the East-West Road. Ugolor said making the details public would promote transparency and accountability in the use of public funds, while enabling communities, motorists and civil society organisations to monitor the project’s implementation. In an open letter to the minister, he welcomed the announcement that the Federal Executive Council approved the N30 billion for repairs to deteriorated sections of the road at its meeting on October 28, 2026. He, however, said the announcement should be followed by clear information on the scope of work, contractors, funding arrangements and completion timelines. “An approval is one stage of delivery. Nigerians also need to know what work has been authorised, who will execute it, how it will be financed and when it will be completed,” Ugolor said. He called on the ministry to identify all sections of the road covered by the approval, including the states, communities, kilometre points and length of each intervention. He specifically asked whether the package included the damaged Kira section in Rivers State and other locations recently affected by flooding. Ugolor also urged the ministry to publish the engineering scope, bill of quantities and completion standards, clarifying whether the funds would cover temporary repairs, permanent reconstruction, drainage improvements, bridges, culverts or road elevation. On procurement, he asked Umahi to disclose the contractors and supervising consultants, as well as whether the interventions involved new contracts, variations to existing contracts or other delivery arrangements. He further requested details of the procurement process, relevant approvals and applicable clearances from the Bureau of Public Procurement. The activist also sought clarification on the source of funding, asking the ministry to distinguish between the amount approved, funds released, payments made to contractors and sums certified against completed work, including the dates of each transaction. Ugolor called for an explanation of how the N30 billion approval related to existing East-West Road contracts and the previously announced reconstruction of approximately 400 kilometres between Edo and Cross River states. He urged the ministry to publish a consolidated schedule showing the boundaries, costs and responsibilities of the different interventions to prevent overlaps or uncertainty over project delivery. On road safety and durability, Ugolor called for the publication of relevant drainage, flood-risk and geotechnical assessments. He said the ministry should explain how the designs would address water flow, road elevation and the safety of neighbouring communities, including consultation and compensation arrangements where applicable. The publisher also asked the ministry to disclose when contractors had been or would be mobilised, the expected completion dates, measurable project milestones, traffic management arrangements and the officials responsible for monitoring progress. Ugolor urged relevant committees of the National Assembly to scrutinise the approval and track the expenditure through to the completion of the work. He also called on state governments, host communities, transport associations and civil society organisations to seek access to project information to enable them to monitor implementation. “The Common Good Letter supports urgent repairs and a transparent, adequately funded programme for the wider East-West Road,” he said. He urged Umahi to provide a consolidated public explanation accompanied by the approval, procurement, funding and implementation records. “Public money must deliver safe roads, measurable progress and lasting relief,” Ugolor added. title: Women domestic workers earn 48% of other employees’ wages – ILO
body: Women employed as domestic workers worldwide earn an average of 48% of the monthly wages of other employees, highlighting persistent gender-based inequalities in the sector, according to the International Labour Organisation (ILO). In its latest report, The State of Domestic Work in 2025: 15 Years After Convention No. 189, the ILO said women account for 77.2% of domestic workers globally and are disproportionately concentrated in cleaning and direct-care occupations. The report found that male domestic workers earn an average of 65.8% of the monthly wages of other employees, compared with 48% for their female counterparts. The figures underscore the persistent wage disparities affecting women in a sector that provides essential household services, including cleaning, cooking and caring for children, older persons and people with disabilities. The ILO estimates that 80 million people aged 15 and above are employed as domestic workers worldwide, up from 75.6 million in 2019. However, 66.5 million of these workers, representing 83.1% of the global domestic workforce, remain in informal employment, often without effective labour and social protection. The organisation said domestic workers earn an average of 53.3% of the monthly wages of other employees, while those in informal employment earn just 48.7%. The report also found that 35.2% of domestic workers work at least 49 hours per week, with 14.6% working 60 hours or more. The ILO has called for stronger implementation of its Domestic Workers Convention, 2011 (No. 189), and Recommendation No. 201 to improve wages, expand social protection, strengthen working-time safeguards and ensure decent working conditions. It also urged governments and other stakeholders to strengthen labour-law enforcement, promote social dialogue and collective bargaining, and invest in decent care jobs. Patrick Belser, Chief of the ILO’s Informal Work Branch, said progress in some countries showed that change was possible, but more needed to be done to address informality and the widening wage gap. “We cannot claim to value care while undervaluing the people who provide it,” he said, calling for the rights outlined in the convention to be translated into effective protection for domestic workers.

title: KuCoin suspends services in Russia and Belarus
body:
The exchange cited legal and regulatory compliance in its reason for cutting off services to users based in the two countries, currently the targets of international sanctions.
Cryptocurrency exchange KuCoin announced that it would immediately suspend services for its users in Russia and Belarus, citing legal and regulatory compliance concerns.
In a Thursday notice, KuCoin said it had suspended access to all products and services for users based in Russia and Belarus. According to the exchange, it would offer an “orderly exit process” to allow users to withdraw assets.
“Compliance is at the core of our operations and guides our decisions on where and how we offer our services,” said the exchange in a Thursday X post regarding the service suspension.
The move comes as many crypto companies are complying with international sanctions led by the United States and Europe against Russia and Belarus over the war in Ukraine. KuCoin is headquartered in the Seychelles.
Separately, Russia’s central bank on Thursday approved the National Association of Securities Market Participants, commonly known as NAUFOR, as a self-regulatory body for crypto exchanges and custodians. The central bank’s registry currently includes 23 crypto exchanges and eight digital custody institutions, with registered entities required to join a self-regulatory organization within 90 days.

title: Ukrainian Producer Oleg Kokhan: ‘The World Must See Ukraine Beyond War and Victimhood’
body:
Oleg Kokhan is a Ukrainian theater and film producer and founder of SOTA Cinema Group, known for his collaborations with prominent Ukrainian directors, including Kira Muratova and Myroslav Slaboshpytskyi.
In 2026, he was invited to join the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, the organization behind the Oscars. In this interview with Kyiv Post, Kokhan discusses the international prospects for Ukrainian cinema, the need to decolonize the global cultural landscape, and the transition from festival success to a fully fledged global film industry.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Kyiv Post: You are one of five Ukrainian producers invited to join the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences this year. Academy membership opens up new professional opportunities. What does this mean for Ukraine? How do you plan to use this access to tools of global influence?
Oleg Kokhan: The entry of Ukrainian producers into the Academy is not simply a personal professional victory or a status symbol. It expands our presence on the world’s most influential film platform. Until now, Ukraine has more often been an object of attention for global cinema: People discussed us, sympathized with us, and foreign filmmakers made films about us. Academy membership gives us the right and the tools to become full-fledged participants and help shape the global cinematic agenda. We gain a direct voice in determining the best, but more importantly, we gain the opportunity to build a network of cultural influence.
This means converting attention into real industry collaboration and, consequently, creating new films. It means advocating for Ukrainian films and working systematically to ensure that Hollywood is no longer surprised by our ability to make world-class cinema, but instead begins to see Ukraine as an equal, strong partner with unique experience and talent.
Hollywood has worked with Russia for decades and continues to do so despite its imperialist policies. What still prevents the global film industry from recognizing the real causes of Russia’s war against Ukraine?
Two things stand in the way: The inertia of comfort and the optical illusion in which the West has lived for more than a century.
Hollywood is an enormous, pragmatic corporate machine. For decades, Russian culture invested billions of dollars in creating the myth of “great Russian culture” – Dostoevsky and ballet. This myth was convenient, aesthetically packaged, and marketed as a universal brand of Eastern Europe. Everything around it – Ukrainian, Georgian, and Kazakh culture – was viewed by the Western film world through a Moscow-centric lens as “provincial folklore.”
When the full-scale war began, the West faced an uncomfortable realization: This “humanistic ballet” and “great literature” had produced real rapists and war criminals. Yet the inertia of thought still leads many in Hollywood to separate Putin from Russian culture, failing to understand that Russian culture itself has been and remains the principal source of legitimacy for Russian imperialism.
Our task as producers is not simply to call for a boycott, although that is critically necessary, but to decolonize the Western perspective. We must offer our own distinctive, profound, and competitive content that proves one thing: The center of European culture today is in Kyiv, not Moscow.
“War Through the Eyes of Animals” explores the humanitarian and environmental consequences of war through the eyes of different living creatures. What inspired you to create this particular cinematic testimony to Russian aggression?
The impulse came from a universal code that we did not invent but that can break through the “wall of war fatigue” around Ukraine that has formed across the world.
During a major war, the information space becomes saturated with images of violence, destruction, and human suffering. Unfortunately, the human psyche has defense mechanisms: Over time, Western audiences subconsciously shut themselves off from other people’s pain to preserve their own peace of mind.
Animals in this war are utterly defenseless witnesses and victims. They have no political convictions, do not take up arms, and cannot call for help. They are the ultimate metaphor for innocence. When we show the tragedy of this war through the eyes of a dog, a goat, or an eagle, we reach straight into the heart of any person, regardless of whether they live in New York, Tokyo, or Paris.
“War Through the Eyes of Animals” is an anthology film that shifts Ukrainian trauma from a narrow geopolitical context into the realm of a global environmental and humanitarian catastrophe. It is testimony that hostile propaganda cannot refute.
The world premiere of “War Through the Eyes of Animals” took place at the Tribeca Festival in the US last year, while its Ukrainian premiere was held at the Odesa International Film Festival on World Animal Day. Based on your observations, how have Western and Ukrainian audiences responded to the meanings the filmmakers sought to convey?
The reactions differ greatly in emotional intensity, but they are equally profound in substance.
For Western audiences, particularly at Tribeca, the film was a genuine cultural and psychological shock. It showed them that war destroys not only infrastructure but also the biosphere, ecosystems, and humanity itself. Through this film, Western viewers experienced guilt and a powerful sense of empathy, connecting with our pain through their own love of animals.
For Ukrainian audiences, the film became a form of therapy and a mirror reflecting their own dignity. In Ukraine, compassion for animals on the front lines and in de-occupied cities remains one of the key markers of our civilizational difference from the enemy. Our soldiers rescue kittens from shelling and lead horses and wild animals to safety. For Ukrainians, “War Through the Eyes of Animals” affirms our moral superiority and our love of life.
Poster of the War Through the Eyes of Animals
The world has grown accustomed to seeing Ukraine through the lens of war. What Ukrainian stories should reach international screens next to change that perception?
The world must see Ukraine not as a “victim,” but as a country of brave, progressive, and talented people. We need to move beyond documenting trauma alone. The next wave of Ukrainian cinema must offer the world:
Universal genre stories with a distinct national identity – high-quality psychological thrillers, historical dramas, and intellectually ambitious mainstream cinema; stories of our transformation – about people who, amid the greatest catastrophe of the 21st century, are building new institutions, developing technologies, rethinking ethics, and changing the world; and a profound reexamination of our heritage – stories about our avant-garde figures, from artists to military leaders and philosophers, that demonstrate that Ukraine has always been part of European modernism.
We must stop asking the world for empathy. We must give the world cinema that inspires admiration, respect, and intellectual curiosity.
You have worked with Kira Muratova, Myroslav Slaboshpytskyi, and other exceptional directors. What still prevents Ukrainian cinema from claiming its rightful place in the global market?
Working with true artists makes one thing clear: We have never lacked talent or originality of vision. Muratova represents the absolute avant-garde of world cinema, while Slaboshpytskyi made a film that transformed the global understanding of cinematic language. So what prevents us from becoming consistent players in the global market? The lack of a sustainable industry ecosystem.
There is a systemic shortage of venture-style producing expertise: Cinema is an art, but the film industry is a tough business. There is a lack of consistent state policy and institutional continuity – the market cannot develop when the rules change every year and transparent competitive procedures are replaced by chaos. There is also isolation from private capital – our business community has yet to learn to view cinema as a tool for capitalization and national branding.
Cinema is an industry. Without strong institutions, a transparent market, and international co-productions, even the most outstanding genius remains an isolated flash of brilliance rather than part of a system.
What changes are needed for Ukrainian films to secure wider international distribution and more frequent Oscar nominations?
We need a clear, pragmatic three-part strategy.
International co-production as the standard: Ukrainian films should not be developed in an “internal bubble.” From the idea stage onward, we must bring in European and American partners, funds, and international sales agents. This immediately provides a guarantee of distribution in foreign markets.
Aggressive, professional promotion – Oscar campaigns: Making an Oscar shortlist or receiving a nomination is not a lottery. It requires a costly, mathematically calculated marketing and PR campaign in the US. The state and private businesses must pool resources to finance these promotional tours and screenings.
Quality standards and market discipline: We must abandon our tendency to be lenient with ourselves. Our products must meet the highest international standards in screenwriting, sound design, and special effects.
What are your plans and ambitions for the near future?
My main strategic goal is to transform Ukrainian cinema from a film culture known for festival successes into a globally operating industry. As for specific projects, they include a cinematic tribute to Kira Muratova, a major documentary project, and two historical films. We must create cinema that does more than document the past or trauma – it must shape the image of a victorious, strong, and modern Ukraine of the future.
Myroslava Makarevych has more than 30 years of experience as a journalist and editor. She has worked for BBC Ukrainian Service; for a number of publishing houses in Ukraine, like HFS (ELLE Ukraine), Edipresse and Sanoma Media (Sensa.Ukraine). She collaborates with various socio-political media including Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, zn.ua; nv.ua. She is the author of 8 original fairy tale books for children, and 4 publicist books.

title: Three people killed in EUFOR helicopter crash in Bosnia and Herzegovina
body:
BELGRADE, October 29. /TASS/. A helicopter belonging to the European Union Force in Bosnia and Herzegovina (EUFOR) crashed near the city of Brcko, killing three people, the Klix news portal reported.
According to the report, no civilians were injured and no infrastructure was damaged. An investigation has been launched. Police, firefighters and ambulance crews have arrived at the scene, and the area has been cordoned off.

title: Africa records 4.2 million increase in domestic workers since 2019 – ILO
body: Africa recorded an increase of 4.2 million domestic workers between 2019 and 2025, the largest rise among the world’s regions, according to the International Labour Organization (ILO). However, 93.3% of domestic workers on the continent remain in informal employment, often without effective labour and social protection, the organisation has warned. The findings are contained in the ILO’s report, The State of Domestic Work in 2025: 15 Years After Convention No. 189, which examines developments in the sector since the adoption of the Domestic Workers Convention in 2011. The report indicates that the growth in Africa’s domestic workforce has occurred alongside persistent challenges in securing formal employment and adequate protection for workers. Globally, an estimated 80 million people aged 15 and above work as domestic workers, up from 75.6 million in 2019. Of this number, 66.5 million, representing 83.1% of the global domestic workforce, remain in informal employment. Domestic workers provide essential household services, including cleaning, cooking and caring for children, older persons and people with disabilities. Yet many continue to face low wages and inadequate working conditions. The ILO estimates that domestic workers worldwide earn an average of 53.3% of the monthly wages of other employees. Those in informal employment earn even less, at 48.7%. The report also found that 35.2% of domestic workers globally work at least 49 hours per week, while 14.6% work 60 hours or more. The ILO is calling for stronger implementation of its Domestic Workers Convention, 2011 (No. 189), and Recommendation No. 201 to expand social protection, improve wages, strengthen working-time safeguards and promote decent working conditions. It also recommends accessible worker registration, effective minimum-wage policies, stronger labour-law enforcement and greater investment in decent care jobs. The organisation says improving conditions for domestic workers will be increasingly important as demographic changes, migration and growing care needs reshape labour markets worldwide.

title: Canada Invests Up to $1.6 Billion in Cohere for Sovereign AI
body: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the next great technological transformation. It is imperative to Canadians’ prosperity, security, and sovereignty that we build and govern these technologies on our own terms. The opportunity to cement that autonomy is now. The decisions we make today will determine whether Canadians have that choice – to use secure, sovereign, Canadian-made AI – for decades to come. To that end, the Prime Minister, Mark Carney, announced the Government of Canada’s commitment to making an equity investment of up to $1.6 billion in Cohere . This is a commercial investment, announced alongside private investors, including NVIDIA, Bell, and Schwarz Group. Founded in Toronto, Cohere builds secure AI systems for businesses and governments. Its technology gives organisations greater control over where sensitive data is stored, how it is used, and who can access it. The government’s planned landmark investment will enable Cohere to scale and compete in the global AI market. Cohere will now be able to develop far more advanced models and products, scale up its computing infrastructure, and expand its Canadian workforce to serve more businesses and governments in Canada and around the world. Building this capability at home ultimately means that Canadian businesses and governments will have more choice in how they adopt AI and greater control over their sensitive information. Cohere is a Canadian success story that is projected to be a leader in sovereign AI. By taking an equity stake, Canada will share in the company’s success from the opportunities created through Cohere’s growth. READ: Cohere and Accenture Partner to Deliver Sovereign AI for Defence As part of this investment, Cohere will: Create at least 1,000 new high-paying Canadian technical jobs by 2030. Commit at least $1.7 billion to additional computing infrastructure in Canada by 2030. Maintain its Canadian incorporation and Canadian headquarters. Invest in research partnerships in Canada and create opportunities for students and recent graduates. Keep working with the Canadian AI Safety Institute to champion the safe development and use of advanced AI. The investment is for Canadians, by Canadians. It will be made in stages, with regular reporting on progress against the company’s commitments, including jobs and investment in Canada. This approach will give Cohere the capital to expand and hold the company accountable to deliver benefits to Canadians. Canada’s ambition is to build advanced AI here at home, help Canadian businesses put it to work, and create opportunities for Canadian talent. This investment is part of that mission: strengthening our ability to develop and operate secure AI, compete globally, and ensure Canadians share in Cohere’s success. “Canada’s investment in Cohere is an investment in choice, in security, and in our ability to live our lives as we choose. Today, true sovereignty depends on our ability to build, adopt, and govern AI on our own terms. The bigger and faster Cohere can scale up their models and operations, the more businesses and governments can control where sensitive data is stored, how it is used, and who can access it. We need this technology. That’s why this company’s growth has been so extraordinary. It is in all our interests for Cohere to succeed, and now all Canadians will have a share in that success.” — The Rt. Hon. Mark Carney, Prime Minister of Canada “It is not enough for great companies to start in Canada. We want them to grow here, build here, and create good jobs here. That means giving Canadian entrepreneurs the conditions to turn ambitious ideas into globally successful businesses. Investing in Cohere sends a clear message: you should not have to leave Canada to build a company that succeeds around the world. We are backing Canadian talent and giving Canadians a stake in that success.” — The Hon. Evan Solomon, Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario “We founded Cohere in Canada with the belief that this country could build AI companies capable of competing at the highest level globally. This investment helps accelerate that vision by expanding our ability to attract world-class talent, build frontier AI systems, and develop secure, sovereign technology from Canada for customers around the world. As AI becomes increasingly critical to economic growth and competitiveness, organisations need solutions that give them greater control over their data, infrastructure, and how AI is deployed. We’re proud to be growing from Canada, creating high-value jobs and innovation here at home, and grateful for the Government of Canada’s support as we help build the future of sovereign AI.” — Aidan Gomez, Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of Cohere ADDITIONAL INFO Canada’s equity investment in Cohere will total up to approximately $1.6 billion and will be made in stages. Founded in Toronto, Cohere builds secure AI systems for businesses and governments that need greater control over their data. Cohere’s recent merger with Aleph Alpha brings together Canadian and German AI expertise. Investments from NVIDIA and Schwarz Group in this financing round strengthen Cohere’s international partnerships and its ability to serve businesses and governments in Canada and around the world.
