title: Mozambique welcomes Russian investment — President
body:
MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Mozambique has invited Russian companies to invest in its economic development and build sustainable partnerships, Mozambican President Daniel Chapo announced at the plenary session of the Russia-Africa summit.
"Russia has consistently supported us throughout the 50 years of our independence," he said. "We are committed to continuing our cooperation with the Russian Federation and attach great importance to developing relations between Russia and Africa. Mozambique intends to expand ties with Russia in infrastructure, transport, logistics, agriculture, energy, tourism, digital transformation, and green energy. We invite Russian companies to invest in Mozambique and establish reliable partnerships."
Chapo underscored the significance of the partnership with Russia in combating terrorism, extremism, and organized crime. "We are making efforts to strengthen political dialogue and explore new opportunities for cooperation between Russia and Africa," he noted.
According to the Mozambican President, the summit in Moscow will help deepen political dialogue and economic engagement between Russia and Africa.

title: Masdar starts construction on 200MW solar energy project in Malaysia
body: Abu Dhabi clean energy company Masdar has started construction on its first project in Malaysia, set to be one of the largest floating solar developments in South-East Asia. The 200MW Chereh Dam solar photovoltaic project in Parang state is being built by a consortium that also includes Malaysia's Citaglobal construction company and investment firm Tiza Global, Masdar said on Thursday. The project's financing was finalised on Tuesday with about 580 million ringgit ($142.9 million) raised from three international lenders, Masdar said. Plans for the development were first unveiled last December , and at the time showed that the value of the project was about $208 million. The Chereh project, which is poised to generate clean electricity to power the equivalent of 100,000 homes, will create about 1,500 jobs and is set to open up economic opportunities in Pahang, Masdar said. The development combines Masdar’s expertise in floating solar projects, including its work on the 145MW Cirata project in Indonesia, with Citaglobal’s infrastructure and energy development capabilities, and Tiza's project development and local stakeholder engagement experience, Masdar said. Masdar chief executive Mohamed Al Ramahi said it also emphasises the strategic importance of Malaysia and the broader South-East Asia region, as electricity demand rises, the potential for renewable energy grows and investments continue to flow. "Chereh marks an important milestone in our long-term commitment to Malaysia and our expansion across Southeast Asia," he said. "By combining Masdar’s global floating solar expertise with strong local partnerships, we will support Malaysia’s energy ambitions while creating jobs and new economic opportunities in Pahang." Masdar, jointly owned by Taqa, Adnoc and Mubadala, has developed projects in various countries, with a combined capacity of more than 65GW. Its entry into Malaysia follows previous moves in Asia. The company signed agreements to develop power plants, including what was then South-East Asia's largest floating solar plant, in Indonesia , and to build renewable energy projects with a capacity of 1GW in the Philippines . In August, Masdar launched its second battery energy storage system project in the UK, as the company continues to boost its presence there amid higher demand for clean energy. In July, Masdar and ScottishPower completed a major construction stage at a $5.42 billion offshore wind farm project off the English coast, which is set to be one of the largest in the world. The Chereh project "reflects how our natural resources can be used responsibly to contribute to Malaysia’s renewable energy ambitions, while bringing opportunities for local communities and industry", said the Sultan of Pahang, Abdullah Ri'ayatuddin Al Mustafa Billah Shah.

title: 59% of Ukrainians read books regularly. What is the Ministry of Culture doing to grow that number?
body:
Tetyana Berezhna, Vice Prime Minister of Ukraine for Humanitarian Policy – Minister of Culture
Russia is burning Ukrainian books by the million. Ukrainians continue to choose books in Ukrainian: according to a new study, 87% of readers surveyed had read or listened to books in Ukrainian over the past year.
These two realities define our responsibility as a state. We must help the book sector withstand these attacks and give Ukrainians access to books that interest them. Sustaining that interest in the years ahead depends on the range of titles published in Ukrainian and how accessible they are.
The Ministry of Culture of Ukraine commissioned a comprehensive study, Reading in Ukraine: Behaviour, Motivation and Tools for Engagement , conducted by Gradus Research with support from the Believe in Yourself Foundation. The researchers combined 41 in-depth interviews with book sector professionals and people who had returned to reading with a survey of 2,200 Ukrainians aged 14 and over.
Over the past year, 59% of respondents had read or listened to books at least several times a month. One-third did so at least several times a week.
At the same time, 70% of readers surveyed had experienced a break from reading lasting six months or longer. Of those who had taken such a break, 35% had returned to regular reading, while another 62% now read occasionally.
This is an important finding for policies to encourage reading. Reading habits change with people’s lives. Work, parenthood, relocation and exhaustion all affect the time and attention someone can give to a book. A change in routine, a recommendation from someone close or a compelling story can help bring them back.
Support therefore matters at different stages of life: when children first discover books, when teenagers develop their own tastes and when adults rediscover an interest in literature.
During the war, books have taken on particular emotional significance. Among readers, 32% say reading helps reduce anxiety, 30% say it helps them recover emotionally and 28% say it helps them cope with stress. Among those who returned to reading after a break, the most frequently cited reason was a psychological need for rest, support or relief from stress. This was selected by 34%.
Participants in the in-depth interviews also described exhaustion that makes it difficult to concentrate. We should take this experience into account when encouraging people to read. Some need a novel that offers a moment of respite; others need a book that helps them make sense of what they have lived through. A wide range of literature and formats allows people to choose what meets their needs at a particular moment.
Of all respondents, 37% said that coming across an interesting book had encouraged, or could encourage, them to read more. This was the most common answer. Among those who had returned to reading after a break, 31% recalled seeing a book that caught their interest.
The opportunity to encounter books in everyday life therefore matters: to browse a title, talk to a bookseller or discover new releases on a library shelf.
Only 34% of respondents believe their town or community has enough bookshops. Another 22% say there are too few, while 21% say there are none at all. Where people live has a significant impact on their access to literature.
The Government has already adopted a resolution developed by the Ministry of Culture to reimburse bookshops for the cost of renting their premises. The first phase will cover communities with populations of up to 100,000. The first payments are planned for the first quarter of 2027, covering rent paid in the fourth quarter of 2026.
Bookshops will use the reimbursed funds to purchase books or pay for titles already sold. This will help booksellers stay in business and publishers receive payments sooner.
For a community, a bookshop can also be a place to meet authors, join discussions and discover contemporary Ukrainian literature. Supporting bookshops gives people more opportunities to participate in cultural life close to home.
Library Acquisitions Must Reflect Readers’ Interests
Among respondents, 73% know of a library in their town or community where they can borrow books free of charge. This is an extensive network that needs to develop in line with communities’ needs.
Among those who do not use libraries, 19% cited a lack of titles that interest them, while 12% pointed to a shortage of new releases. In small towns, the share of people who say libraries lack books that interest them reaches 27%.
Acquisitions should therefore begin with readers’ requests. Librarians know which authors visitors are looking for, which books teenagers are waiting for and which titles families with children borrow. This knowledge should shape library collections.
For the first time since 2021, the draft state budget for 2027 includes funding to purchase new books for libraries. The Ministry of Culture is working to replenish public library collections, while school libraries fall within the remit of the Ministry of Education and Science. We plan to build the public library programme around an assessment of communities’ needs.
Together with our partners, we are also working to improve library spaces. Libraries in Rohatyn, in the Ivano-Frankivsk region, and Bilohiria, in the Khmelnytskyi region, became the first pilot sites for the Libraries for All programme. Up-to-date collections, welcoming spaces and professional advice should help people find books they connect with—and return for more.
Among readers aged 18–24, 91% had read or listened to books in Ukrainian over the past year. The state has an important role in sustaining this interest and giving young people the means to choose their own reading.
From the launch of the eKnyha programme in December 2024 to the end of June 2026, young Ukrainians purchased more than 549,000 books through the scheme. State support translated into books that readers chose for themselves, while also supporting the book sector.
We are working to extend eKnyha to parents of newborns. We look to the Verkhovna Rada to support this expansion so that families can receive assistance to buy books from the beginning of a child’s life. After all, a child’s introduction to reading often begins with time spent with their parents, the sound of their voices and a first favourite story.
As children grow, they need room to make their own choices. Contemporary literature for reading for pleasure should therefore also be available in school libraries. The opportunity to try different genres, discover authors and share impressions with friends helps children develop their own tastes as readers.
In 2027, we also plan to expand the Tysiachovesna programme to include the book sector. Support for new Ukrainian publications should go hand in hand with the development of bookshops, libraries and interest in reading.
I measure the results of this work by the opportunities it creates for people. Can a child choose an interesting book at the library? Can a young person afford literature that reflects their own tastes? Can an adult reader find the title they need in their community?
The study gives us a basis for making decisions and assessing their results. We need to understand how bookshops perform after receiving support, whether readers borrow newly acquired library books and how young people’s interest in reading develops.
Books are the depths of the sea: Whoever dives down to the bottom, Though the effort be great, Brings wondrous pearls to the surface.
For every reader, these “pearls” are different: new knowledge, a better understanding of themselves or support through a difficult time. Ukrainian literature gives us the opportunity to reflect on our experiences, discover the world and form our own opinions.
Our task as a state is to broaden that choice. To ensure that libraries receive the books their readers are waiting for, that bookshops can operate in communities and that literature for different ages and interests is published in Ukrainian. To help everyone find the book that sparks a love of reading—or brings them back to it.
We cannot choose the book that will captivate someone. But we can give them more opportunities to find it.

title: Ghana at risk of missing 2030 methane emissions target, AMA warns, as stakeholders push for more funding and waste separation
body: Ghana risks missing its target of cutting methane emissions from the waste sector by 30 percent by 2030, officials of the Accra Metropolitan Assembly (AMA) have warned, citing funding shortfalls and weak waste collection. The warning came on Wednesday at the Accra LOW-M Institutional and Climate Finance Roundtable at the Africa Regent Hotel in Accra. The event was organised by the AMA and the Green Africa Youth Organization (GAYO), with the Global Alliance for Incinerator Alternatives (GAIA) and C40 Cities. It brought together the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, the Ministry of Finance, the Environmental Protection Agency and its Ghana Carbon Markets Office, the private sector and informal waste workers. Victor Kotey, the AMA’s Climate Change Focal Point, said the country was off track. “Looking at the trajectory, if we don’t put a lot more effort into this, we may not be able to achieve the 2030 [target],” he said. “If you are not getting the right investment in the right quantum, it will be very difficult to achieve this.” He said the Assembly would not be able to implement about half of the 20 priority actions in its 2020–2025 climate action plan, largely because of a lack of money. The warning comes a week after the United Nations Environment Programme’s annual Emissions Gap Report found that if current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8°C within this century, with methane emissions heading in the opposite direction of what countries agreed to. Ghana is among the countries backing the Global Methane Pledge, under which signatories work towards a collective effort to reduce global methane emissions by at least 30% from 2020 levels by 2030. Ghana’s waste sector commitments under its Nationally Determined Contributions include building three landfills with 50 percent methane recovery, doubling the country’s waste-to-compost capacity, and building 200 biogas facilities. Methane is produced when organic waste rots without oxygen in dumpsites and landfills. Engineer Godfred Fiifi Boadi, Head of Climate Action, Sustainability and Partnerships at the Ministry of Local Government, said that “over 20 years it is 60 to 100 times more potent than carbon dioxide”. Desmond Alugnoa, Africa Programme Manager of GAIA, said Africa as a whole is falling short. “I must admit that we are not doing as much as we could,” he said, adding that the money committed and the political will do not match what countries have promised. The roundtable centred on the Accra LOW-M (Lowering Organic Waste Methane) Portfolio, a plan to turn organic waste into compost and biogas instead of sending it to landfills. Accra aims to collect at least 50% of organic waste separately by 2030, and to divert at least 30% of organic waste by 2040. Fathia Selasi Charway-Glover, Project Coordinator on GAYO’s Zero Waste Cities Project, said more than 55 percent of Accra’s waste is organic, and the plan depends on separating it at source. “We need the bylaws, we need the institutional backing from governments to ensure that this is possible,” she said. Ing. Boadi said government is building more facilities to get waste to the right places for treatment. “There is also some innovations that have been announced by the Minister for Local Government with regards to the construction of additional final disposal site facilities across the regions, and also quite a number of waste transfer stations,” he said. Mr Alugnoa said cutting food waste would also make a big difference. “If we are able to avoid the tonnage that is coming from those places by conserving our food and ensuring food security, we are also going to achieve much of our climate targets,” he said. Mr Kotey urged households to stop dumping and burning waste. “Please pay for waste collection services and make sure your waste is collected and properly treated,” he said. Ms Charway-Glover said everyone has a part to play. “If you cook and you feel like, oh, I don’t want to eat this tomorrow and you throw it away, you are part of the problem,” she said. “And so as we are part of the problem, it is the same way we need to be part of the solution.” The roundtable is expected to produce a six- to 12-month action plan for the portfolio, naming the institutions responsible for each task and setting out how it will be financed. END.

title: Russia, Nigeria sign customs cooperation agreement to ease business, trade
body:
NAIROBI, October 29. /TASS/. Russia and Nigeria have concluded an agreement on cooperation and mutual assistance in customs matters, aimed at facilitating business operations in both countries, the Trade Representation of the Russian Federation in Nigeria, Togo, Mali, and Burkina Faso announced on its Telegram channel.
The document was signed on the sidelines of the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow. According to the Trade Representation, the agreement will strengthen collaboration between the two nations' customs authorities and foster a more favorable environment for bilateral trade.
Valery Pikalev, Head of the Federal Customs Service of Russia, and Bashir Adewale Adeniyi, Comptroller-General of the Nigeria Customs Service, inked the document. This marks the first such agreement between the two states, with drafting efforts underway since 2023.
The agreement provides for information exchange required for customs control, joint efforts to combat customs offenses, and cooperation in professional training and development for specialists.
Furthermore, the sides discussed tariff preferences during the meeting. Nigeria benefits from the Eurasian Economic Union’s (EAEU) unified system of tariff preferences, meaning import duty rates on certain Nigerian goods are 25% lower than those established by the EAEU’s Common Customs Tariff.

title: Kallas may be among greatest disappointments in EU history — newspaper
body:
BERLIN, October 29. /TASS/. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has become one of the biggest disappointments in the bloc’s history, having participated in no talks with Russia on Ukraine, Berliner Zeitung columnist Nicolas Butylin wrote.
Throughout the various stages of negotiations, "no one in Moscow, Washington or Beijing showed any interest in her," he noted. "Kallas played no part in this entire process, either as a participant or as someone initiating contact. Yet just six weeks ago, Kallas said in an interview with Finnish broadcaster Yle that she would answer a call from [Russian President] Vladimir Putin or Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov if one came."
Butylin said that in the same interview, Kallas "admitted her own unsuitability for this diplomatic task," stating that she "cannot act as a full-fledged mediator because the West supports Ukraine." For that reason, "Kallas should not be surprised that others are doing the job for her," he concluded.

title: NPP rejects reports of changes to Minority leadership in parliament
body: The New Patriotic Party (NPP) has rejected reports that it is considering changes to its parliamentary leadership, saying no discussions have taken place to replace Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin and his team. The party’s General Secretary, Justin Kodua Frimpong, said the NPP was satisfied with the current leadership of the Minority Caucus and had no plans to reshuffle the team. Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, October 29, he accused those spreading the reports of attempting to create divisions within the party’s parliamentary ranks. “Let me state it categorically. The party has never had any meeting. The party has never thought about even deliberating to change the leadership in Parliament. We have not,” he said. Mr Kodua Frimpong added that those seeking to create confusion among the parliamentary leadership and the Minority Caucus would not succeed. Meanwhile, he has cautioned party members seeking to position themselves as running mate to the NPP’s flagbearer for the 2028 general election through social media campaigns. He said the party’s constitution does not provide for the selection of a running mate through a competitive process or public campaigning. According to him, the decision rests with the party’s flagbearer in consultation with the National Council. “There is nowhere in our constitution which says that the running mate is selected through a contest or through a campaign; so the people who are busily urging bloggers to promote themselves, you are wrong,” he said.

title: Maritime Unions Sound Alarm Over Jones Act Waiver Compliance, Foreign Crews and National Security
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
Oil tanker lines up to sail under Califronia's Golden Gate Bridge. Photo by Andy Randy Shutterstock
Nine maritime labor organizations say the Trump administration’s prolonged Jones Act waiver raises serious questions about compliance with federal law, including reporting requirements, immigration restrictions and the use of foreign vessels in domestic commerce.
Nine U.S. maritime labor organizations are raising fresh concerns over the Trump administration’s ongoing Jones Act waiver, warning that foreign-flagged vessels may be conducting domestic voyages without meeting federal reporting requirements and other legal safeguards intended to protect American mariners and national security.
In an October 27 letter to House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Ranking Member Rick Larsen (D-Wash.) and Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee Ranking Member Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.), the unions questioned whether the waiver complies with restrictions enacted under the Fiscal Year 2023 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).
The letter comes as the administration’s Jones Act waiver, first issued March 17 amid disruptions caused by the war with Iran, approaches its November 15 expiration following two extensions. The waiver allows certain foreign-flagged vessels to transport cargo between U.S. ports, temporarily setting aside the Jones Act’s requirement that domestic waterborne cargo move aboard U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and U.S.-crewed vessels.
At issue is whether the waiver meets the NDAA’s requirement that such exemptions be granted only when “necessary in the interest of national defense to address an immediate adverse effect on military operations.”
The unions argue that the extent of foreign-vessel activity under the waiver is difficult to reconcile with that standard.
“The Administration, meanwhile, has provided Congress and the public with little of the required information regarding the need for the waivers and the availability of U.S. vessels as required by law,” the organizations wrote.
They also allege that some waiver recipients have submitted inadequate documentation, missed mandatory reporting deadlines or failed to report their voyages altogether.
Under federal requirements, vessel operators must submit post-voyage reports to the Maritime Administration within 10 days, including details about the vessel, cargo, ports visited and why the voyage served national defense interests.
According to the unions, many operators have provided generic explanations or simply responded “not applicable” when asked to explain the national defense justification for their movements.
Foreign Crews Raise Additional Legal Questions
The labor organizations also raised concerns about the use of foreign mariners aboard vessels operating in U.S. domestic commerce, including potential violations of immigration, employment and tax laws.
The letter specifically questions whether foreign crewmembers holding D-1 visas are legally permitted to work aboard vessels transporting cargo between U.S. ports.
“Immigration law, for example, prohibits foreign crewmembers holding a D-1 visa from engaging in domestic commerce, yet many waiver operations appear to employ precisely such D-1 visa mariners,” the unions wrote.
The organizations also pointed to recent Internal Revenue Service guidance raising questions about U.S. tax obligations for foreign vessel operators and mariners participating in domestic transportation.
They argue that allowing foreign crews to perform domestic shipping work without meeting comparable legal, licensing and security requirements puts American mariners at a competitive disadvantage.
The letter further raises national security concerns, citing reported use of the waiver by Chinese state-owned shipping company COSCO and a separate instance involving Russian mariners.
“These concerns are especially troubling because the Jones Act waiver authority was intended to strengthen national security,” the organizations wrote. “Instead, the program appears to have enabled hundreds of domestic voyages by foreign vessels crewed by foreign mariners operating under exemptions from laws that Congress never intended to set aside.”
The unions cite media reports alleging espionage activity involving COSCO vessels near U.S. coastlines, but the letter does not establish that any vessel operating under the waiver engaged in espionage.
The latest letter adds to mounting congressional scrutiny of the waiver, including questions raised by Carbajal earlier this month over foreign-vessel reporting and compliance with federal law.
As gCaptain reported on October 19, Carbajal asked Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to explain how the department is enforcing immigration, tax and maritime requirements aboard foreign vessels operating under the waiver.
That inquiry followed gCaptain’s September reporting identifying evidence of at least 14 previously unreported domestic tanker voyages and a possible 15th, expanding on a Bloomberg Government investigation that found foreign vessels had transported more than $40 million in petroleum products without appearing in MARAD’s public waiver records.
A gCaptain review of MARAD data published September 16 counted 255 completed movements under the original waiver and its first extension. The additional voyages suggested the official tally was incomplete.
MARAD previously told Bloomberg Government that it lacks legal authority to compel operators to submit required reports. Jones Act enforcement falls to U.S. Customs and Border Protection.
The administration has since tightened its waiver procedures. Under rules introduced with the August 17 extension, operators must submit vessel availability requests before conducting a voyage, allowing MARAD to assess whether a qualified U.S.-flag vessel is available. The Department of War then determines whether the movement qualifies under the waiver.
Whether those changes have addressed the broader compliance concerns remains an open question.
Carbajal has requested a response from DHS by October 31.
The October 27 letter was signed by leaders of nine maritime labor organizations, including the Seafarers International Union, American Maritime Officers, Marine Engineers’ Beneficial Association, Masters, Mates and Pilots, Sailors’ Union of the Pacific, American Radio Association, Marine Firemen’s Union, AFL-CIO Maritime Trades Department and AFL-CIO Transportation Trades Department.
“American mariners stand ready to support the nation’s energy, transportation, and national security needs,” the unions wrote. “We ask only for a faithful enforcement of the laws enacted by Congress.”

title: GAYO, AMA hold roundtable to secure funding and institutional backing for Accra’s methane reduction plan
body: The Green Africa Youth Organization (GAYO) and the Accra Metropolitan Assembly (AMA) have held a roundtable to get government institutions and funders to commit to Accra’s plan to cut methane emissions from waste. The Accra LOW-M Institutional and Climate Finance Roundtable: Advancing Coordinated Action and Climate Finance for Urban Methane Reduction, held on Wednesday at the Africa Regent Hotel in Accra, focused on the Accra LOW-M (Lowering Organic Waste Methane) Portfolio. The plan aims to cut methane emissions from the city’s waste by at least 30 percent by 2030, mainly by turning organic waste into compost and biogas instead of sending it to landfills. The meeting, co-organised with the Global Alliance for Incinerator Alternatives (GAIA) and C40 Cities, brought together the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, the Ministry of Finance, the Environmental Protection Agency and its Ghana Carbon Markets Office, the private sector and informal waste workers. Fathia Selasi Charway-Glover, Project Coordinator on GAYO’s Zero Waste Cities Project, said the aim was to get each institution to take responsibility for its part of the plan. “Today, we are essentially here to bring together all institutions across government offices and across the roles of each of these institutions when it comes to the implementation of the portfolio,” she said. She explained that LOW-M is a global initiative supported by the Climate and Clean Air Coalition. It was launched at COP28 to encourage cities to set targets for reducing organic waste and methane by 2030. She said more than 55 percent of Accra’s waste is organic, and that the plan depends on separating it at source. Desmond Alugnoa, Africa Programme Manager of GAIA, said the portfolio was designed to bring scattered efforts under one plan. “This is to help coordinate all the implementation activities that are happening within the city and beyond the city,” he said. He added that informal waste workers would be central to educating households on separating their waste, and that he was looking to the Ministry of Finance to commit budget to collection, composting and biogas. The AMA says it needs that support. Victor Kotey, the Assembly’s Climate Change Focal Point, said waste management is expensive and the Assembly cannot raise enough revenue on its own. “Investment is a problem in the waste sector and in the other sectors as well,” he said. He warned that without more effort and money, Ghana may not meet its 2030 target. Engineer Godfred Fiifi Boadi, Head of Climate Action, Sustainability and Partnerships at the Ministry of Local Government, said the plan builds on existing national efforts, including compost plants, biogas facilities and faecal sludge treatment plants. “There are many interventions across the country that helps to divert this organic waste from actually entering landfills,” he said. The roundtable is expected to produce four outcomes: a responsibility matrix naming the lead institution and focal person for each action, a six- to 12-month action plan, a pipeline of projects seeking funding, and a tracker to monitor commitments made at the meeting. Organisers say the outcomes will be shared with participants in early November, with follow-up on commitments through to December. END.

title: Honeywell to Invest $500 Million in New Arizona Manufacturing Facility
body:
Honeywell Aerospace plans to significantly expand its manufacturing capacity for commercial aviation and defence programmes. The company will invest $500 million in a new 300,000-square-foot facility in Tempe, Arizona, with production scheduled to begin in late 2028. The site will also support priority defence programmes and next-generation aerospace technologies. Honeywell Aerospace is expanding its Tempe campus near Phoenix with a new advanced manufacturing facility designed to meet growing demand from both commercial and defence customers . The company said the $500 million investment will add approximately 300,000 square feet of production space and support current as well as future aerospace programmes. Digital manufacturing and automation The new plant will feature an integrated digital production system, modular robotics, automated inspection, digital twins and an end-to-end digital thread linking engineering and manufacturing processes. Honeywell also plans to increase its level of vertical integration by bringing more complex machining capabilities in-house. According to the company, this area of the supply chain is currently constrained, and additional internal capacity is intended to improve resilience and reduce dependence on external suppliers. Support for next-generation systems The Tempe facility will support production of next-generation products including the Assure advanced actuation system and Attune vapor-cycle cooling subsystems. Honeywell said the site will also provide additional capacity for current programmes and for approximately $15 billion in new Control Systems programme wins. The facility is also intended to support priority production of critical defence technologies covered by a supplier framework agreement signed with the U.S. government in March. Around 600 new jobs The new facility is expected to create around 600 permanent jobs over time, strengthening Honeywell Aerospace’s engineering and skilled manufacturing workforce in Arizona. Construction of the plant is also expected to support more than 1,000 local jobs. The facility will be located close to Honeywell Aerospace’s global headquarters in Phoenix. Honeywell Aerospace employs more than 36,000 people worldwide and supplies technologies for commercial air transport, business aviation, defence and space platforms. More capacity for defence and aerospace programmes The investment reflects the growing pressure on aerospace and defence manufacturers to increase production while also making supply chains more resilient. Honeywell is therefore not only adding physical capacity, but also investing in automation, digital manufacturing and deeper in-house production. The new Tempe facility is intended to support higher output for both existing programmes and future commercial and military requirements. Source: Honeywell Aerospace

title: Mayor and entrepreneur: Transparency International calls for dismissal of Georgian officials over business ties
body: TI identifies 24 officials heading private companies Transparency International Georgia (TI) has identified 24 serving public officials who simultaneously hold directorships at 30 private companies, in violation of anti-corruption legislation. The officials include mayors, deputy mayors, heads of municipal councils and representatives of state agencies. Georgian law prohibits public officials from simultaneously engaging in business activities. TI says officials whose violations are confirmed must be dismissed. Under the law, newly appointed officials have 10 days to relinquish their positions as directors of commercial organisations. Failure to comply requires them to leave public service. Georgia: Billionaire Ivanishvili meets ruling party leaders – what is known about their talks after silent video release Talk reportedly included jailed ex-PM Gharibashvili and other fallen Ivanishvili allies. What else was disclosed – and what was reportedly decided behind closed doors? According to the list published by Transparency International Georgia, the officials named include: Merab Bekaia – deputy head of Tbilisi’s Isani district administration and director of private company Hydraulic Service +. Nino Vashakidze – deputy head of Tbilisi City Hall’s Property Management Agency and director of two private companies, Bidara and Il Gudauri. Guram Sagaradze – head of the Foreign Ministry’s International Economic Relations Department and director of private company Kospot. Shota Andriadze – deputy director of the state-run Municipal Development Fund and director of private company Aipi. Tamta Kvelaidze – deputy head of the National Wine Agency and director of private company Wine Events and Consulting. Temur Gasviani – deputy minister of justice and civic integration of the Autonomous Republic of Abkhazia and director of private company Strada. Archil Jakel i – deputy director of the State Services Agency of the Autonomous Republic of Abkhazia and director of two private companies, Konka and Iveron Construction Company. Giorgi Nachkebia – mayor of Martvili and director of private company Buduli. Berdia Chankseliani – deputy prosecutor for Ambrolauri, Lentekhi, Oni and Tsageri municipalities and director of private company Chankseliani Marani. Mikhail Tarakhchev – deputy director of Adjara’s public broadcaster and director of three private companies, Inform-Mobile Georgia, Mai Kavkasia and Suzhou Machinery and Equipment – Georgia. Valentina Naveriani – deputy mayor of Bolnisi and director of private company Levnli. Giorgi Dolidze – deputy chair of Tskaltubo Municipal Council and director of private company Victoria. Jaba Khozrevanidze – chair of the People’s Power party faction in Adigeni Municipal Council and director of private company Blebi. Giorgi Shavreshiani – chair of the People’s Power party faction in Lentekhi Municipal Council and director of private company Tvibi-001. Archil Chachanidze – chair of a commission of Khashuri Municipal Council and director of two private companies, Transit Service 888 and Trapizontransport Company. Mamuka Sinauridze – deputy chair of the People’s Power party faction in Kutaisi Municipal Council and director of private company Rustaveli Art Group. Irakli Dzadzamia – deputy chair of the ruling Georgian Dream party faction in Tsalenjikha Municipal Council and director of private company Global Construction Group. Nodar Asatiani – deputy chair of the Georgian Dream party faction in Tskaltubo Municipal Council and director of private company Asani Construction. Otar Sulashvili – deputy chair of the Georgian Dream party faction in Tskaltubo Municipal Council and director of private company Prometheus. Ucha Khutsishvili – deputy chair of the Georgian Dream party faction in Kazbegi Municipal Council and director of private company Take Energy. Giorgi Gibradze – head of Bolnisi City Hall’s Spatial Planning and Infrastructure Department and director of two private companies, G and N Business Group and Pagi. Solomon Gorashvili – head of Dedoplistskaro City Hall’s Infrastructure, Spatial Planning, Architecture and Construction Department and director of private company Mirzaani. Roland Abuladze – head of Khulo City Hall’s Healthcare and Social Protection Department and head of the Adjara Clan cooperative. Bidzina Mekvevrishvili – deputy chair of the Georgian Dream party faction in Akhmeta Municipal Council and head of the Magraani agricultural cooperative. 'One cashbox' for two parties: Transparency International Georgia study According to the study, a significant share of the pro-government People’s Power’s funding comes from people who previously financed the ruling party. What the law says Article 13 of Georgia’s Law on Combating Corruption restricts public officials from engaging in business activities and managing private companies. The aim is to separate public and private economic interests and reduce the risk of conflicts of interest. At the same time, the law allows public officials to own shares in commercial enterprises, which gives them a different legal status from that of a company director. Transparency International Georgia argues that simultaneously holding public office and managing a private company creates corruption risks. The organisation calls on the government to take action in accordance with the law.

title: Nigeria reviews national security strategy to address terrorism, cyber threats, misinformation
body:
The Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA) has inaugurated a committee to review Nigeria’s National Security Strategy (NSS) 2019 and develop a new framework to address emerging security threats, including terrorism, banditry, kidnapping, misinformation, and cybercrime, among others.
The 33-member committee is chaired by Sarkin Bello, a retired Nigerian Army major general, who is deputised by Emeka Onumajuru, also a retired major general.
The National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu, inaugurated the committee on Thursday, 29th October. The committee is expected to submit its final draft of the NSS 2026 to the NSA by 27 November.
Represented by the committee’s chairperson, Mr Ribadu said the review was necessary because Nigeria’s domestic, regional and global security environments had changed significantly since 2019.
He added that the new strategy would serve as an overarching framework for coordinating national security, resilience and sustainable development.
The NSA said the strategy must reflect current realities, anticipate future disruptions and support the government’s national objectives under President Bola Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda, particularly in human security, economic transformation and national cohesion.
“Nigeria demands a strategy that is realistic and implementable,” he said, urging committee members to work with resource institutions and relevant stakeholders to produce a comprehensive and actionable document.
He assured the committee that ONSA would provide the administrative, technical and logistical support required to complete the assignment.
Mr Onumajuru said the country’s changing security environment required a thorough reassessment of its strategic priorities.
He said conventional security threats, including terrorism, insurgency and banditry, had become intertwined with non-kinetic challenges such as cyber threats, economic instability, food insecurity and climate change.
“The National Security Strategy 2026 must be an inclusive, forward-looking and highly actionable blueprint,” he said.
Mr Onumajuru said the committee would work with its secretariat and consult resource institutions, private-sector leaders and traditional rulers to develop a comprehensive strategy.
He said the committee’s composition, which includes representatives of the armed forces, intelligence agencies, government ministries, civil society and academia, would help ensure a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach to national security.
He urged members to begin work immediately, stressing the need for rigorous analysis, professional integrity and constructive engagement to meet the submission deadline.
“Together, we will deliver a strategy that firmly safeguards the sovereignty, unity and future prosperity of the Federal Republic of Nigeria,” he said.

title: Alleged Cyberbullying: Sowore Seeks Adjournment, Trial Resumes November 3
body: The trial of the presidential candidate of the African Action Congress (AAC), Omoyele Sowore, over alleged cyberbullying was stalled on Thursday at the Federal High Court in Abuja following his absence and a letter seeking an adjournment. At the mention of the case, prosecuting counsel, Akinlolu Kehinde (SAN), noted that the defendant was absent from court. Defence counsel, T. O. Etonyeaku, who said she was holding the brief of Sowore’s lead counsel, Adeyinka Olumide-Fusika (SAN), told the court that the politician was in Ekiti State for his presidential campaigns. Etonyeaku subsequently prayed the court for a stand-down to enable another senior lawyer, who was earlier in court before the commencement of proceedings, to arrive and conduct the defence. However, the presiding judge, Justice Mohammed Umar, drew the attention of both lawyers to a letter written to the court by Sowore and asked Kehinde whether he was aware of it. The prosecution counsel denied being copied on the letter, arguing that it was wrong for an accused person represented by a lawyer to bypass counsel and write directly to the court without copying the other party. He added that since there was no evidence that Sowore had discontinued the services of his lawyer, Olumide-Fusika, he ought not to have written personally to the court. Kehinde, however, conceded to an adjournment in the interest of justice. The prosecuting lawyer also noted that the defence was yet to respond to the written address he filed, as ordered by the court, on the issue of whether he could be subpoenaed to testify as a defence witness. Justice Umar subsequently adjourned the case until November 3 for the adoption of addresses and continuation of the defence. Sowore is being prosecuted by the Department of State Services (DSS) over posts he published on X, formerly Twitter, and Facebook in August 2025, in which he described President Bola Tinubu as a “criminal” and accused him of lying about the level of corruption in the country.

title: Marconi Technologies Receives U.S. Army Orion Radio Order
body: The U.S. Army has awarded Marconi Technologies a delivery order for the latest Orion long-range mission packages (LRMP), giving units the organic assets to connect across long distances and rugged terrain, without depending on satellite links. The delivery order makes Marconi responsible for the radio, networking and power components of the Army’s Terrestrial Line-of-Sight (TRILOS) modernization capability, putting the newest generation of systems in warfighters’ hands now, ready for the current fight. Next-gen Orion radios will provide mobile, long-range, high-capacity backbone communications Each LRMP delivers the high-capacity, low-latency connectivity the Army requires across its tactical command and control backbone. That backbone is built around decision speed, collapsing the time between sensing something on the battlefield and commanders acting on it. “We’ve reinvented the software-defined Orion radio line to continue to carry out the U.S. Army’s most demanding communication missions as we have in the past,” said Alain Cohen, CEO of Marconi Technologies. “This delivery order places the latest and most capable long-range tactical radio in the Army’s hands; it’s also a testament to how well and diligently the U.S. Army team has partnered with industry to push the art-of-the-possible.” The Orion is a sixth-generation software-defined tactical radio built for high-throughput communications in contested environments. It’s designed for missions demanding frequency agility and survivability, whether on the move or at the quick halt. title: Death toll from train collision in Spain rises to 74 — newspaper
body:
MADRID, October 29. /TASS/. At least 74 people have died in a train collision in Spain’s Toledo Province, El Diario newspaper reported.
Earlier reports put the death toll at 69.
On the morning of October 28, two passenger trains traveling along the Madrid-Seville route collided near the town of Urda in Toledo Province, in the autonomous community of Castile-La Mancha. The trains were carrying a total of more than 540 passengers.

title: Nsaa Play unveils Chop Money, offering Ghanaians chance to win prizes for GHS5
body: Gaming company Nsaa Play has launched Chop Money, a mobile raffle platform that allows Ghanaians to enter prize draws for GHS5 per ticket. The platform was unveiled at the Accra City Hotel on Thursday, October 29, 2026, offering participants the chance to win smartphones, electronics, shopping vouchers and everyday essentials. Chop Money can be accessed by dialling *2727# on any mobile phone, including basic handsets, or through its website, www.chopmoneygh.com. Users do not need to download an application or have an internet connection to participate through the USSD option. The first raffle will open in November 2026, with five winners scheduled to be drawn on December 4. A test raffle held after the launch saw participants win fuel vouchers, shopping vouchers and a mobile phone. “Our ambition is to make participating straightforward and accessible, while giving people an exciting way to engage with prizes that are relevant to their everyday lives,” Nsaa Play Limited General Manager Albert Aryee said. Akua Serwaa Adu Darko, a representative of the National Lottery Authority (NLA) Caritas Team, said the platform had met the required standards and received the Authority’s approval to operate its raffle draws. “I want to use this opportunity to encourage Ghanaians to participate fully in this promotional activity because they are duly recognized by NLA. They’ve gone through all the necessary regulatory approvals and so they have our backing to have this promotional activity.” Participants can review available prizes and the rules for each raffle before purchasing tickets. Each valid ticket counts as one entry, while participants may buy multiple tickets where the rules permit.

title: Ondo approves state burial for Fasoranti
body: By Dayo Johnson, Akure Ondo State Governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa, has set up a committee to organise a state burial for the late Afenifere leader, Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti, who died at the age of 100. According to a statement issued in Akure by the governor’s Chief Press Secretary, Prince Ebenezer Adeniyan, the committee will work with the Fasoranti family and the leadership of Afenifere to organise a befitting burial for the elder statesman. The committee is chaired by the state Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Dr Kayode Ajulo, SAN, while Apostle Eniola Olushola will serve as secretary. Other members are Hon. Gbenga Fasua, Mr Gbenga Atiba, Mrs Kosemani Kolawole, Rt. Hon. Bakkita Bello, Hon. Idowu Otetubi, Erelu Modupe Martins, Mr George Asonja, Esq., Mr Muyiwa Ogunyemi, Hon. Stephen Abitogun and Mr Adetunji Gbenga. Adeniyan said the state government decided to honour Fasoranti with a state burial in recognition of his contributions to Ondo State, Yorubaland and Nigeria. He said Aiyedatiwa believed the late Afenifere leader deserved to be celebrated for his life of service, wisdom and selfless leadership. The governor also reaffirmed the government’s commitment to ensuring that the burial reflects Fasoranti’s contributions to society. The committee is expected to coordinate the arrangements in consultation with the family and Afenifere leadership to ensure a dignified farewell for the late nationalist. title: Alyoshki residents did not want to leave for Ukraine, local resident says
body:
SIMFEROPOL, October 29. /TASS/. None of the residents of the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region wanted to leave for Ukraine, local resident Svetlana told reporters in response to a question from TASS.
"No, none of the people I know wanted to leave for Ukraine. As for what the Ukrainian authorities are saying about this, they can say whatever they want," she said.
The Russian Defense Ministry reported that, as of 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27, the Russian Armed Forces had ceased fire on the Kherson front and established a "regime of silence" in preparation for a humanitarian operation near Alyoshki.
Earlier, Russia and Ukraine, with the assistance of US First Lady Melania Trump, agreed to a ceasefire in Alyoshki to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid and prepare for the evacuation of civilians through a designated safe corridor.
Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki critical on September 21. Shelling and drone attacks by Kiev have rendered the delivery of food and medicine to the town impossible. Just over 1,000 of Alyoshki’s former 20,000 residents remain in the town.

title: Sacha Baron Cohen publicly apologizes to Kazakhstan for ‘Borat,’ 20 years after the film’s release
body: British actor Sacha Baron Cohen has publicly apologized to the people of Kazakhstan for his portrayal of Borat in the 2006 film of the same name. “Borat” follows Borat Sagdiyev, a fictional journalist from Kazakhstan who travels to the United States to make a documentary, encounters American culture, and finds himself in all sorts of comical situations. “I want to apologize to the people of Kazakhstan for the first time ever because Borat has got nothing to do with Kazakhstan,” the actor said on the podcast “Happy Sad Confused.” Baron Cohen said he had developed an earlier version of the character for the BBC, with a different name and Albanian nationality. His name and nationality later changed depending on which television channel was paying for the show. “I would just say, ‘Oh, that character already belongs to the BBC. I’ve got a completely new character, this guy’s called Alexi Krickler, he’s from Moldova,’” Baron Cohen said. The actor reiterated that at some point he had chosen Kazakhstan as a place “that no-one knows anything about.” He emphasized that he doesn’t even know what a Kazakh accent sounds like. Before recounting a complaint from the Kazakh Embassy, he apologized for being unable to imitate a Kazakh accent and said he would use Borat’s accent for the anecdote because his knowledge of Central Asian accents was limited. Baron Cohen described the apology as his first for the character he created, though he has had to defend Borat ever since the film came out. “The joke is not on Kazakhstan. I think the joke is on people who can believe that the Kazakhstan that I describe can exist,” the actor said in a 2006 interview with Rolling Stone. Over the years, Kazakhstan’s authorities have shifted from hostility toward “Borat” to acceptance. In 2005, the country’s Foreign Ministry threatened to sue Baron Cohen and claimed his show had been commissioned for political ends to tarnish the international reputation of Kazakhstan and its people. In 2006, shortly before the film’s release, the country’s authorities paid for a four-page advertising supplement in The New York Times and the International Herald Tribune touting Kazakhstan’s achievements in the 21st century. Although “Borat” was not officially banned in Kazakhstan, it never screened in the country’s movie theaters after its world premiere. The film also did not receive a theatrical distribution license in Russia. Over time, attitudes toward Borat in Kazakhstan softened. In 2017, Czech tourists in Astana got off with a small fine for walking around dressed as Borat (Baron Cohen himself offered to pay it). In 2020, Kazakh Tourism, the company responsible for promoting tourism within Kazakhstan, adopted his catchphrase “Very nice!” as the country’s official tourism slogan. By then, a sequel to “Borat” had been released worldwide, and the Kazakh diaspora in the United States continued to oppose it. In November 2020, the Kazakh American Association called for “Borat 2” to be excluded from consideration for Oscar, Golden Globe, and other award nominations.
