title: Manhunt continues for convicted murderer who escaped from Tennessee prison
body:
The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation has announced that the reward for information leading to the arrest of Jacob Morley , a man convicted of murder who escaped from a Tennessee prison on Sunday , has raised to $15,000 as authorities continue their manhunt for the escaped inmate.
The TBI said that the following rewards are being offered for information leading to the arrest: $7,500 from the Tennessee Governor’s Office, $2,5000 from TBI and $5,000 from the U.S. Marshals Service.
“Tennessee Governor Bill Lee’s Office and the U.S. Marshals Service have increased the reward as the search continues. If you have any information on Jacob Morley, please call 1-800-TBI-FIND. Stay vigilant and aware of your surroundings. Morley is considered dangerous,” the TBI said in the update.
Morley, who was serving a life sentence for killing a co-worker four years ago, was found to be missing from the Northwest Correctional Complex (NWCX) late on Sunday.
“At approximately 11:30 pm on October 25, 2026, staff at NWCX confirmed Morley was unaccounted for and immediately conducted an emergency count and search of the facility,” the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a news release .
“Further review of security cameras confirmed Morley breached the perimeter fence and exited the facility in his TDOC uniform,” the Tennessee Department of Correction said.
“Morley is serving a life sentence for a conviction in Carter County for first-degree murder, aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, evading arrest, and vandalism. He is 28 years old, 5’11” tall, and weighs approximately 240 pounds. He has brown hair and green eyes,” the news release added.
The TBI released surveillance video from a farm, showing Morley open a truck’s unlocked driver’s side door and drive off at around 1 a.m. on Monday.
Firefighters in Hornbeak, about 19 kilometres east of the farm, said on social media that investigators confirmed their cameras captured footage of the truck driving by their station about 15 minutes later.
By Tuesday afternoon, the TBI announced that the vehicle stolen by Morley was found abandoned in Marion, Illinois.
“Morley’s whereabouts remain unknown, and locating him continues to be an urgent priority for law enforcement,” the TBI added.
“Public safety is our top concern. We are working around the clock with our local, state, and federal partners to track down Morley as quickly as possible,” authorities said.
By Wednesday, Marion Police Chief David Fitts told NBC News that Morley has no known connection to the town where the truck he is accused of stealing was found.
“What we have seen kind of leads us in the direction that he’s not still here. But that doesn’t mean that we’ve stopped looking,” Fitts added.
There have also been no confirmed sightings, according to Fitts.
“There’s really nowhere for him to go here where he wouldn’t be recognized. His face is all over the news,” Fitts said.
“I have no idea why he would come here, other than I-57 is a major interstate and it runs right through the middle of our town,” Fitts said. “And I don’t know, maybe he was low on gas and just pulled off. I don’t know.”
Morley is serving a life sentence for killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022, according to The Associated Press.
Birchfield’s body was found in a box under Morley’s home after he had been missing for a few weeks. The two lived in Carter County, in eastern Tennessee.
Along with first-degree murder, Morley was convicted of aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest, The Associated Press reports.
When Morley saw deputies at his home, he led officers on a chase that ended in North Carolina, authorities said.
Birchfield’s sister, Carrie Norman, took to Facebook after news of Morley’s escape spread.
“I’ve been following this all day. Im really disappointed with the Justice System. VINE , Is a joke. Who notified me that a convicted murderer is on the loose, my best friend,” she wrote.
“Has the Sheriff called to reassure the victims that he’s working on keeping us safe, NO. So my advice to everyone in this AREA! Lock your doors, load your guns, check your cameras,” she added.
In a statement to ABC News , Norman said she was “reliving this horrible tragedy all over again.”
“I find myself asking the public for help to find my brother’s murderer when he should be in prison locked away,” she added.
Eric Mohler, Birchfield’s cousin, told CBS affiliate WREG that he doesn’t understand how Morley could “just walk out of prison.”
“He killed my cousin in cold blood. I mean, I wouldn’t put it past him doing it again, you know?” said Mohler. “Definitely watch out. People, be careful!”

title: Russia, Tanzania intend to deepen cooperation in energy, other sectors — Novak
body:
MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has met with Mwigulu Lameck Nchemba, Prime Minister of Tanzania, on the sidelines of the third Russia-Africa Summit to discuss cooperation prospects in energy, trade, finance, and banking, the Russian government announced.
"Tanzania has come a long way and is now rightfully considered an economic development leader in East Africa, which opens up new opportunities for mutually beneficial cooperation," Novak emphasized. "Russia is committed to further expanding political dialogue, parliamentary and interdepartmental exchanges, and deepening engagement in geological exploration, natural uranium extraction, energy, industry, transport, logistics, agriculture, tourism, finance, and investment."
Novak noted that Tanzania’s participation in the summit underscores the high level of bilateral relations and a shared interest in their continued development. The event creates new avenues for deepening Russia’s partnership with African nations, where Tanzania, as a key partner on the continent, can play a significant role, the government added.

title: Russian rights group documents at least 69 deaths among victims of political persecution since 2022
body: At least 69 people subjected to politically motivated persecution by Russian authorities have died in Russia since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to a report published by Memorial’s Political Prisoner Support human rights project to mark the Day of Remembrance for Victims of Political Repression. Illness and lack of medical care were the most common causes of death, accounting for 29 cases documented by the group. At least 20 people died from beatings, torture, or their aftereffects, and 10 died by suicide. One person died as a result of a hunger strike, and another — Alexey Navalny — was deliberately killed in a penal colony. The causes of death of eight others remain unknown. The group recorded the most deaths in 2024, when 26 people died. Another 13 died in 2025, and 16 died in the first 10 months of 2026, with October not yet over. The average age of those who died was 51. The youngest on the list, Ukrainians Daniil Dakhov and Pavel Grimak, were both 18. The figures include people who died in pretrial detention centers and penal colonies, as well as during searches, under house arrest, and shortly after their release. Memorial’s report recounts the stories of all 69 people who died. Meduza has reported in detail on some of them, including Ukrainian journalist Viktoria Roshchyna, pianist Pavel Kushnir, scientist Dmitry Kolker, Arctic researcher Valery Mitko, biker Kirill Buzmakov, and activist Anatoly Berezikov. title: GDIT puts Vion mission partner environment technology through its paces during Pacific exercise
body: General Dynamics Information Technology’s Vion mission partner environment kit was incorporated into the U.S. military’s recent Olympus Fires exercise in the Pacific, the company announced Thursday. The exercise came as the Defense Information Systems Agency and other military components are working to boost information sharing among allies. The demonstration of GDIT’s Vion system capabilities was the culmination of years of effort and internal investment by the company, according to Jason Myers, vice president of GDIT’s defense agencies business. “We’re actually selling it as that integrated hardware and software bundle. So, kind of view it as four different layers, if you will, of the … mission-ready tech stack: deployable cloud hardware, a secure zero-trust platform, the common data-centric services, and then the [command-and-control] mission applications,” Myers said in an interview ahead of the official announcement. “A lot of these pieces have really been in the works. But one of the things that was really critical to me this year was really doubling down to make sure that we’re putting this into users’ hands. And so that’s where a lot of these culminations really came together. And then we had certain goals we wanted to set for ourselves. You know … it’s easy to say ‘zero trust,’ it’s easy to say ‘AI.’ You know, they’re very buzzwordy. But how do you actually operationalize them? How do you influence a mission advantage? And that’s where we really felt like we came together … and we wanted to test that out at exercise and prove it. And now we feel very comfortable with what we’ve been able to go ahead and demonstrate,” he added. The deployment of the Vion system in an exercise had multiple elements to it. “First and foremost is the ability to have our own core services, right? So, when we talk about our own core services, it’s having secure AI-enabled collaboration tools, so offering real-time translation services. One of the things that people take for granted on translation is it’s been around a very long time. But that being said, it’s very tabular in nature, right? X word equals Y other word. And in the military context, that’s really difficult. Military jargon, acronyms, codes — all of those things really do play and complicate typical translation services. And so, having AI assistance to understand the context of what you’re trying to say was really, really paramount. And we used that with a number of our foreign partners,” Myers told DefenseScoop. The tech offers advanced voice, video, chat and email collaboration tools, according to GDIT. AI-assisted software development is another capability Vion brings to the table, Myers noted. Recent real-world conflicts have highlighted the importance of software innovation. “There are certain elements where, as we’ve seen in Ukraine, the ability to adapt, overcome [is critical]. You’re going to have new sensors, you’re going to have new drone feeds, you’re going to have all these things that you’re going to have to provide the warfighter, but you’re not going to have … a software development team necessarily sitting there next to those warfighters. So, how do you give somebody that’s maybe never developed before, the ability to go and build that? And that’s exactly what we were able to demonstrate on Vion with the exercise. And probably the most paramount one was how do you solve problems rapidly?” Myers said. “There were a number of customers that had interesting dynamics with their network. And they were able to take all of their network diagnostics, put it into Vion and our … secure AI-assisted platform, and not just identify what the problem was, but actually get [information telling them] here’s what you need to go fix, here’s what the fix is,” he said. As an example, Myers described a situation where some video elements were impacted. “We were able to use AI to say, ‘here’s the problem, here’s some of the logs,’ and within minutes we were back up and running and able to federate those services again,” he told DefenseScoop. Zero trust and identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) are key elements of the tools, Myers suggested. “Anybody that has a laptop and is connected to Vion has access to all of our foundational capabilities. But really the major advancement as well is the ability to then federate those services with our foreign partners. So now our foreign partners actually can reach into Vion and get access to those services as well,” he said. An aim is to prevent under-sharing and over-sharing of sensitive information. “By using our identity management, we know exactly who is trying to request access, and then leveraging that with the data tagging on the back end, we’re able to make sure that only those right partners with the right clearances and the right accesses can get access to that data,” Myers told DefenseScoop. GDIT sees a lot of demand from the U.S. military and its allies for the types of capabilities that Vion offers, Myers said, though he declined to identify specific potential customers the company is in talks with. The firm used its own money to develop Vion, he noted, an indication that the contractor had confidence that it could sell it to government buyers. “I wanted to take a risk, right? I wanted to go and say ‘we know the customer space, we know what you need,’” Myers explained. “Vion was completely built by GDIT, and we had to go prove [the effectiveness of the technology] in exercise.” GDIT isn’t fully on contract with the Pentagon for the Vion system, he told DefenseScoop. “Now the next steps are, we’ve got a couple customers who have actually stated that they plan on supporting our accreditation and broader scale deployment across a number of different organizations,” Myers said. “Our focus was let’s prove it. And now the customer has said ‘you did prove it [and] we’re going to help you scale this.’” The post GDIT puts Vion mission partner environment technology through its paces during Pacific exercise appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: 2027: Makinde pledges to revive South-East industries
body: …Promises to tackle 25% interest rates, expand long-term financing By Chinedu Adonu ENUGU — The presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Seyi Makinde, has pledged to tackle high interest rates and improve access to long-term financing to revive industries, expand businesses and create jobs in the South-East if elected president in 2027. Makinde, the Oyo State governor, made the pledge during a town hall meeting with stakeholders from the region in Enugu, where he identified manufacturing as a critical driver of economic growth, employment and poverty reduction. He said the South-East’s economic potential extended beyond trading to industrial production, particularly in commercial and manufacturing centres such as Onitsha and Nnewi in Anambra State. According to him, businesses cannot expand production or employ millions of Nigerians when interest rates remain high and long-term credit facilities are difficult to access. “Yes, trading is something this zone is synonymous with, but so is manufacturing. If you go to Onitsha and Nnewi, you will discover that the South-East is not just about trading; manufacturing is also thriving here. “You cannot expand manufacturing and employ millions of people when interest rates are at 25 per cent and long-term financing facilities are unavailable. These are two challenges we will tackle decisively,” he said. Makinde said his proposed economic reforms would shift Nigeria away from dependence on the sharing of federal allocations towards production, industrial expansion and wealth creation. “The responsibility of government is to create a conducive environment for businesses to thrive. That is precisely what we will do. We will create an enabling environment for businesses to flourish throughout the country,” he said. Drawing on his private-sector experience, the governor said access to long-term financing was essential for economic expansion, arguing that Nigeria’s financial system remained dominated by short-term loans largely suited to trading. “I come from the private sector. I started paying workers’ salaries at the age of 29, and now I am 58. I have been paying salaries from then until today, so I understand when an economy is expanding. “One indication of an expanding economy is the availability of long-term financing within the economic system. Right now, bankers can tell you that what we have been experiencing is mainly short-term financing facilities meant for trading,” he said. He said expanding manufacturing would help address unemployment, particularly among young people, and pledged to support entrepreneurs capable of creating sustainable jobs. Makinde cited the commissioning of the headquarters of Capital Sage, a conglomerate in Ibadan, as an example of the employment opportunities businesses could generate when given the right conditions to grow. Beyond industrial development, the APM candidate said his economic agenda would prioritise skills acquisition to improve young people’s employment prospects and support business expansion. He disclosed that his campaign had partnered with SkillResert Nigeria to train one million young Nigerians in skills intended to make them employable within a short period. According to him, the initiative formed part of his plan to move the economy away from dependence on public revenue distribution towards productive activities capable of generating wealth and employment. Makinde also identified unemployment and poverty as challenges requiring deliberate government intervention, warning against allowing economic hardship to deepen divisions along ethnic and religious lines. “My message to you today is this: please reject all forms of division, whether along religious or ethnic lines. The challenges we face do not recognise religion or ethnicity. “What we should do is create opportunities for our people, particularly our teeming young population, so that we can address hunger and grinding poverty and move our people from poverty to prosperity,” he said. On governance, Makinde said rebuilding public confidence in government would be central to his proposed administration, arguing that sincerity and trust between leaders and citizens could help address many of the country’s challenges. He cited his administration’s experience in Oyo State, where he said efforts had been made to bridge the trust deficit between the government and the people. The governor outlined four pillars of his proposed national development agenda: resetting the economy, restructuring the security architecture, reforming the education system and rebuilding the socio-political space. He said the party was developing its manifesto through consultations with Nigerians across the six geopolitical zones to ensure that its policies reflected the needs of the people. Makinde disclosed that the manifesto would be launched on November 4, 2026, adding that the Enugu town hall meeting marked the final session in the party’s series of zonal consultations. He also questioned the Federal Government’s continued borrowing despite claims of improved revenue collection and substantial external reserves, arguing that economic management should translate into tangible benefits for businesses and ordinary Nigerians. The APM candidate urged voters in the South-East to support his presidential ambition, acknowledging the region’s political importance and promising to take his campaign message to every part of the country. Earlier, the APM national chairman criticised the state of the economy and called on President Bola Tinubu to support Makinde’s presidential ambition. “Every Nigerian is aware that this country has not had it this bad. What is needed in this country is a reset. Nigeria is a major oil producer, and we do not know how we moved from around ₦200 to ₦1,400,” he said. The chairman questioned why Nigerians were not benefiting sufficiently from increases in international petroleum prices, given the country’s status as an oil-producing nation. He also expressed concern over the country’s security challenges. Recalling Makinde’s support for Tinubu through the G5 governors during the 2023 presidential election, the chairman urged the President to reciprocate the gesture. “Last time, you supported the president through the G5 governors. Now it is your turn, and the president should support you. I am calling on President Bola Tinubu to step down and support Seyi Makinde,” he said. The Director-General of the campaign, Felix Hyat, also appealed to South-East residents to support Makinde, citing his policy proposals and leadership experience. Hyat lamented the economic difficulties facing households, saying many Nigerians were struggling to meet their family needs. “It is unfortunate that our people can no longer cope with family demands because of the bad economy. It is time for the young people to vote them out,” he said. He also commended Makinde’s choice of a security expert as his running mate, describing the ticket as capable of addressing the country’s challenges. The post 2027: Makinde pledges to revive South-East industries appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Russia’s October losses hit record high of 49,040 with three days left, Ukraine says
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine’s Defense Forces inflicted an estimated 49,040 personnel losses on Russian forces in October as of 29 October, setting a new monthly record since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s General Staff said. The figure points to the growing human cost of Russia’s war against Ukraine. Ukraine’s military says Russian losses are rising faster than Moscow can replenish its units, making it increasingly costly for Russia to sustain its offensive operations. October losses surpass previous record The previous monthly record was set in December 2024, when Russian forces suffered an estimated 48,670 personnel losses, according to the General Staff. October’s total had already surpassed that figure by 370 personnel as of 29 October, with three days remaining in the month. The General Staff reported an average of about 1,750 Russian personnel losses per day in October so far. Russian losses rise sharply in 2026 Ukraine’s General Staff reported 26,090 Russian personnel losses in February 2026, followed by 46,230 in September. By 29 October, the October figure had reached 49,040. The figures indicate a sharp increase in reported Russian losses over the past several months. Explore further Russia now loses more soldiers than it recruits. But the war won’t end because of that. Ukraine says losses exceed Russia’s ability to replenish units The General Staff said the pace of Russian personnel losses exceeds Russia’s ability to replenish its military units. According to the Ukrainian military, the rising toll makes each month of the war increasingly costly for Moscow. The figures refer to total personnel losses and do not distinguish between those killed and wounded. They are estimates published by Ukraine’s military and could not be independently verified. Ukraine’s Defense Forces said they would continue inflicting losses on Russian forces until Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine ends. title: Private military company destroys more than 60 targets using automated turrets
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Ministry of Defense reported this.
“The Ministry of Defense and the Brave1 defense innovation cluster are continuing their efforts to integrate automated turrets into the air defense system . More effective systems in service mean more lives saved and a safer sky over Ukraine,” the statement reads.
The Ministry of Defense noted that Brave1 began developing automated turrets back in 2024. Today, such systems are not merely experimental technologies but an integral part of the air defense system.
They are already in service with the Ukrainian Air Force and are destroying enemy threats, including “Banderole” rockets and “Geran-5” drones.
Automated turrets have already destroyed more than 60 targets as part of the private air defense project.
In the last month alone, these systems have destroyed dozens of enemy unmanned aerial vehicles over Kyiv.
“This is the result of systematic work, which proves that the latest Ukrainian developments are capable of effectively countering air threats both on the front lines and over cities, thereby protecting critical infrastructure,” the ministry emphasized.
The private air defense project is being implemented in accordance with Resolution No. 1506 of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine dated November 19, 2025.
It allows companies to provide additional protection for their employees, production facilities, and energy infrastructure, which are systematically subjected to attacks by enemy drones.
In addition, this decision allows for the rapid scaling up of air defense capabilities without placing an additional burden on the Ukrainian Defense Forces’ air defense system.
As reported by Ukrinform, nearly 100 enterprises have joined the pilot project to integrate enterprises —regardless of ownership structure—into Ukraine’s air defense system.

title: Germany plans electronic surveillance of Russia, Belarus from Lithuania — vice admiral
body:
LONDON, October 29. /TASS/. Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr, plan to use their unit in Lithuania to monitor Russia and Belarus with electronic warfare equipment, Vice Admiral Thomas Daum, head of the Bundeswehr’s cyber forces, told Reuters .
German troops intend to gather data on radar systems and other equipment emitting radio waves in Russia and Belarus, he said. The unit is scheduled to be fully deployed in 2027.
According to the report, German troops are testing electronic warfare systems in Lithuania, including drone detectors, signal interceptors, jammers and sensors designed to relay battlefield data to remote analysts.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected claims that Russia plans to attack NATO countries. Russian President Vladimir Putin has described such statements by Western politicians as attempts to frighten their own populations and justify increased military spending. Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the alliance is pursuing "unbridled militarization" and using the portrayal of Russia as a threat to justify its members’ decision to raise defense spending to 5% of GDP.

title: COSCO Profit Jumps Most in Two Years as Turmoil Supports Rates
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
(Bloomberg) — Cosco Shipping Holdings Co. earnings jumped the most in two years as persistent geopolitical disruptions rerouted trade routes, tying up more of its vessels for longer while container rates surged.
Third-quarter net income rose 81% to 17.2 billion yuan ($2.6 billion), with transpacific sailings the biggest growth driver, according to a Thursday filing.
Cosco’s strong showing foreshadows a bumper season for some of its global peers. Earnings estimates for Europe’s A.P. Moller-Maersk A/S and Hapag-Lloyd AG have ticked up since July.
Japan’s Nippon Yusen KK’s raised outlook surpassed analyst expectations earlier on Thursday, while Taiwan’s Evergreen Marine Corp. is set for its most profitable quarter since 2024 when it reports next month.
Global supply chains remained stretched throughout the quarter as vessels continue to route sailings between Asia and Europe around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope to avoid the Middle East.
That’s pushed spot rates for a 40-foot container near two-year highs, a level that held for most of the quarter, according to Drewry World Container Index data.
Container spot rates are likely to stay where they are, with transpacific spot rates remaining firmly anchored near post-pandemic highs amid resilient US trade flows, said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Lindsay Chen.

title: CAR Tightens Border Checks As DR Congo Ebola Cases Rise
body: As the Democratic Republic of Congo grapples with its deadliest Ebola epidemic in history, the neighbouring Central African Republic has tightened frontier controls, with daily checks on the many travellers crossing the border. With the vast majority of the 10,000 cases recorded to date in Africa’s latest outbreak of the deadly virus having been logged in the DRC, officials in the Centrafrican capital Bangui are worried about the disease spilling over the Oubangui river dividing the two nations. At the M’Poko Bac pier, in the Bimbo district southwest of the capital, travellers who have just crossed the river from the DRC wash their hands under the watchful eye of a health worker, before having their temperature taken. “Passengers arriving by canoe dock at the entry point. Then they disembark one at a time,” explained Maldiana Bagalama, tasked with health screening at the site. “One of our colleagues is there to direct them to the hand-washing station. Next, we brief them on the situation, then direct them to the tent for temperature checks and registration,” Bagalama added. Fears that an outbreak which has killed almost 5,000 people will reach the CAR are fuelled by the presence of the virus in the three Congolese regions bordering the country. On top of that, the DRC and CAR share a porous and largely unmonitored frontier stretching for more than 1,500 kilometres (930 miles). While the DRC is the epicentre of the outbreak, the virus has nonetheless spread to several other regions on the continent, with several cases reported in Kenya and one detected as far west as Nigeria. Ebola, transmitted through contact with bodily fluids and which causes a severe haemorrhagic fever, has already claimed more than 15,000 lives in Africa over the past 50 years. Despite the risks, economic activity continues apace along the Oubangui river. Fishermen, canoe operators, sellers of fresh fish and many others all depend on the vital waterway linking between the two countries. ‘Constant Contact’ “We are worried because we work right here, by the river, and if Ebola reaches here we shall be the first to fall victim to it. We’re asking the ministry of health to take far greater precautions,” said Neige, a fishmonger and mother-of-three. A few metres away, Foxy Yeti Nzapa, 25, ferried passengers by canoe. A father-of-two, he fears that travel between the two countries may expose him to the virus. “It’s hard to find work in the Central African Republic and this is my only source of income. My concern is that the people we bring back from the other side might also put us at risk, given that we provide transport between the two countries without any protection. It’s dangerous,” he said. “From over there, we sometimes hear this or that person has died of Ebola. I could also become infected. So we need preventive measures to protect ourselves, as we are in constant contact with the other side,” Foxy insisted. His concern is shared by the Centrafrican authorities, which insist that they have toughened their border controls. Never Too Prepared “We have entry points staffed by health workers, the Water and Forests Department, Customs, Civil Protection and Internal Security Forces,” explained Dr Valentin Nebanga, departmental head at the Ministry of Health. “All passengers, both those arriving and departing, are systematically screened by community health workers. “They take their temperatures and ask travellers a number of questions using a standardised form,” Nebanga added. In addition to those checks, the authorities have launched awareness-raising campaigns. Neighbourhood chiefs, community leaders and religious figures are being drafted in to pass on prevention guidelines to residents. For Nebanga, preparedness also means keeping the public engaged and making sure that they understand the importance of protective measures, particularly while there are no reported cases in the CAR. Yet around the river, residents’ growing concerns are starkly visible in their daily lives. For those who make a living from river transport, fishing or trade, avoiding travel is not always an option. “We’ve not had any cases yet, but our biggest challenge remains retaining staff and keeping them engaged,” said Nebanga. But “we are never fully prepared”, he conceded. AFP The post CAR Tightens Border Checks As DR Congo Ebola Cases Rise appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Lithuania plans to introduce universal military conscription for men ages 18–22 starting in 2032
body: Lithuania’s State Defense Council has decided to introduce universal conscription in 2032, President Gitanas Nausėda said. Universal conscription will apply to men ages 18 to 22 , replacing the current selective draft . Women will still be able to volunteer for military service. Lithuania currently drafts about 5,000 young people each year. Nausėda said the annual intake under universal conscription would be about 7,500 young men, based on demographic trends and the number of conscripts fit for service. The 2032 start date was chosen to give the military time to prepare its infrastructure for the larger intake. Lithuania abolished compulsory military service in 2008. It reinstated conscription in 2015 amid “ increased threats ” following Russia’s annexation of Crimea. Lithuania requires nine months of military service, or three months for those with specialized military qualifications. Baltic security The Baltic states fear a Russian invasion. title: 2027: Tinubu lacks energy to govern, Obi says
body: …Urges South-East to shun ethnic politics By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki ABAKALIKI — The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, has questioned President Bola Tinubu’s competence and energy to govern Nigeria, urging him to leave office and rest. Obi spoke at an NDC town hall and stakeholders’ meeting held at the Citi-Hub Centre, Mile 50, Abakaliki, Ebonyi State, where he urged Nigerians to unite behind candidates based on their qualifications and capacity to deliver good governance rather than ethnic considerations. He cautioned the South-East against division, insisting that voters in Ebonyi and other parts of the country should support him based on his credentials, not because he is Igbo. “Let nobody divide the South-East. I don’t want the people of Ebonyi to vote for me because I am from the South-East. I don’t want you to vote for me because I am an Igbo person. “My dear people, I want you to vote for me because I am qualified to be the President of this country. I want you to vote for me because I am the leading candidate,” he said. The former Anambra State governor challenged Tinubu to explain his administration’s record over the past three years, particularly the use of funds borrowed by the Federal Government. “I want President Tinubu to come to Abakaliki to tell the people what he has done in the past three years. I want him to come to Abakaliki to tell you what he used the money he has been borrowing to do for the past three years,” Obi said. He also questioned the President’s reported time spent outside Nigeria, arguing that he should be able to travel across the country to account for his administration’s performance. “President Tinubu does not have the competence to run Nigeria. He does not have the energy to run Nigeria. He should pack his things, go home and rest,” Obi said. Outlining his proposed priorities if elected president in 2027, Obi said his administration would declare emergencies in key sectors, including national unity, security, education, healthcare, corruption and food production. On national unity, he said his government would seek to reduce ethnic divisions and ensure that appointments reflected the federal character principle. “We must unite this country. Our pride should not be consideration of employment, this or that. We will operate federal character for all the jobs we have. So, we must unite the country,” he said. On security, Obi promised decisive action against insecurity and pledged to equip security agencies to protect lives and property. “We will declare emergency in the security of lives and property in Nigeria. We will deal with insecurity decisively. Nobody will be in charge, we will be in charge,” he said. He specifically promised stronger action against kidnappers targeting schoolchildren, saying his administration would ensure that security agencies pursued those responsible and protected vulnerable communities. “If I am President of this country, kids come to school and somebody takes them into the bush, we will be in the bush with such person. They will not be there alone, we will be there with those kids,” he said. On corruption, the NDC candidate pledged to ensure that public funds were used for public benefit and that offenders faced prosecution, regardless of their position. “We will declare emergency in corruption. I will fight corruption like nobody has fought it before. Public money must be used for public good, nobody will steal our money again. If you do it, you will go to jail starting from the President,” Obi said. He also promised to prioritise education, citing the large number of Nigerian children out of school and pledging to reduce the figure. “We will declare emergency in education. We have over 18 million children out of school, we must reduce it,” he said. On food security, Obi said his administration would support farmers to return to their farms, increase agricultural production and boost exports. “We have vast lands, our farmers must go back to farm, be able to cultivate, give us what we eat and be able to export,” he said. He further pledged to strengthen healthcare delivery by ensuring that every political ward in the country had access to functional healthcare facilities. “We will declare emergency in health. We must have a functional healthcare in all the political ward of Nigeria. Every ward must have it, we have the resources to do it,” he said. title: KuCoin crypto exchange halts services for Russian, Belarusian users
body:
MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. KuCoin cryptocurrency exchange discontinues provision of services to users in Russia and Belarus, the trading platform said.
"At KuCoin, compliance has always been fundamental to our operations. In line with applicable legal and regulatory requirements, KuCoin will discontinue services for users in Russia and Belarus effective immediately. This will comprehensively cover access to all KuCoin products, services, and features," the crypto exchange said.
"We recognize this may cause inconvenience to affected users, and we are committed to an orderly termination process that allows affected users to close positions and withdraw their assets," KuCoin said. Affected users will receive notices with the relevant deadlines and the procedure for positions closing, the crypto exchange added.

title: In Arctic, US Army researchers test camo that could adapt to changing landscapes
body: In a future battlespace, boats, vehicles and weapons could deploy and travel with outer shells or coverings that change with the terrain — or even light and time of year — to add an extra layer of concealment. That concept was one of the key testing lines of effort in an Army Corps of Engineers and Army Research Laboratory experiment in Pituffik, Greenland, earlier this year. The whole endeavor was part of a broader testing series organized by the International Cooperative Engagement Program for Polar Research (ICE-PPR) and the Office of Naval Research, a multi-national endeavor that underscores the ever-increasing importance of the Arctic as a warfighting domain. It is also a domain that presents unique challenges for camouflage, said Dr. Tom Douglas, a research chemist and senior scientific technical manager of the Army Corps of Engineers’ Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory Alaska Research Office in Fairbanks, Alaska. “It’s dark for some periods; it’s light for other periods,” Douglas told Military Times in an interview. “Everything can look kind of yellow or orange when the sun’s setting … you’ve got sea ice, which can look kind of gray … You can stand out pretty blatantly in a vast open white field where there’s no vegetation, right? So there’s that, and then thinking about coatings or snow covering things, and maybe making it worse now that your camo doesn’t work.” Anthony Fragoso, a cold regions artificial intelligence lead at CRREL, said that his lab worked with ARL staff during ship-to-shore operations to test “a number of novel coatings,” using sensors to assess the effectiveness of concealment. “If you go beyond the visible, which our adversaries can do, snow in certain wavelengths looks black. But it’s white in visible,” Fragoso told Military Times in a separate interview. “So trying to match that is a challenge.” Researchers, Fragoso said, were inspired by Arctic foxes in Pituffik, which change colors over the course of the year – from white in the winter to brown in the summer. An Arctic fox walks on Svalbard archipelago on August 27, 2020, near Longyearbyen, Norway. It’s best known for its thick, warm fur that is also used as camouflage. (Maja Hitij/Getty Images) “Things that are reversible, flexible is kind of what we’re after,” he said, adding that researchers considered units like the Alaska-based 11th Airborne Division, which also regularly deploys to the Pacific. “They’re the Arctic Angels, but they are also worried about fighting in the jungle,” he said. “So they don’t want to paint stuff white, and then it has to go to Taiwan.” While still at the scientific research and development level, the work is making its way to operational units already, with upcoming plans to test a rapidly deployable coating system on the Army’s Cold Weather All-Terrain Vehicles in Alaska. “The Alaska National Guard is going to fly over it with helicopters, film it with thermal, all that stuff,” Fragoso said. “Everything now is counter-[unmanned aerial systems], so it’s making sure stuff isn’t being spotted from above by a $1,000 drone.” Mike Parker, the cold regions mobility lead for CRREL, emphasized that this effort to test flexible camouflage extends beyond the Arctic. With surveillance from above essentially a given in contemporary warfare, additional layers of concealment, particularly those that can be easily altered to fit changing environments, are in unprecedented demand. “It has to remain flexible, and all aspects of it are on the table,” Parker said. “It doesn’t have to be just a coating; it could be a fabric … anything that can give us the tactical advantage is being evaluated.”

title: Sowore Writes Court, Seeks Adjournment In Cyberbullying Trial
body: The trial of African Action Congress (AAC) presidential candidate, Omoyele Sowore, over alleged cyberbullying was stalled on Thursday after he was absent from court and wrote to seek an adjournment. At the mention of the case before the Federal High Court in Abuja, prosecuting counsel, Akinlolu Kehinde (SAN), noted Sowore’s absence. Defence counsel, T. O. Etonyeaku, who said she was holding the brief of Adeyinka Olumide-Fusika (SAN), told the court that Sowore had travelled to Ekiti State for his presidential campaign activities. Etonyeaku asked the court to stand down the matter to allow another senior lawyer, who had been in court before proceedings began, to arrive and conduct the defence. Justice Mohammed Umar, however, drew the attention of both lawyers to a letter personally written to the court by Sowore and asked Kehinde if he was aware of it. Kehinde said he had not been copied on the letter. He argued that it was improper for a defendant represented by counsel to write directly to the court without copying the prosecution. He added that since there was no evidence that Sowore had discontinued the services of his lawyer, Olumide-Fusika, the defendant ought not to have written to the court personally. The prosecution counsel, however, agreed to an adjournment in the interest of justice. Kehinde also told the court that the defence was yet to respond to a written address he filed, as directed by the court, on whether he could be subpoenaed to testify as a defence witness. Justice Umar adjourned the case until November 3 for the adoption of addresses and continuation of the defence. The Department of State Services (DSS) is prosecuting Sowore over posts he published on X, formerly Twitter, and Facebook in August 2025, in which he described President Bola Tinubu as a “criminal” and accused him of lying about the level of corruption in the country. The post Sowore Writes Court, Seeks Adjournment In Cyberbullying Trial appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Why India Needs To ‘Smell The Coffee’ On Future Warfare
body:
When General David Petraeus, former Director of the CIA and commander of US forces in Iraq and Afghanistan, delivered his prescription for modern warfare at the NDTV World Summit last week, it reverberated sharply through India’s national security corridors. His message was stark: future battlefields will be dominated by drone swarms, cheap autonomous weapons, and algorithmic warfare where traditional maneuver assets like tanks, surface ships, and manned aircraft face extreme vulnerability. In Petraeus’s view, every military on Earth requires a top-to-bottom institutional revolution, unlearning legacy concepts, overhaul of procurement cycles to weekly software iterations, and turning force structures on their heads.
However, when applied to India, a country that only recently nearly went to war with one nuclear neighbour, has an ongoing military standoff with another, how realistic is this radical prescription?
On NDTV’s India Matters, anchored by LivefistDefence.com founder Shiv Aroor, former Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Arun Prakash, a 1971 war hero and naval aviator now a strategic affairs commentator, delivered a sobering, unvarnished reality check from the perspective of India’s military establishment. While acknowledging Petraeus’s insights into Ukraine and the Middle East, Admiral Prakash outlined why India remains dangerously far from executing such a transformation, constrained by structural inertia, political distraction, and a widening technological gap with China.
General Petraeus urged militaries to throw out legacy playbooks and embrace rapid institutional change. But as Admiral Prakash pointed out, the Indian defence ecosystem historically struggles with even routine administrative shifts, making a revolutionary leap nearly unthinkable under current conditions.
“Executing a revolution is not something easy especially in military affairs where… we are very conservative and unfortunately in India even routine issues take years and decades to implement so bringing about a revolution is… a little out of our reach.”
To underline the point, Admiral Prakash highlighted India’s agonisingly sluggish pace of structural reform:
“To take ordinary decisions like reorganizing our 17 commands into theaters has taken 6 years after the government gave an express order directive to the newly minted Chief of Defence Staff… We need to go well back in 2001 when the group of ministers following the Kargil episode directed the constitution of the Strategic Forces Command and the Andaman Nicobar Command—those were the first baby steps towards jointness, but 25 years have passed.”
The root cause, according to the former Navy Chief, lies in a fundamental disconnect at the top of the decision-making pyramid.
“…These things need to originate at the political level… My feeling is that the political establishment is far too much involved in politics and not enough in national security.”
The rapid evolution of unmanned surface vessels (USVs) and loitering munitions in ongoing global conflicts has already altered naval and aerial warfare dynamics, a key point made by Gen Petraeus. Admiral Prakash highlighted how non-state actors and nations without conventional navies are inflicting asymmetric damage on major powers:
“If you look at Ukraine, the country doesn’t have a navy to speak of but they’ve decimated the Russian navy… sank their flagship the Moskva… The Russian Navy is clinging to the east coast of the Black Sea… If you look at Iran, their air force has been decimated by the Americans and the Israelis, and yet they’ve got the Americans on the run—they’ve rained missiles and drones on 14 US bases in West Asia. Tanks and infantry are rarely seen on the Ukrainian battlefield… all these are factors which lead to what we are calling a revolution.”
India stands on the verge of allocating tens of billions of dollars toward heavy capital platforms, including potentially a third aircraft carrier, conventional and nuclear submarines, and 114 Rafale fighters. Admiral Prakash questioned whether committing scarce capital to long-gestation legacy platforms makes sense when the global balance is shifting toward algorithmic warfare.
“We are on the cusp of spending a great deal of money on weapon platform acquisitions whether it’s an aircraft carrier, submarines, or fighter aircraft… Projects like AMCA are about 10 to 15 years from realization. Should we be spending money on these kinds of platforms, or should we switch now and put money into artificial intelligence, algorithmic warfare?”
Comparing India’s technological readiness with Western developments reveals a stark gap:
“The Maven Smart System project was kicked off by the US armed forces… 10 years ago… Today they have something called the Maven Smart System. We don’t even have a large language model. We don’t even have a search engine which we can call Indian.”
Given the time required to build true indigenous technological depth, Admiral Prakash offered a grim tactical assessment:
“If we are going to try to catch up with China, then we need a spell of peace. Therefore, our politicians, our statesmen, and our diplomats need to ensure that we have a 10 to 15-year period of peace… which will allow us the breathing spell to catch up.”
General Petraeus asserted that the human is no longer “in the loop,” but rather “on the loop”, supervising systems that execute targeting at machine speed. Admiral Prakash cautioned against removing human moral judgment from lethal kill chains, citing ethical failures already visible in contemporary combat:
“…Theoretically speaking, it’ll be a sad day if the human being is taken out of the loop because AI is already galloping… There has to be a human being in the loop to exercise ethical caution and precaution… No matter how advanced the systems get, military ethics demands that we keep a man in the loop so the final trigger or the firing button is pressed at the behest of a human being…”
A core theme of Admiral Prakash’s critique was India’s tendency to create national security catchphrases that obscure a lack of concrete capability on the ground.
“We have conclaves, samvads, and seminars… but really are issues of contention subjected to debate and thrown about?… We need to catch the bull by the horns and realize how far astern, how far back we have been left behind. Examples of things like integrated battle groups, Cold Start, preferred security partner, etc.—those all turned into slogans; nothing happened after they were mouthed.”
He singled out critical technology bottlenecks, such as the decades-long struggle to develop an indigenous jet engine:
“Issues like the Kaveri engine… unless we have an aero-engine, our aerospace industry, we can bid goodbye to it … and there again, it’s a lack of political will, lack of funding, lack of intervention at the right point.”
He warned that entering a conflict without addressing these core deficiencies risks severe consequences:
“I think we are chasing too many mirages and issues which are not really of substance. So we need to come down to earth, face the reality, smell the coffee of what’s going to happen tomorrow, and either we gird our loins and tackle the problems, put money where our mouths are… If we go into a conflict with our present organization of 17 commands scattered all over the country and our archaic system of doing things… I don’t see a very happy future.”
The most glaring contrast, according to both Gen Petraeus and Admiral Prakash, in military planning across the Line of Actual Control (LAC) lies in China’s disciplined, step-by-step execution. While Beijing formulates regular Defence White Papers and builds vast industrial capacity, India still lacks a published National Security Strategy.
“China is very clear-eyed and resolute about where it stands… They produce a defence white paper every two years… You can make out what a clear-eyed vision they have… We have even denied the need for a national security strategy. So if we don’t know where we are going, how will we get there at all?”
The disparity in industrial manufacturing capacity is equally striking:
“China’s shipbuilding capacity is about… 20 times that of the USA. They can churn out an aircraft carrier in two to three years, we took 16 years. They’re pushing out destroyers and frigates in matters of weeks and months…”
Admiral Prakash concluded with a call for self-examination, warning against taking refuge in economic headline numbers or grand political slogans:
“We’ve declared ourselves a Vishwaguru already, but technologically we are ages behind China… We repeat ad nauseam that we are the third largest or fourth largest economy in the world. I don’t think that matters, it is the per capita GDP that is going to matter… So I think we need to smell the coffee, keep in touch with reality, especially where national security is concerned.”
General David Petraeus’s vision of future warfare provides an important benchmark for modern militaries. However, Admiral Arun Prakash’s intervention serves as a necessary, sobering reality check. High-concept military theories cannot substitute for clear national security strategy, sustained R&D funding, political focus, and streamlined procurement. Until India moves past slogans and addresses these foundational gaps, adapting to the future of warfare will remain an uphill climb.

title: Former MN-S CEO sues for wrongful termination and breach of contract
body:
Métis Nation – Saskatchewan (MN-S) and former CEO Richard Quintal have entered a legal dispute over the former employee’s claims of wrongful termination and breach of contract.
Quintal filed his suit on his belief he was let go after an employment contract extension due to political pressures from the Provincial Métis Council (PMC). He alleges he did not receive the compensation he says he is owed.
“On or about April 23, 2026, and as a result of what appeared to be political pressure, the President verbally notified the Plaintiff that the Defendants were going in a different direction and that the Plaintiffs employment with the Defendants was going to be terminated without cause,” reads Quintal’s claim.
He claims after several extensions, he was contracted to work in his position until July 31, 2030, at the time of the termination notice. His claim states PMC confirmed he would be let go effective as of May 15, 2026.
Quintal says he was invited to give an exit speech to PMC and MN-S President Glen McCallum made a public statement and video announcing Quintal’s termination
“The Plaintiff (Quintal) received notice that an emergency meeting of the PMC would be happening on May 11, 2026. The meeting took the entire day, and the President notified the Plaintiff in the evening that a new resolution had been passed, which rescinded his termination without cause and placed him on Suspension,” states the claim.
Quintal says he thinks he was put on suspension to evade the cost of firing him. He says the contract stipulated after being fired without cause he would receive the remainder of the Annual Base Salary which would have been payable over the term of the Agreement.
On June 11, Quintal says he received a letter from MN-S stating that an investigation was going to be launched to review the extension of his contract. He says as of Aug, 24, the investigation was continuing.
Quintal is seeking severance payment in the amount he says he is contractually allocated as well as damages.
MN-S has responded to the court action with an intention to defend the allegations.

title: West works to besmirch Russia's partnership with Africa — TASS chief
body:
MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The West is working hard to sully the Russia-Africa partnership, TASS Director General Andrey Kondrashov said during a plenary discussion at the Russia-Africa media forum.
"Russia-Africa cooperation has become one of the main targets of information attacks by Western ill-wishers and their henchmen. Today, when Russia and African nations are working to build an equal partnership, any distortions are especially noticeable and come at a particularly high cost to both sides," he stressed.
Modern fake news is rarely based on crude fabrications, Kondrashov pointed out. Instead, it often relies on "seemingly harmless techniques," the distortion of motives and the use of reputable sources without providing evidence. As an example, he cited a deepfake video featuring Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova. Posted shortly before a Russian delegation’s visit to Kazakhstan, the fabricated video was intended to disrupt the visit but failed after the provocation was promptly exposed.
The TASS director general urged African journalists to pool their efforts to counter fake news. He noted that TASS and its partners had co-founded the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN).
"We brought together 130 experts from 55 countries. This is an effective tool that will allow you to detect fake news almost automatically from the start," Kondrashov said, adding that media outlets could join the organization free of charge and that they did not have to pay membership fees.
The Russia-Africa media forum is taking place in Moscow on October 26-29, bringing together leading Russian and African media outlets. Media leaders are discussing the role of the countries of the Global Majority in the international media landscape, exploring the prospects for the development of media resources as tools to combat disinformation, and assessing ways to "decolonize" media content.
TASS is an information partner of the forum.

title: Nasdaq-listed Canton Strategic Holdings plans tokenized stock trading from Nov. 2
body:
The tokenized shares would carry the same shareholder rights as traditional stock, with round-the-clock trading and immediate settlement under the SEC’s innovation exemption.
Canton Strategic Holdings, a Nasdaq-listed company formerly known as biotechnology firm Tharimmune, announced plans to tokenize its common shares on the Canton Network, with trading expected to begin as soon as Nov. 2.
According to a Thursday announcement, the company partnered with TSV LLC, a trading venue for tokenized securities, and Fairmint, a US Securities and Exchange Commission-registered transfer agent, to bring its shares onto the blockchain. The tokenized shares would carry the same shareholder rights as the company’s Nasdaq-listed stock.
The Nasdaq-traded issue, under the ticker CNTN, currently trade an average daily volume of 757,704 shares, according to Yahoo Finance data. At last look, the stock was up more than 4.5% on the day, trading at roughly $2.13 apiece, with a market cap of $170 million.
Tokenized share trading would be available around the clock through an automated market maker, with transactions settling immediately on the Canton Network. Fairmint would maintain ownership records and oversee compliance with share transfer requirements.
The announcement follows the SEC’s September innovation exemption , which the companies said provides a regulatory path for trading tokenized US stocks on domestic platforms.
Canton Strategic Holdings shifted its focus to digital assets in November 2025 after raising $545 million to build a business around Canton Coin. It changed its name in February and now holds the cryptocurrency, helps operate the Canton Network, and invests in projects built on the blockchain.
Despite its name, Canton Strategic Holdings is not the company behind the Canton Network, which was developed by Digital Asset . However, it has ties to the Canton Foundation through its investments and participation in network governance.

title: UK government urged to expand Israel sanctions to cover Gaza aid blockade
body: British MPs have called on the government to speed up and expand its new sanctions regime against Israel to include those blocking the entry of aid into Gaza. In a letter to Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband , 75 MPs and peers warned that more punitive measures were needed to address the worsening humanitarian crisis in Gaza, which is compounded by delays to the delivery of aid. The UK announced a new sanctions regime in September to target companies trading in illegal Israeli settlement goods and services in the occupied West Bank , as well as violent settlers. The designations are expected to take six months to come into force. But sanctions are also needed to target those blocking aid, including extremists groups, the letter drafted by Liberal Democrat MP Alistair Carmichael said. Labour MPs Rushanara Ali and Abtisam Mohamed , and Liberal Democrat Layla Moran are among the co-signatories. “Make the first designations before winter sets in. Treat cases relating to aid obstruction in Gaza as a priority for assessment, and announce the first designations within weeks rather than months,” the letter said. Israeli ministers and officials who “designed, promoted or enforced” measures that have restricted the entry of the UN's Palestinian agency (UNRWA) and other aid organisations into Gaza should also be sanctioned, the letter said. The signatories also called on the government to mirror EU sanctions against extremist groups that are blocking aid, using a new mechanism that allows for immediate sanctions to be imposed where they exist in other allied governments such as the EU or US. This includes the group Tzav 9, which has been sanctioned by the EU since July 2024 for blocking aid lorries entering Gaza. The politicians urged the government to announce additional aid funds for food, water and shelters for Gaza before winter, with efforts to “mobilise other donors”. The government's new sanctions regime has divided the ruling Labour party. Critics of Mr Miliband's punitive measures warned that they could compromise the UK's security and intelligence-sharing agreement with Israel, or that it could embolden the far-right in Israel. Others fear that the measures are not wide enough to prevent Israel's expansion of its illegal settlements in the West Bank. Sanctions on settlements Earleri this month, the UK introduced the Global Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law Sanctions Regulations 2026, an expansion of existing British sanctions regulation. On Tuesday, Mr Miliband said that these new regulations would allow the government to act more swiftly in designating individuals and organisations on human rights grounds. This includes companies bidding for Israel's controversial E1 settlement project for which applications close on November 19. Mr Miliband said the government would “do all we can to prevent the settlement building in E1 from happening” “We have brought the sanctions regime – not the sanctions regime that is coming in the next six months, but the extension of the GHR sanctions regime – precisely so that we can take swift action,” he said. But he declined to comment on which Israeli ministers or officials could be designated for facilitating the expansion of West Bank settlements. The letter asks the government to use the powers given by the new regulation to designate those involved in blocking aid into Gaza. “The powers now exist. We urge you to use them now, beginning with those responsible for denying and obstructing life saving aid to Palestinians in Gaza,” the letter said. International agencies have repeatedly warned about the lack of attention to the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. Last week, the World Food Programme announced that it had cut its aid deliveries to Gaza due to funding shortages. The number of people helped by the UN agency will drop from 1.6 million to 1.1 million, with meals provided community kitchens to be rationed from 250,000 to 150,000 a day. Unicef also warned that the Sheikh Radwan stormwater basin could be drained within two weeks, but that the Israeli authorities had not allowed the necessary equipment in to replenish it. This risks flooding areas with sewage contaminated water. Aid shortfalls Meanwhile, charities have warned that the UK will miss its aid spending target of 0.3 per cent of gross national income by 2027, after no adjustments to spending were made during the autumn budget announced on Wednesday. The Office of Budget Responsibility forecast on Wednesday that gross national income in 2027 had improved on previous projections. Yet money allocated to the UK aid budget will remain fixed from 2025. This would mean that a shortfall of £320 million below 0.3 per cent of gross national income, according to Bond, a network of British charities in the aid sector. The Labour government made cuts to the UK aid budget in 2025, but committed to spending 0.3 per cent of gross national income by 2027. The previous Conservative government had already reduced the UK's commitments from 0.7 per cent to 0.5 per cent in 2021. The policy changes made in 2025 mean that the original budget allocated then based on available projections would remain fixed even if the UK's economy grew in that time. “The UK aid cuts have already cost lives and forced lifesaving humanitarian, health and climate programmes to close. But failing to meet even the paltry target of 0.3 per cent means the government is failing people facing the worst impacts of conflict, crisis and extreme poverty worldwide,” said Gideon Rabinowitz, director of policy and advocacy at Bond. “The government must urgently fix this injustice, by meeting its 0.3 per cent commitment and setting out a road map for a gradual return to the 0.7 per cent target. The Treasury should also ensure savings made by other departments spending UK aid are returned to the [Foreign Office],” he said.

title: Ukraine and the Netherlands team up on missile defense as Europe plans its own missile killer, free of US approval
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine and the Netherlands are working together on a new missile defense project "Bliksem" may be an effort to develop a ballistic missile interceptor that can hit incoming missiles above the atmosphere It's a rare and valuable capability, and one Ukraine needs—but it won't come quickly or cheaply Ukraine and the Netherlands will collaborate on an air-defense project called "Bliksem," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced during his visit to the Netherlands on Wednesday, 28 October. Zelenskyy didn't offer a lot of details. But if the Bliksem initiative he referenced on Wednesday is the same Bliksem initiative that a consortium of European companies launched this summer , then Ukraine could be in line to acquire one of the world's most powerful missile interceptors. But not quickly. Nor cheaply. Explore further Ukraine fired its first FP-7 ballistic missile in combat. Its maker says next version will do what Ukraine needed since 2022 The pan-European Bliksem project aims to develop a so-called "exo-atmospheric" interceptor. That is, a missile that can fly higher than 100 km—above Earth's atmosphere—in order to hit the most dangerous ballistic missiles during their mid-course phase of flight, before they tip back into the atmosphere and streak down toward their targets. On Wednesday, Zelenskyy and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten met with the heads of Dutch and Ukrainian companies in the defense, energy, and software sectors, Zelenskyy said . "We defined key priorities and decisions that can strengthen our practical economic cooperation: defense production, joint technology and energy projects, industrial development, and, very importantly, satellite technologies and air defense," Zelenskyy said. "Our teams have been tasked with working out a specific air defense project, Bliksem," Zelenskyy continued. "We have already started this work." If the Dutch-Ukrainian Bliksem is the same as the wider European Bliksem, then it's an effort to develop a missile in the class of the American Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) and Standard Missile-3 (SM-3), as well as the US-Israeli Arrow 3. All three are exo-atmospheric. Cued by radars and satellites and boosted 100 km into the sky, they punch right through the hazy Kármán line that delineates the border between the atmosphere and space. Cold of space Chart: Euromaidan Press Up there in the cold vacuum, the interceptors can see clearly with sensitive infrared seekers—and distinguish incoming ballistic missiles from any decoys the missiles may deploy. Thrusters maneuver the interceptors to directly impact incoming missiles, destroying them with kinetic energy rather than explosive warheads. While Germany has a few Arrow 3s, most European powers lack exo-atmospheric interceptors. Their only option for shooting down the heaviest incoming ballistic missiles (such as Russia's intermediate-range Oreshnik) is to hit them in the final seconds of flight, when even a destroyed ballistic missile can cause damage by scattering supersonic debris. To plug that air defense gap, this summer five European companies— Destinus, MBDA, Safran, Airbus, and Thales —signed a letter of intent to form the Bliksem EXO consortium. The goal: to test the interceptor's kill vehicle in space in 2027. The companies signed in Paris at the first meeting of an anti-ballistic coalition that Ukraine launched with nine European countries, including the Netherlands, with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten present. They said the design would draw on Ukraine's experience against Russian missiles. The lead firm, Destinus, is Dutch. Given Zelenskyy's statement, it's possible Ukrainian firms will join the consortium itself. Explore further Ukraine’s answer to Russia’s jet Shaheds: a jet drone named Bars, built to strike Russia and now turned around to hunt them If the timeline holds and any technology Bliksem EXO develops actually works, the result could be a new interceptor rivaling the THAAD, SM-3, and Arrow 3—and one unbound by American export restrictions. Europe could arm itself for mid-course missile defense. Ukraine could, too, significantly stiffen its missile defenses that are in a state of collapse owing to a deepening shortage of American-made Patriot missile interceptors. Don't expect Bliksem to bear fruit quickly or cheaply. The THAAD, SM-3, and Arrow 3 interceptors each needed a decade or more to move through development to deployment. And leaving aside their multi-billion-dollar development costs, the missiles are expensive. A single THAAD interceptor costs $12 million. Even the Americans can't afford to stockpile more than a few hundred THAADs at a time. A Bliksem interceptor could eventually—and at great cost—lend Ukrainian forces a capability they currently lack: an active defense against a big ballistic missile like the Russian Oreshnik. Ukraine is also building its own anti-ballistic system, FREYJA, with European partners. Zelenskyy wrote on 21 October that officials had found ways to speed it up so it reaches testing by the end of this year. But neither project will solve a much more urgent problem: how to shoot down the dozens of smaller ballistic missiles Russia has been launching at Ukrainian cities every month. Ukraine got only 24 Patriot interceptors from the US in three months and needs about 350 a month, Zelenskyy told ABC News on 23 October. Meanwhile, Russia produces 55–60 Iskanders a month, according to Ukrainian military intelligence. To stop the ballistic barrage, Ukraine simply needs more Patriots—and soon.

title: Pentagon treating military base freezer malfunctions as suspected cyberattack, officials say
body: The Pentagon is treating the spate of mysterious freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the United States in August as a suspected hack, according to four officials familiar with the matter. One of the officials said the military investigators were in touch with their French counterparts about a similar cyberattack on commercial freezers that disrupted supermarkets there earlier this month. Reuters was not able to ascertain how far along the Pentagon’s investigation was or whether it had reached any conclusions about what happened or who might be responsible. When asked about the investigation, the Pentagon said that a unit of Cyber Command — the military’s cyber force — was “working in close coordination with interagency and law enforcement partners.” It did not elaborate. The US Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division said its Cyber Field Office was involved in the investigation and that it was working with French law enforcement to better understand “the refrigeration outages in Europe.” The late August malfunctions in the United States affected at least six commissaries — on-base stores where military personnel buy their food — according to a Reuters review of the military bases’ contemporaneous Facebook posts and website updates. In at least one of the cases, the freezers did not simply stop working; the cooling units’ temperatures were cranked up overnight, yielding mounds of wilted or melted food in the morning. The Fort Huachuca, Arizona, Facebook account explained on August 26 that its freezer “went into defrost mode where it heated up all the food. Trust us when we say it was ‘spoiled.'” The spate of rogue freezer behavior and the possibility of cybersabotage were first reported on August 28 by a recently created blog called Signal and Silence. The involvement of military investigators and their contacts with the French were reported by the newspaper Stars and Stripes and Britain’s Daily Telegraph, respectively. The news that the investigators were treating the incident as a suspected hack is being reported here for the first time. The French Embassy in Washington said it would have no comment. French freezers fried If confirmed to be a cyberattack, the refrigerator malfunctions would be another illustration of how vulnerable critical infrastructure — in this case cold storage — can be to hackers. The French freezer cyberattack overrode the temperature controls on commercial cooling units in more than 350 establishments, leading to dramatic scenes as supermarkets’ frozen food aisles were cleared of spoiled merchandise. The French hack involved cranking the temperature inside the units up rather than merely knocking them offline, similar to what happened in Fort Huachuca in Arizona. Some French refrigeration units had the temperature turned up so high they caught fire. The French attack’s total costs could add up to tens of millions of euros nationwide, one supermarket owner estimated earlier this month. The French cyberattack appeared to have ​been easy to pull off, experts previously told Reuters. The Danish firm Danfoss, whose controllers ran many of the stricken units, said that many of the devices were obsolete or were running outdated firmware, which could have made it easy for hackers to break in. Reuters could not establish whether Danfoss or any other brand of freezer controller were in use at the affected US bases. Danfoss did not return messages seeking comment. Chilling hacks Refrigeration plays a critical role in the distribution of fresh food and the sabotage of cold storage facilities over the internet has long been seen as a nightmare scenario, alongside the loss of electricity or water plants. Earlier this year, the Global Food Safety Initiative, an industry body, called on food safety professionals and IT leaders to work together to ensure “robust cybersecurity” for refrigeration technology, noting that “a hacked cooling system is just as dangerous as a broken one.” Hackers have previously sabotaged fridges and freezers both in the United States and elsewhere. Danfoss has said that, in 2022, hackers either targeted or broke into supermarkets in Russia and Israel that were using obsolete versions of its cold storage controllers. In December of last year, federal prosecutors in Los Angeles accused a Ukrainian woman of being part of a hacker group that knocked out the refrigeration at a meatpacking facility in 2024, ruining more than 2,000 pounds of meat. The root problem was that controllers that were initially conceived as isolated interfaces that would be serviced by an in-person technician were increasingly being connected to the internet, said Bill Moore, the chief executive of industrial cybersecurity firm Xona Systems. Concerns about online exposure were not unique to cooling systems, he said, but they could have particularly serious consequences there. “It can definitely disrupt the supply chain for food,” he said.

The Danish firm Danfoss, whose controllers ran many of the stricken units, said that many of the devices were obsolete or were running outdated firmware, which could have made it easy for hackers to break in. Reuters could not establish whether Danfoss or any other brand of freezer controller were in use at the affected US bases. Danfoss did not return messages seeking comment. Chilling hacks Refrigeration plays a critical role in the distribution of fresh food and the sabotage of cold storage facilities over the internet has long been seen as a nightmare scenario, alongside the loss of electricity or water plants. Earlier this year, the Global Food Safety Initiative, an industry body, called on food safety professionals and IT leaders to work together to ensure “robust cybersecurity” for refrigeration technology, noting that “a hacked cooling system is just as dangerous as a broken one.” Hackers have previously sabotaged fridges and freezers both in the United States and elsewhere. Danfoss has said that, in 2022, hackers either targeted or broke into supermarkets in Russia and Israel that were using obsolete versions of its cold storage controllers. In December of last year, federal prosecutors in Los Angeles accused a Ukrainian woman of being part of a hacker group that knocked out the refrigeration at a meatpacking facility in 2024, ruining more than 2,000 pounds of meat. The root problem was that controllers that were initially conceived as isolated interfaces that would be serviced by an in-person technician were increasingly being connected to the internet, said Bill Moore, the chief executive of industrial cybersecurity firm Xona Systems. Concerns about online exposure were not unique to cooling systems, he said, but they could have particularly serious consequences there. “It can definitely disrupt the supply chain for food,” he said.
